en: The Second Chapter.

[In this second chapter, titled "Non-contradiction" (Avirodha), in the first quarter (pāda), the removal of contradictions to the Vedānta harmony is accomplished through the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Kāraṇāda, and others, as well as by the arguments employed by the Sāṃkhya and other schools.
1. The Section on Smṛti. Sūtras 1–2.

In the first chapter, it was established that the Omniscient Lord of All is the cause of the origin of the world— just as clay, gold, and so forth are the causes of jars, golden ornaments, and the like—
and that He is the cause of its maintenance by virtue of being the ruler of the world once it has originated.
Like a magician with respect to his illusion,
it is the cause for the withdrawal of the extended universe back into its own self;
and like the earth with respect to the fourfold host of living beings.
And it has been established through the demonstration of the consistency (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts that this very [Self] alone is not the Self of all;
furthermore, the theories of the Pradhāna and other causes have been refuted on the grounds of their lack of scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*).
Now follows the removal of contradictions with Smṛti and reasoning (*nyāya*) regarding our own position.

The second chapter is commenced in order to demonstrate that the doctrines of Pradhāna and so forth are supported by fallacious reasoning, and that the processes of creation and so on are consistent across all Vedānta texts.
Therein, he first introduces and then refutes the objection regarding contradiction with Smṛti.
If it is argued that this entails the fault of leaving no room for other [authoritative] traditions (smṛti), we say no, because that would entail the fault of leaving no room for other traditions.
Regarding what was stated— that Brahman alone, being omniscient, is the cause of the world— that is incorrect.
Why? Because it would entail the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis.
"Smṛti" refers here to the tradition known as the Tantras composed by the Supreme Sage and accepted by the learned, as well as other Smṛtis that follow them;
if [your view were correct], these would be rendered without scope.
For in those [Smṛtis], the insentient *pradhāna* is propounded as the independent cause of the world.

As for the Smṛtis of Manu and others, they remain within their proper scope by providing the matters required by the collection of duties characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
for instance, [they state] that for this caste, at this time, the initiation (*upanayana*) is to be performed according to this rule.
Such is the conduct,
such is the study of the Vedas,
and such is the union with a partner in dharma.
Likewise, the Vedic texts enjoin various duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma) for the sake of human goals;
however, there is no scope for the Smṛtis of Kapila and others regarding such matters to be performed,
for they were composed solely with reference to right vision (samyagdarśana) as the means to liberation.
If there were no room for those [Smṛti texts] even in that case, it would follow that they are utterly purposeless.
Therefore, the Vedāntas must be interpreted in a manner that does not contradict them.

But how can the meaning of the Śruti, which has been determined through reasons such as "because it sees" (*īkṣati*) and so forth to be that Brahman alone—the omniscient cause of the world—is now challenged once again by the objection regarding the fault of leaving no room for Smṛti?
For those of independent intelligence, there is no need for the objection that [the Smṛtis] must be accepted as authoritative.

However, most people, being of dependent intelligence, are unable to ascertain the meaning of the Śruti on their own; they would therefore rely upon Smṛtis composed by renowned authors and, by means of them, seek to understand the meaning of the Śruti.
Furthermore, people might not place their trust in an exposition composed by us due to their great respect for the authors of the Smṛtis.
It is remembered that the knowledge of Kapila and others, who were seers (*ṛṣis*), was unimpeded;
and there is a Śruti text: "He who in the beginning supported with his knowledges the seer Kapila when he was born, and beheld him as he was being born" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.2).
Therefore, it is impossible to consider their doctrine to be non-conformable with reality. Furthermore, they establish their meaning by relying on mere reasoning;
for this reason as well, there is a renewed objection that the Vedāntas must be interpreted by the strength of memory (Smṛti).
His [the opponent's] concentration is not [valid], because it would entail the fault of leaving no room for other *smṛtis*.

If the doctrine of God as the cause were refuted on the grounds that it leaves no room for *smṛtis*, then likewise other *smṛtis* that maintain God as the cause would also be rendered without any room.

We shall cite those passages: having introduced the supreme Brahman with the words, "That which is subtle and unknowable," and having stated, "For He is the inner self of all beings and is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)," he says, "From that, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest (avyakta) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) was produced.
Likewise, elsewhere also, he says, "The unmanifest, O Brahmin, is completely dissolved into the qualityless Puruṣa."
And thus, in the Purāṇa: "Therefore, hear this summary: Nārāyaṇa, the ancient one, is all this; at the time of creation he creates everything, and at the time of dissolution he consumes it again.
And in the Bhagavadgītā: "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world" (BhG 7.6).
Furthermore, Āpastamba recites with reference to the Supreme Self itself: "From Him all bodies originate; He is the root, eternal, and everlasting" (Dharmasūtra 1.8.23.2).
Thus, in numerous instances, the Lord is revealed in the Smṛtis as both the efficient cause and the material cause.

Since I shall provide an answer by means of the authority of Smṛti for one who opposes me on the strength of Smṛti, this presentation of the fault regarding the lack of scope for other Smṛtis is made.
However, the purport of the Śrutis regarding the doctrine that God is the cause has already been demonstrated.

Furthermore, when there is a conflict among the Smṛtis, and it is necessary to either accept one or reject the other, those Smṛtis that follow the Śrutis are authoritative and independent, while the others are not.
As it is stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa*: "In case of contradiction, however, [the Smṛti] would be non-authoritative, for there exists [contradictory] inference" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.3).
Nor can it be conceived that anyone perceives objects beyond the senses without the aid of scripture, for there is no such cause [for such perception].
If it is argued that this is possible because perfected beings (siddhas) such as Kapila possess unimpeded knowledge, we say no; for even their perfection is dependent upon other factors.
For success depends upon the performance of dharma,
and that dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā).
Consequently, the meaning of an injunction established prior [to human existence] cannot be called into doubt on the basis of the words of a person whose own existence is established only later.

Even in the case of a hypothesis based on the authority of perfected beings (*siddha*), since there are many such perfected beings, when contradictions among their traditions (*smṛti*) arise in the manner already demonstrated, there exists no means of determination other than recourse to the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Furthermore, even for one whose intellect is dependent [on others], it is not appropriate to have an arbitrary partiality toward a specific tradition without cause;
for if such partiality were to occur in anyone toward anything, it would lead to the undesirable consequence that the truth could never be established due to the infinite variety of human opinions.
Therefore, even in his case, wisdom should be directed toward the true path by means of pointing out contradictions in his Smṛti and by discerning what does and does not fall within its scope.

As for the scriptural passage cited which demonstrates Kapila’s excellence in knowledge, one cannot place faith in the Sāṃkhya doctrine— even if it contradicts the Śruti— on the basis of that passage alone, because the term "Kāpila" is merely a commonality of name.

And because the recollection of another Kapila—namely Vāsudeva, the son of Sagara and the tormentor [of his enemies]—is [possible], and because a vision of something else that lacks attainment is not a means of proof;
furthermore, there exists another Vedic revelation proclaiming the greatness of Manu: "Whatever Manu said is indeed medicine" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.10.2).
And Manu says: "Beholding himself in all beings and all beings in himself, he who sacrifices to the Self indeed attains self-sovereignty."
(12.11) Thus, by praising the vision of the self-nature of all, it is understood that the doctrine of Kapila is being censured; for Kapila does not accept the vision of the self-nature of all,
because he maintains the distinction between individual selves.

And in the *Mahābhārata* as well, after deliberating on the question, "O Brahmin, are there many Puruṣas, or is there indeed only one?", and having set forth the opposing view— "O King, there are many Puruṣas according to those who investigate Sāṃkhya and Yoga"— it refutes that [view] with the following: "Just as a single womb is said to belong to many Puruṣas..."
In that same way, I shall describe that universal Person who is preeminent in qualities.
Having begun with these words: "My inner self, yours, and those of others who are situated within bodies—all these are witnessed by Him; He cannot be grasped by anyone, anywhere."
With the universe as his head, the universe as his arms, and the universe as his feet, eyes, and nose,
he moves alone among all beings, wandering at will according to his pleasure.
Thus, the state of being the self of all is definitively established.

And there is a scriptural text regarding this state of being the self of all: "When for the one who knows, all beings have become the Self alone, then what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that oneness? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7).
Such is the nature [of his system].

Therefore, it is established that Kapila’s treatise is contrary to the Vedas and contrary to the words of Manu who follows the Vedas, not only because of his conception of independent primordial matter (prakṛti), but also because of his conception of the plurality of selves (ātman).
For the Veda possesses independent authority regarding its own subject matter, just as the sun does with respect to visible forms.
The words of human beings, however, depend upon other sources and are mediated by the memory of the speaker; thus, there is a distance [between them and direct perception].
Therefore, it is not a defect that the Smṛti finds no scope when its subject matter contradicts the Veda. //1//

The summary verse (saṃgrahaśloka) states: "In the second [chapter], there is no contradiction with Smṛti and Tarka; the other [systems] are defective; and there is no contradiction with the Śruti concerning the past enjoyer, nor with the Śruti concerning the subtle body (liṅga). The Supreme Sage (paramarṣi) is Kapila.
Others [the doctrines] were composed by Āsuripañcaśikha and others;
the meaning is that they would understand the scriptural sense in a figurative (upacarita) manner.
"Subtlety" means being beyond the reach of the senses (atīndriyatva).
"Incomprehensibility" means being inaccessible to other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"The bodies" refers to Brahmā and the others. "Eternal" means immutable (*kūṭastha*).
In the event of conflict with Śruti, the authority of Smṛti is to be disregarded and rejected;
for it is only when there is no such conflict that the inference of Śruti occurs.
[This refers to] the burner of one who is being burned.
All [the deities] are its heads because it is reflected everywhere;
the same should be applied to the universal arms and so forth.
Furthermore, why would the consequence of leaving no room for traditional scripture (*smṛti*) be a fault? It is not a fault.
And because the others are not perceived (BBs 2.1.2):

those other things than the *pradhāna*—namely, the *mahat* and so forth—which are not conceived in the Smṛti as being transformations of the *pradhāna*, are not found either in the Veda or in the world.
As for the elements and the sense organs, they can indeed be remembered because they are well-known from both the world and the Veda.

However, because the great principle (*mahat*) and the others are well-known from non-Vedic sources, a Smṛti [text] regarding them is not tenable, just as there is no such Smṛti for the sixth sense-object.

As for the fact that in some places there appears to be a scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) directed toward them, that too has been explained as not being so intended in the commentary on *Brahma-sūtra* 1.4.1, which states, "And for some, it is based on inference" (*ānumānikam apy ekeṣām*).
The intention is that since the Smṛti concerning the effect is unauthoritative, it is logical that the Smṛti concerning the cause is also unauthoritative.

Therefore, even for this reason, the objection that it would result in the Smṛti being rendered untenable is not a valid fault; however, he will refute the reliance on reasoning starting from the sūtra "Because of the difference in nature" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.4). // 2 //
2. The Section on the Refutation of Yoga. Sūtra 3: "By this, Yoga is refuted.
By this refutation of the Smṛti of Sāṃkhya, it should be understood that the Smṛti of Yoga is likewise refuted; thus [the author] extends the argument by analogy.

Even there, in contradiction with the Veda, the Pradhāna is postulated as an independent cause, and effects such as the Mahat and so forth—which are established neither in common worldly experience nor in the Veda—are likewise postulated.
Now, if this is the case, since the same logic applies, this matter is already covered by the previous [section]; for what purpose is it being extended [to this point] again?
For there is here a further doubt:

yoga is indeed prescribed in the Veda as the means for attaining right vision, in such passages as, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5),
and "Holding the body straight and even" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8).
In the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, an elaborate exposition of the method of yoga is seen, preceded by the arrangement of the seat (*āsana*) and other requisites.

Furthermore, thousands of Vedic indicative marks (*liṅga*) concerning the subject of yoga are found, such as: "They consider that steady control of the senses to be yoga" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.18), and "This knowledge and the entire rule of yoga" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.18).
And such passages as these exist.
Furthermore, in the Yogaśāstra as well, it is accepted that "Yoga is the means for the vision of reality" (*atha tattvadarśanopāyo yogaḥ*), precisely as a means for right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

Therefore, because it shares a portion of its subject matter with what is already established [in the Vedas], the Yoga-smṛti, like the Aṣṭaka-smṛti and others, shall likewise not be subject to refutation.
This further doubt is also removed by extension [of the previous reasoning],
because we observe that even when there is agreement regarding one part of the subject matter, there may still be disagreement regarding another part of the subject matter, as previously stated.
Although there are many Smṛtis concerning the inner self (adhyātma), an effort has been made specifically to refute the Sāṃkhya and Yoga Smṛtis.
For Sāṃkhya and Yoga are renowned in the world as means for attaining the supreme human goal, are accepted by the learned, and are reinforced by inferential marks as well as by Vedic revelation.
"Having known that Cause, which is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one is released from all fetters" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13).
However, this is a refutation [of the view] that the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) is attained through the knowledge of Sāṃkhya independent of the Veda, or by the path of Yoga.

For the Śruti excludes any means to the supreme good other than the Vedic realization of the oneness of the Self, stating: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journeying" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).
For those Sāṃkhyas and Yogas are indeed dualists; they do not perceive the oneness of the Self.

As for the teaching stated, "That cause is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga," it should be understood that it is Vedic knowledge and meditation alone that are denoted by the words Sāṃkhya and Yoga there, due to their close proximity [to the Vedic path].
Insofar as they do not contradict [the Vedas], the Sāṃkhya and Yoga traditions are indeed accepted as having scope.

For example, the purity of the Puruṣa, well-known from such scriptural passages as "For this Puruṣa is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.16), is admitted by the Sāṃkhyas through their description of the Puruṣa as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).

And thus, even by the Yogas, through the instruction on renunciation and so forth— such as "Now the wandering mendicant, wearing discolored garments, shaven-headed, without possessions" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 5)— that very state of being established in cessation, which is well-known from the Śruti, is followed. By this, all [objections based on] reasoning and Smṛti texts are to be refuted.
If it is argued that those [means] also assist in the knowledge of reality through reasoning and logical proof, let them indeed assist;

however, the knowledge of reality arises from the Vedānta texts alone, as evidenced by: "One who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.7) and "I ask you about that Person who is known through the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
This is established by such scriptural passages as these.
[FN: That body in which the three—the chest, the neck, and the head—are elevated is called "three-elevated" (tryunnata).
Reasoning (tarka) is inference (anumāna), which is a means of knowledge to be supported.]
The distinction is that "origination" (*upapatti*) is the reasoning of favorability (*anugrāhikā yukti*). The section on "having different characteristics" (Sūtra 4.1.2):
"It is not so because of its having different characteristics; and its being such [as the world] is from scripture. (BBs 2.1.4)
The objection against the position that Brahman is both the efficient cause and the material cause of this world—based on the authority of Smṛti—has been refuted.
Now, the objection based on reasoning (tarka) is being refuted. But how can there be any room for an objection based on reasoning when the meaning of the scripture has already been determined?
But surely, just as with *dharma*, scripture ought to be independent regarding *brahman*.
This support would hold if this object were inaccessible to other means of knowledge and cognizable through scripture alone, like *dharma* which consists of things to be performed;
however, *brahman* is understood as having a fully established nature.
Furthermore, when a thing is already established, there is scope for other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), as in the case of earth and so forth;

and just as when there is mutual contradiction among scriptural statements (śruti), the others are interpreted in accordance with one, so too when there is contradiction with other means of valid cognition, the scripture should be interpreted in accordance with them alone.
Furthermore, reasoning (*yukti*), which establishes an unseen object through its similarity to what is seen, is closer to direct experience (*anubhava*);
whereas scripture (*śruti*) is more remote, as it denotes its own meaning merely through tradition (*aitihya*).
Moreover, the realization of Brahman—which culminates in direct experience—is held to be the means for liberation by way of removing ignorance, and is intended as having a visible fruit.

The Śruti as well, by enjoining reflection (*manana*) in addition to hearing (*śravaṇa*) in the statement "it is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon," shows that reasoning (*tarka*) must also be respected in this matter.
Therefore, a further objection based on reasoning is raised with the words, "Not so, because of its being of a different nature.
This refers to what was stated previously: that the conscious Brahman is the cause and the material source (*prakṛti*) of the world.
That is not tenable.
Why?
Because this transformation is of a different character from its primal nature.
For this world, which is intended to be the effect of Brahman, is observed to be different from Brahman—being insentient and impure;
whereas Brahman is heard in scripture to be different from the world—being sentient and pure.
Furthermore, a relationship of material cause and effect is never seen to exist between things that are so fundamentally different.
For modifications such as necklaces do not have clay as their material cause, nor do bowls and the like have gold as their material cause;
rather, modifications endowed with clay are produced from clay alone, and those endowed with gold from gold alone.

Likewise, this world, being insentient and endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion, must be the effect of a cause that is itself insentient and consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and not of something of a different nature.
Furthermore, this world must be understood as distinct from Brahman because it is observed to be impure and insentient.

Indeed, the world is impure because it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion; because it is the cause of joy, anguish, despondency, and so forth; and because it comprises the manifold diversity of high and low states such as heaven and hell.
Moreover, this world is insentient because it functions as an instrument for a sentient being by entering into the relationship of effect and cause with respect to that sentient being.
For when there is equality, the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary does not exist;
indeed, two lamps do not benefit one another.
[Objection: But surely even a conscious cause will benefit the enjoyer according to the analogy of a master and a servant. [Reply: No.
Even in the case of master and servant, it is only the unconscious portion that renders service to the conscious one.

For that part consisting of the conscious elements such as the intellect (*buddhi*) which constitutes the appropriation of one conscious being, is what benefits another conscious being; the conscious being itself does not benefit or harm another conscious being, for the Sāṃkhyas maintain that conscious beings are without distinctions and are non-agents.
Therefore, cause and effect are insentient;
furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whatsoever for the sentience of wood, clods of earth, and the like.
Moreover, this distinction between the sentient and the insentient is well-established in the world.
Therefore, because it is of a different character from Brahman, this world does not have Brahman as its material cause.

Furthermore, someone might argue: "Having heard that the world has a conscious being as its material cause, I shall understand the entire world to be conscious by the very force of that [scriptural statement];
for we observe the persistence of the nature of the material cause within its modification."
However, the non-manifestation of consciousness will result from a specific modification [of the material substrate].

Just as the consciousness of selves, though possessing manifest consciousness, is not manifested during states such as deep sleep or fainting, so too the consciousness of wood, clods of earth, and the like will not be manifested.

And precisely because of this distinction between manifestation and non-manifestation, as well as the presence or absence of form and other qualities, there will be no contradiction in the relationship of primary and subordinate between causes and effects and between selves, even though there is no difference in their sentience.

And just as, despite the lack of distinction in their earthiness, meat, soup, rice, and so forth, possess mutual utility due to the specificities inherent in each individual item, so too will it be here. For this very reason, the established distinction [between them] will not be contradicted; by that means, the difference characterized by sentience and insentience may also be somehow resolved.
However, the distinctness characterized by purity and impurity is certainly not being set aside;
nor can the other kind of distinctness be set aside either. Thus he says: "And its suchness [is known] from scripture.
For if this consciousness of all things were not understood in this way, one would merely speculate—relying solely on scripture—based on the hearing that everything has consciousness as its nature.
And that is contradicted by the scripture itself,
because from the scripture as well, suchness is understood;
by "suchness," he means its being distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti).

The scripture itself, by teaching the insentience of a certain portion in the passage, "Both the conscious and the unconscious" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), declares that the unconscious world is distinct from the conscious Brahman. (4) [FN:
*Avaṣṭambha* means an illustrative example.]
"By mere tradition" means by way of being beyond direct perception.
Pleasure, pain, and delusion are the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* respectively.
"Excellence" (*atiśaya*) is the connection with attributes that possess arising and passing away; its absence is "non-excellence" (*niratiśayatva*).
The other [aspect] consists of the nature of being conscious and unconscious.
But is it not the case that consciousness is also heard of in some instances regarding the elements and the senses, which are otherwise considered unconscious?
For example: "The earth spoke," "The waters spoke" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.1.3.2.4).
Thus, there are scriptural passages concerning the elements that attribute consciousness to them, such as: "That fire thought" and "Those waters thought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3, 4).
There are also passages concerning the sense organs, such as: "These vital breaths, disputing among themselves as to who was the best, went to Brahmā" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.7).
Thus, [the passage] beginning with "They said to Speech, 'Chant for us'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.2) concerns the sense organs. To this, he recites the following reply:
"But there is designation by means of the presiding [deities], on account of distinction and following after.
The word "but" (tu) dispels the doubt.
Indeed, one should not suspect that the elements and the senses possess consciousness on the basis of such scriptural passages as "The clay spoke."
Because this is a designation based on presiding deities (*abhimānin-vyapadeśa*).

It is the conscious deities who preside over clay and so forth, as well as those who preside over speech and so forth, that are designated in connection with activities such as speaking and conversing—which are appropriate for conscious beings—and not merely the elements or the sense organs.
Why?
[This is known] through specific distinction and through conformity.
For the specific distinction between the enjoyers and the elements and sense-faculties—characterized by the differentiation between the conscious and the unconscious—has been stated previously;
and this [distinction] would not be possible if everything were conscious.

Moreover, in the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), the Kauṣītakins qualify them with the word "deities" (*devatā*) in order to exclude the notion that they are mere instruments and to include an intelligent presiding agent, as in: "These deities, indeed, were disputing among themselves for the sake of superiority" (2.14), and "All these deities, having recognized the highest good in the vital breath... (2.14).
Furthermore, conscious deities who are present everywhere and possess self-conceit (*abhimānin*) are understood from the *mantras*, *arthavādas*, *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and so forth.
And such scriptural passages as, "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth" (*Ai. Ā. 2.4.2.4*), show that a deity who assists the instruments is present within them.

Furthermore, in the supplementary passage of the dialogue on the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), it is said: "Those vital breaths, having approached their father Prajāpati, said... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.7).
Here, they go to Prajāpati in order to determine which among them is the best;

and by his word, through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*)—that is, by the departure of each one in turn—they come to understand the preeminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Furthermore, the scriptural passage, "To him [is offered] the bali-oblation" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.13),

and others of a similar nature, which follow the same pattern of worldly usage as we and others employ, confirm that the designation refers to the presiding deity. Likewise, in the statement, "That fire thought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), it should be understood that this act of seeing is attributed to the Supreme Deity herself, who, as the presiding controller, is present within her own transformations.
Therefore, this world is indeed different in character from Brahman;
and because it is of a different character, it cannot have Brahman as its material cause—having been thus challenged, [the author] provides the following rebuttal. (5) [Note:
*saṃvadana* means dispute.]
The ellipsis is "they distinguish speech and the others as being superior to breath and the others.
For the sake of *ahaṃśreyas*, that is, for each one's own superiority;
*niḥśreyasa* means preeminence.
But it is indeed seen.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
As for what was stated—that this world does not have Brahman as its material cause because of their dissimilarity—[it is refuted as follows].
This is not an absolute rule;

for in the world, we observe the production of hair, nails, and so forth from things like human beings who are well-known as sentient, and the production of scorpions and the like from things like cow dung which are well-known as insentient.
[Objection: But surely the bodies of humans and the like, which are themselves insentient, are the causes of insentient things such as hair and nails;
and the bodies of scorpions and the like, which are themselves insentient, are the effects of insentient things such as cow dung. [Reply:
It is said in response: even so, there remains a distinction, for some insentient thing becomes the locus (*āyatana*) of consciousness, while other [insentient things] do not.

Furthermore, there is this great transformational distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*) between things such as a person and their hair or nails, due to the difference in their essential forms and so forth;
likewise between cow dung and a scorpion.
Moreover, if there were absolute similarity, the very relationship of material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) would vanish.

Now, it might be argued that there exists some nature such as "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) which persists from men and so forth in their hair and nails, or from cow-dung and so forth in scorpions and the like.
In that case, one could likewise observe a nature characterized by "existence" (*sattā*) belonging to Brahman persisting in ether and other effects.

Furthermore, regarding the objection that the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause because of their difference in character (*vilakṣaṇatva*), do you mean by this "difference in character" the non-persistence of the *entire* nature of Brahman, or the non-persistence of *any* [part] of it?
It should be stated that this refers to consciousness (*caitanya*).
In the first alternative, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total annihilation of all primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*);
for, in the absence of some excellence (*atiśaya*), there can be no such thing as a transformation of primordial matter.
In the second case, there is the fallacy of the unestablished (asiddhatva),
for it has been stated that the nature of Brahman, characterized as existence (sattālakṣaṇa), is observed to persist in space and other such things.
In the third case, however, there is an absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭāntābhāva).
For what instance, unconnected with consciousness, could be cited against the proponent of Brahman (the Brahmavādin) as being seen to have a non-Brahman nature?
This is because it is accepted that the entire aggregate of existing things has Brahman as its material cause.
Furthermore, contradiction with scripture is indeed well-known.
This is because it has been established that the purport of the scriptures is that conscious Brahman is both the cause and the material nature (*prakṛti*) of the world.
As for the argument that other means of knowledge might apply to Brahman because it is an already existing entity (*pariniṣpanna*),
that too is a mere fantasy.
For, because of the absence of form and other [sensory qualities], this object is not within the range of direct perception;

and because of the absence of logical marks and so forth, it is not within the range of inference and the other [means of knowledge]. Rather, this object is to be understood solely through scripture, just like *dharma*.
And thus says the Śruti: "This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning; it was declared by another alone for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.9).
"Who indeed knows, who here has truly proclaimed—from what this creation arose? (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.30.6).
Thus, these two verses demonstrate that the cause of the world is difficult to comprehend even for perfected beings who are lords.
There is also a Smṛti text: "Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable—one should not attempt to apply reasoning to them";
and also: "This is said to be unmanifest, inconceivable, and immutable" (Gītā 2.25).
"Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin;
for I am the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect" (Gītā 10.2)— and other passages of this kind.
As for the claim that the very Word (śabda), by enjoining reflection (manana) as distinct from hearing (śravaṇa), indicates that reasoning (tarka) must also be respected:
this pretext does not allow for the introduction of dry reasoning here.
For it is only reasoning supported by scripture (śruti) that is resorted to here as an auxiliary to direct experience (anubhava).

The non-attachment of the Self [to the world] follows from the mutual deviation between the states of dreaming and waking; its nature as the non-differentiated Reality beyond the phenomenal world (niṣprapañca-sadātmatva) follows from its merging into the Being (sat) through the abandonment of the phenomenal expansion (prapañca) during deep sleep;

and its non-distinction from Brahman follows from the fact that the phenomenal world originates from Brahman, according to the principle of the non-difference of cause and effect—such is the nature of this [teaching].
And by the sūtra, "Because reasoning is not firmly established" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.11), [the author] will demonstrate that mere reasoning is deceptive.
This applies even to one who, relying solely on the strength of scriptural statements regarding an intelligent cause, speculates that the entire world is conscious. For him as well—

Regarding the scriptural statement on the distinction between consciousness and non-consciousness— "consciousness and non-consciousness"— this can indeed be applied to sentience through the processes of manifestation and non-manifestation.
However, for the opponent [the Sāṃkhya], even this scriptural statement of distinction is not tenable.
How so?
For here it is proclaimed that the Supreme Cause exists as the very self of the entire world, according to the text: "It became both the conscious and the unconscious.
In this regard, just as the state of being unconscious is not possible for that which is conscious because of their contradictory natures, [so too is the reverse].
Thus, even for that which is insentient, the state of being sentient is not tenable.
Since the argument regarding the difference in characteristics has already been refuted, the cause must be accepted exactly as stated in the scripture. [Note:
"Pāriṇāmika" means consisting of the specific transformation found in things such as hair.]
This understanding, born from the Vedānta scriptures, is not to be set aside by mere reasoning—that is, by one's own speculative conjecture—nor is it subject to sublation;
or rather, the meaning is that it is not to be attained through reasoning alone.
Rather, when it is explained and awakened by another skillful teacher, it leads to right knowledge, that is, to direct realization.
"O most beloved, O dearest one"—this is Yama’s address to Naciketas.

"Whence has this emission—the creation of space and so forth—arisen? From what has it obtained its existence? Truly, who knows that in its essence? No one. Who has declared it? No one has been a declarer.
"Deceptiveness" means the failure to establish a specific nature for the object.
If it is argued that [the effect] is non-existent, we say no, because that would be a mere negation.

(BBs 2.1.7) If Brahman—which is conscious, pure, and devoid of sound and other qualities—were held to be the cause of an effect that is its opposite, namely unconscious, impure, and possessed of sound and other qualities, then the effect would necessarily be non-existent prior to its production.
If it is argued that this would follow as a consequence, and that this is undesirable for you who maintain the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*),
we reply: this is not a fault.
Because it is a mere negation;
for this is a mere negation, and there is no object to be negated by this negation.
Indeed, this negation cannot negate the existence of the effect prior to its production.
How so?
For just as this effect exists even now as having the nature of its cause, it is understood that it existed likewise prior to its production;
for even now, this effect does not exist independently, apart from the nature of its cause.
This is because of scriptural passages such as, "Everything abandons him who knows everything as other than the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).
However, the existence of the effect as the causal Self is indistinguishable [from that of the cause] prior to its production.
[Objection: Is it not the case that Brahman, being devoid of sound and other qualities, is the cause of the world? [Reply: Certainly.
But an effect characterized by sound and other qualities does not exist—either prior to its production or now—in a state devoid of its causal nature.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the effect is non-existent prior to its production;
we shall explain this in detail in the discussion on the non-difference between cause and effect. // 7 //
"In the case of dissolution, there would be the same contingency; therefore, it is inconsistent.

(BBs 2.1.8) Here [the opponent] says: If it were admitted that the effect—characterized by properties such as grossness, having parts, insentience, finitude, and impurity—has Brahman as its cause, then at the time of dissolution (*apīti*), i.e., during the cosmic reabsorption (*pralaya*), the effect, being merged back, would attain non-distinction from the cause.

One might object that the cause should be defiled by its own attribute; thus, since upon dissolution the cause—namely Brahman—would likewise incur defects such as impurity just like the effect, this Upaniṣadic doctrine that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world is inconsistent.

Furthermore, since all distinctions would reach a state of non-distinction, there would be no cause for regulation during subsequent production, and thus production could not occur with the distinction between enjoyers and objects of enjoyment; therefore, it is inconsistent.

Furthermore, if it is admitted that the enjoyers—who have attained non-difference from the supreme Brahman—undergo rebirth even when the causes such as karma have dissolved, then there follows the undesirable consequence of the rebirth of even those who are liberated; thus, [the doctrine] is inconsistent.
Alternatively, if this world were to remain distinct from the supreme Brahman even during dissolution, then in that case, dissolution itself would not be possible.
Furthermore, since an effect that is not distinct from its cause is impossible, this [position] is indeed inconsistent. // 8 //
To this it is replied:
"But not so, because of the existence of examples" (BBs 2.1.9). Indeed, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in our own philosophical system.
As for what was stated— that the effect, when merging into the cause, would defile the cause with its own properties— that is not a valid objection.
Why?
Because there is a lack of supporting examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For there do exist examples where an effect, upon returning to its cause, does not defile the cause with its own specific properties (*dharmas*).

For instance, transformations such as bowls and the like, which have clay as their material cause (*prakṛti*) and exist in various states—high, low, or intermediate—do not, when they return again to that material cause, defile it with their own properties.
They do not merge;

even the modifications of gold, such as bracelets and the like, do not merge with the gold by means of their own specific qualities upon dissolution. Likewise, the fourfold collection of beings, which is a modification of earth, does not merge with the earth by means of its own specific qualities upon dissolution.

But for your position, there is no illustrative example whatsoever. Indeed, even the process of merging (*apīti*) would be impossible if the effect were to persist in the cause by means of its own specific attributes.

Furthermore, even if the effect and the cause are non-different, we shall explain under *Brahma-sūtra* 2.1.14, "On account of the word 'originating material' and so forth," that it is the effect that possesses the nature of the cause, and not the cause that possesses the nature of the effect.
To say that "the cause would merge with its own nature even while in the state of being an effect" is an understatement;
for this same undesirable consequence applies equally to the state of persistence as well,
since you admit the non-difference between cause and effect.
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6);
"The Self alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2);
"This immortal Brahman alone is before [us]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).
For by such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1), it is taught without distinction that the effect is non-different from its cause at all three times.
In this regard, the resolution is that because the effect and its attributes are superimposed through ignorance (avidyā), the cause is not affected by them.
This [principle] remains the same even upon reabsorption.
Furthermore, there is this other illustration: just as a magician is not touched by the illusion he himself has projected throughout the three periods of time, because it lacks substantial reality.
In this way, the Supreme Self also is not touched by the illusion of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra-māyā),
just as a single dreamer is not touched by the illusion of seeing a dream, because he remains unaffected by the transition between waking and dreaming.
Thus, the one Witness of the three states is not touched by the three states, which are subject to change;
for this appearance of the Supreme Self in the form of the three states is merely *māyā*, like the appearance of a rope in the form of a snake and so forth.
Regarding this, it has been said by the Teachers who know the tradition of the meaning of the Vedānta: "When the individual soul (*jīva*), sleeping through beginningless *māyā*, is awakened..."
"When one awakens to that which is unborn, sleepless, dreamless, and non-dual" (Gauḍapāda Kārikā 1.16).
In this regard, what was stated—that upon dissolution, the cause would also incur defects such as grossness just like the effect—is incorrect.

Furthermore, as for the claim that, since all distinctions reach a state of non-distinction, no regulating cause can be established for their subsequent emergence through differentiation—this too is untenable.
This too is not a fault, precisely because there exists a supporting illustration.

For just as even in deep sleep, meditative absorption, and so forth, although a natural state of non-differentiation has been attained, differentiation occurs again upon awakening—just as before—because false knowledge has not been removed; so it is here as well.

And there is a scriptural passage on this point: "All these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know, 'We are merging into Being. Whatever they may be here—a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—becoming that, they become so again" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2, 3).

For just as even though the supreme Self is without division, the empirical usage of division— obstructed by false knowledge— is seen to persist unimpeded like a dream, so too, even after dissolution,
the power of division must be inferred as being likewise obstructed by false knowledge.
By this, the objection that there would be the consequence of the liberated souls being born again is answered.
Because false knowledge has been sublated by right knowledge,
that other alternative which was further imagined at the end— namely, that even after dissolution this world would remain distinct from the supreme Brahman—
is also refuted simply by the fact that it is not accepted.
Therefore, this Upaniṣadic view is consistent.
[9] (FN: *apigacchat* means merging;
the state of differentiation is the period of maintenance.)
The statement that they do not know while being unified in Brahman is an expression of ignorance.

The statement regarding their differentiation here—meaning that prior to waking from deep sleep they become divided by birth and so forth, and at the time of rising again they become exactly as they were—is intended to show that [the opponent's view] suffers from the same defects as its own position. (BBs 2.1.10)
Moreover, these faults common to the opponent would manifest within your own position as well.
How so? It is said:
first, as for what was asserted—that this world is not of the nature of Brahman because of its dissimilarity—[that argument fails].
This [objection] applies equally even to the theory that the Pradhāna is the material cause,

because it is admitted that the world, which possesses sound and other qualities, arises from the Pradhāna, which is devoid of sound and other such qualities. And for this very reason— namely, the admission that an effect of a different nature arises— the consequence of the doctrine of *asatkāryavāda* (the non-existence of the effect prior to its production) is equally applicable before the production [of the world].
Nevertheless, since it is admitted that the effect is merged into its cause, the same undesirable consequence applies here as well. Thus,

when all modifications in which every particularity has been obliterated have reached a state of non-distinction upon dissolution, those specific determinations belonging to each individual person— which existed prior to the dissolution, such that "this is the material cause for this person" and "that is the material cause for that person"— cannot be restricted in the same way during subsequent production, because their cause is absent.

If a restriction were accepted without any cause, then because of the equality of the absence of a cause, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even those who are liberated would be bound again. If it is argued that some particular differences attain non-distinction upon dissolution while others do not, then those which do not attain it would fail to be effects of the Pradhāna; thus, these defects, being common to both positions, should not be raised against either one, and this very fact confirms their lack of faultiness.
Because it must necessarily be relied upon. (10) [Note:
*prāduṣyuḥ* means "they would manifest.
If it is argued that, because reasoning is not firmly established, the object may be inferred otherwise, even so, there follows the consequence of no liberation. (BBs 2.1.11)
For this reason as well, one should not oppose a matter that is accessible through scripture by means of mere reasoning alone;
for in such a case, reasonings— which lack scriptural authority and are based solely on human imagination— are unstable,
because imagination is unrestrained.

For instance, logical arguments (tarka) that have been conceived with great effort by some experts are seen to be refuted by other, more expert individuals; and those very arguments, having been conceived by them, are in turn refuted by yet others. Thus, because of the diversity of human intellects, it is impossible to rely upon the stability of logical arguments.
Now, if it be argued that the reasoning accepted by someone of renowned majesty— be it Kapila or another— is established, even so, there is still no establishment [of truth],
because we observe mutual contradictions among those founders of systems (tīrthakaras) of renowned majesty who are approved [by others], such as Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, and the rest.
To this it may be said: otherwise we shall infer in such a way that the fault of instability will not occur;
for it cannot be said that reasoning itself does not exist as something established.
Indeed, even this instability of reasonings is established by means of reasoning alone.
Because some forms of reasoning are seen to be unstable, other reasonings of that same class are also unstable.
And if all reasoning were unstable, it would follow that worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) would be destroyed;
for the world is observed to act toward the future time—just as in the past and present times—in order to attain pleasure and avoid suffering.

Furthermore, when there is a conflict regarding the meaning of the scriptures, the determination of the correct meaning is accomplished precisely by means of reasoning (*tarka*) in the form of an investigation into the function of the sentences, through the refutation of fallacious meanings.
Manu also holds this view: "One who desires purity in dharma should thoroughly understand the triad of perception, inference, and the scripture consisting of various traditions."
Thus [it is said]:
"He who examines the instruction on Dharma given by the seers with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures— he, and no other, knows Dharma."
And speaking thus [in verses 12.105–106]:
"This very lack of foundation is indeed the ornament of reasoning;
for it is in this way that one must understand faultless reasoning by means of the relinquishing of [faulty] reasoning."
If it is argued that there is no proof whatsoever that one must be a fool simply because one's ancestors were fools,
and therefore the instability of reasoning (*tarkāpratiṣṭhāna*) is not a fault—
even so, the consequence remains that liberation is impossible.

Although in some matters the stability of reasoning (*tarka*) is observed, nevertheless, regarding this present subject, there inevitably follows the fault of instability, resulting in the impossibility of liberation through reasoning.
For this extremely profound reality of existence, which is the basis for liberation, cannot even be conceived without recourse to scripture (*āgama*).
Indeed, because it lacks form and other sensory qualities, this matter is not within the range of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, we have already stated that because there is an absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, there can be no inference or other such means of knowledge [regarding the Self].
Moreover, it is the accepted position of all proponents of liberation that liberation results from right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
And that right knowledge is of a single form, because it depends upon the reality of the object itself.
For that object which exists in a single form is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
In the world, knowledge having that as its object is called "correct knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*), such as [the cognition] "fire is hot.
This being the case regarding correct knowledge, it is untenable for there to be conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) among persons.

However, regarding the cognitions based on reasoning (*tarka*), disagreement is well known due to their mutual contradiction. For it is well known in the world that what one logician has established as "this alone is correct knowledge" is refuted by another; and what he has established is then refuted by yet another. Thus it is renowned in the world.
How could there be a correct cognition arising from reasoning that has as its object a single, non-abiding form?
Furthermore, the proponent of *pradhāna* is not the best among those who know reasoning, such that he would be accepted by all logicians and we could thereby accept his view as correct cognition.

Nor is it possible to assemble all past, future, and present logicians in one place and at one time, so that their consensus might constitute a correct cognition whose object is a single form and a single meaning.

Since the Veda is eternal and serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge, it is established that its subject matter is fixed; therefore, the validity of the knowledge produced by it cannot be denied by any logicians—past, future, or present.
Thus, it is proven that this very knowledge derived from the Upaniṣads is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).

Otherwise, since right knowledge would be impossible elsewhere, the consequence would be that liberation from saṃsāra could never occur. Therefore, by the authority of scripture and by reasoning that conforms to scripture, it is established that conscious Brahman is both the cause and the material source (prakṛti) of the world. [Note: "Reasoning" (tarka) here refers to that which is supported by scripture, as opposed to mere independent speculation.]
The purity of Dharma; the definitive distinction from non-Dharma; the state of being exceedingly profound; the state of being beyond the reach of scripture; the unfitness for the objects of desire;
the true nature of existence as residing in the cause, which is non-duality.
Liberation from bondage consists in the state of being exclusively one with existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidekatānatva).
Section on the Acceptance by the Learned (Śiṣṭaparigrahādhikaraṇa): Sūtra 12. By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained. (BBs 2.1.12)

Because it is closely related to the Vedic philosophy, because it is endowed with the force of more weighty reasoning, and because it has been accepted in some respects by certain learned persons who follow the Vedas, we have now refuted the objection based on reasoning that was raised against the Vedānta texts concerning the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause.

Now, fearing that some of dull intellect might again raise objections against the Vedānta texts by resorting to the doctrines of the Atomists (Aṇuvādins) and others, [the author] extends the previous argument by the maxim of "defeating the chief wrestler" (*pradhānamallanibarhaṇanyāya*). "Parigrahāḥ" means those who accept; "aparigrahāḥ" means those who do not accept; thus, they are the "non-acceptors" of the learned (*śiṣṭas*), such as Manu, Vyāsa, and others. By this very reason—the refutation of the doctrine of Primordial Matter (*Pradhāna*) as the cause—[the objection is rejected].

Those theories of atomic and other causes which are not embraced by any [scriptural authority] in any respect should also be understood as having been explained as refuted and rejected; for the reasons for their rejection are identical, and nothing further need be suspected here. Even in its mere similarity, the supreme profundity of the cause of the world consists in its being unfathomable by logic, the instability of logic, the lack of liberation even through otherwise-inferred reasoning, and contradiction with scripture—such are the characteristics of this kind.
Refutation. // 12 //
5. The Section on the Becoming the Enjoyer (Bhoktrāpatti-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 13:
"If it be argued that there would be no distinction because of the becoming of the enjoyer, [we reply] it would be as in the world.
Otherwise, however, the doctrine of Brahman as the cause is challenged by means of reasoning alone.

Although scripture (*śruti*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own domain, it must nevertheless become subordinate when its object is sublated by another means of knowledge,

as is the case with mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Likewise, even reasoning (*tarka*) would be unestablished outside of its own domain, such as in the case of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
What follows if this is so?
It follows that it is improper for the Veda to subvert an object established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
But how can an object established by another means of valid cognition be subverted by the Veda?

To this it is replied: For this distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is well-established in the world; the enjoyer is the conscious embodied self, and the objects of enjoyment are the sense-objects such as sound and so forth, just as Devadatta is the enjoyer and rice is the object of enjoyment.
And the non-existence of that distinction would follow if the enjoyer were to undergo the state of being the enjoyed.
Or else, the object of enjoyment would attain the state of the enjoyer;
for, since these two are non-different from Brahman, the supreme cause, it would follow that they undergo a mutual transformation of states.
And it is not proper to subvert this well-known distinction.
If someone should object: "Just as the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is observed in the present, so too must it be postulated for the past and the future.

Therefore, because this well-established distinction between enjoyer and enjoyed would otherwise result in non-existence, this determination that Brahman is the cause is untenable"—one should reply to him: "It may be so, as in the world.
This distinction is indeed possible even in our position, because it is observed to be so in the world.

For instance, although the foam, waves, ripples, and so forth—which are modifications of the ocean—are non-different from the ocean which consists of water, a worldly transaction characterized by their mutual distinction and mutual conjunction is nevertheless observed.
And yet, even though they are non-different from the ocean consisting of water, those modifications such as foam and waves do not become one with each other.
Nor, despite their not becoming one with each other, do they become different from the nature of the ocean.
In the same way here as well, there is neither a mutual transformation of the enjoyer and the enjoyed,
nor will there be any otherness from the supreme Brahman;
even though the enjoyer is not a modification of Brahman.

For it is heard that the very creator, remaining unmodified, enters into his own creation and becomes the enjoyer, as stated in the passage: "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

Nevertheless, for him who has entered into the effect, there exists a distinction caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as there is for space (*ākāśa*) due to limiting adjuncts such as jars and the like.

Therefore, even though there is non-difference from the Supreme Cause, Brahman, the distinction characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed is established through the analogy of the ocean and its waves; this has been stated. (13) [FN:
"Having another purpose" means having a figurative meaning.]
Differentiation is birth;
or rather, the refutation has already been stated by the word "even so" (tathāpi).
Section on the Origin [of the World], Sūtras 14–20.
"The non-difference from that [cause] is established on account of the words concerning 'origin' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth.
Having provisionally accepted this empirical distinction characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the rebuttal was stated as "it would be as in the world.
However, this distinction does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), because the non-difference of those two—the effect and the cause—is understood.
The effect is the world consisting of manifold diversity, such as space and so forth;
the cause is the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, it is understood that from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is non-difference from that cause, meaning the effect has no existence apart from it.

Why? Because of the words concerning "clinging" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. First, there is the word concerning "clinging": [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1] "For one who has not heard this, there is clinging to name-and-form. And so on. Here, "clinging" means attachment. This is because it is used in that sense elsewhere, as in: "He clings to the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6). Furthermore, the word "clinging" is used in the sense of material cause; for example, in the passage: "From clay, indeed, one knows all earthen things; the modification is only a name, arising from speech; the reality is simply 'clay'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.6). Therefore, since the word "clinging" is used here in the sense of material cause, it is established that the individual soul is non-different from Brahman. Furthermore, the word "origin" (samutthāna) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "From food, indeed, life-breath arises" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.9.1). Moreover, the word "modification" (vikāra) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "The modification is only a name, arising from speech; the reality is simply 'gold'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.6). Therefore, since the word "modification" is used here in the sense of material cause, it is established that the individual soul is non-different from Brahman. Furthermore, the word "transformation" (pariṇāma) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "By the transformation of water, indeed, the moon arises" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3). Furthermore, the word "manifestation" (vivarta) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "By the manifestation of ether, indeed, the wind arises" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1). Furthermore, the word "becoming" (bhava) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "From fire, indeed, smoke becomes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1). Furthermore, the word "arising" (udbhava) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "From the earth, indeed, herbs arise" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1). Furthermore, the word "production" (janman) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "From the Self, indeed, the vital breaths are produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Furthermore, the word "birth" (janman) is used in the sense of material cause, as in the passage: "From the Self, indeed, these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
