Having proposed that by means of the knowledge of one [thing] there is the knowledge of all, and in view of the need for an illustration, it is said: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the reality is simply 'clay'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1).

This is what is meant: when a single lump of clay is known in its ultimate sense as having the nature of clay, everything made of clay—such as jars, bowls, and water-pots—becomes known, because there is no difference in their being of the nature of clay.

For whatever modification there is, beginning with speech, is merely a name based on speech; it is commenced as "the pot," "the cup," or "the water-jar. But in reality, no such thing as a modification exists at all.

"For this is merely a name; it is unreal, while 'clay' alone is real"—this illustration of Brahman has been handed down in the scripture. From the word *vācārambhaṇa* heard therein, it is understood that even in the case of the subject of the illustration, the entire aggregate of effects does not exist apart from Brahman.

Furthermore, having stated that fire, water, and food are the effects of Brahman, the text declares that the effects of fire, water, and food do not exist apart from fire, water, and food, by means of the passage beginning:
"The fire-nature of fire has departed; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the three forms alone are real" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1).

From the phrase "from the word regarding the origin" (*ārambhaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ*), by the word "etc. (*ādi*), [the following passages are included]: "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; thou art That" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7);
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6);
and "Brahman alone is all this" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).

Furthermore, one should cite the collection of statements intended to establish the oneness of the Self, such as "All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2) and "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19).
And otherwise, the knowledge of all things could not be accomplished through the knowledge of one.
Therefore, just as the spaces within a jar, a water-pot, and so forth are non-different from the great space,

and just as the water of a mirage and the like are non-different from the saline desert and so forth— because their nature is seen and then lost, and because they cannot be defined by way of their own essential nature— [so too is the case here].
Thus, it should be understood that this entire manifold of objects of enjoyment, enjoyers, and so forth, does not exist apart from Brahman.
Now, an objection may be raised: Brahman is multiform;
just as a tree possesses many branches, so too Brahman is endowed with the activity of manifold powers (*śakti*).
Therefore, both unity and diversity are indeed real.
For example, "tree" represents unity while "branches" represent diversity;
and just as there is unity in the nature of the ocean, there is diversity in the nature of its foam, waves, and so forth.

Just as there is unity in the nature of clay and plurality in the forms of jars, bowls, and so forth, so too, through the aspect of unity, the practical application of liberation will be established by means of knowledge;
whereas through the aspect of plurality, the worldly and Vedic applications based on the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) will be established.
And thus, the examples of clay and so forth will be appropriate;
however, this would not be the case, because in the example, truthfulness is determined to belong to the material cause alone, as in the statement: "Only 'clay' is real."

Furthermore, because the phrase "a mere beginning in speech" (vācārambhaṇa) expresses the unreality of the entire collection of modifications, and because in the case of the illustrative example as well, the text—by stating "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth"—determines the reality of the single supreme cause alone, and because the text "That is the Self; thou art That, O Śvetaketu" teaches the identity of the embodied soul with Brahman.
For this identity of the body with Brahman is taught as something already self-evident, not as something to be accomplished through further effort.

Therefore, when this scriptural identity with Brahman is understood, it sublates the natural sense of being the embodied self, just as the cognition of a rope and so forth sublates the cognitions of a snake and so forth.

And when the identity of the embodied self [with Brahman] is sublated, all its natural worldly activity based upon that identity is likewise sublated; it is for the sake of establishing such activity that another aspect of difference from Brahman would have to be postulated.
Furthermore, Scripture shows this:
"But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
By such passages, [the text] declares the non-existence of the entire empirical transaction— characterized by action, agent, and result— for one who perceives Brahman as the Self.
Nor is it proper to say that this absence of empirical transaction is restricted to a particular state,
because the identity of Brahman and the Self expressed in "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) is not dependent on any particular state.

By means of the illustration of the thieves, [the text] shows that for one who intends falsehood there is bondage, while for one who intends truth there is liberation (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16), thereby demonstrating that unity alone is the single ultimate reality,

whereas plurality is a manifestation of false knowledge. For if both were real, how could a living being, even when engaged in the sphere of worldly transaction, be said to be "one who intends falsehood"?

And by refuting the perception of difference in the passage, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19), [the scripture] demonstrates this very point;
moreover, in such a view, it is not logically tenable that liberation results from knowledge.
For it is not admitted that any false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) removable by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is the cause of saṃsāra.
Indeed, if both [unity and diversity] were real, how could it be said that the cognition of diversity is removed by the cognition of unity?

[Objection: But if one-ness alone is admitted as absolute, then worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), would be contradicted because they would lack an object (*nirviṣayatvāt*), due to the non-existence of diversity.
Just as the cognitions of a person and so forth regarding a post and the like [are sublated when the truth is known],
so too the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions, because it depends upon duality, would be contradicted in the absence of that [duality]; likewise,
the scripture concerning liberation would also be contradicted in the absence of that, since it depends upon the distinction between the disciple, the teacher, and so forth.
And how can the reality of the oneness of the Self, as propounded by a scripture of liberation that is itself unreal, be established?
To this it is replied: this is not a fault, because all worldly transactions are indeed established as real prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self.
It is like the conventional behavior in a dream prior to awakening.

For as long as there is no realization of the true oneness of the Self, no one develops the cognition of unreality regarding the modifications characterized as means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and their results.

Indeed, abandoning its natural state of being the Self that is Brahman, every living being perceives only those very modifications through ignorance, with the sense of "I" and "mine" as belonging to itself.
Therefore, prior to the awakening to the Self as Brahman, all worldly and Vedic activity is entirely justified;

just as for an ordinary person who has fallen asleep and is seeing various high and low objects in a dream, there exists a cognition that is certainly regarded as direct perception until awakening, and at that time, there is no intention that it is a mere semblance of perception— so it is in this case.
But how can the realization of the true identity of Brahman as the Self be established by means of an untrue Vedāntic statement?
For one does not die from being bitten by a rope-snake,
nor is the purpose of drinking or bathing accomplished by the water of a mirage.
This is not a fault,
because effects such as death are observed to be caused by the poison of fear and the like,
and because effects such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water are observed for one in the state of dreaming.
If it should be argued that even its effects are unreal,

we reply: although the effects— such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water— experienced by one in the state of dreaming are unreal, nevertheless, the cognition of them is indeed a real result, because it remains unsublated even for one who has awakened.

Indeed, no one who has awakened from a dream, considering the effects seen in the dream—such as being bitten by a snake or bathing in water—to be false, would also consider the cognition of those effects to be false.
By this non-sublation of the cognition of the dreamer, it should be understood that the doctrine of the self being merely the body is refuted.
And so says the Śruti: "When, during rites performed for desired ends, one sees a woman in dreams..."
"In that dream-vision one should recognize prosperity" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.9);
thus, [the text] shows the attainment of true prosperity through an unreal dream-vision.
Likewise, when certain portents have appeared in direct perception, one should know: "He will not live much longer."

Having said this, [the text] shows that true death is indicated by various such dream-visions, which are themselves unreal, through such statements as: "Now, if one sees a black man with black teeth in a dream, he kills him.

And this is well known in the world among those skilled in the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that by such a dream-vision a good arrival is indicated, and by such [another], a bad arrival.
Likewise, the comprehension of the true letters such as *ka* and so forth is seen to arise from the comprehension of the false letters represented by lines.
Furthermore, this final means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishes the oneness of the Self; beyond this, nothing further remains to be desired.

For just as in the world, when it is said "one should sacrifice," there arises a desire to know what [is to be sacrificed], by what [means], and how, it is not so when it is said "That thou art" or "I am Brahman"—nothing else remains to be desired.
This is because the realization has as its object the unity of the Self of all things.
For when this [realization] exists, there would be an expectancy for some remaining object;
however, apart from the unity of the Self, there is no other remaining object that could be expected.
Nor can it be said that this comprehension is not possible,
because of such scriptural passages as, "He understood that from him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.16.3).
Furthermore, because there are injunctions for the means of realization— such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, as well as the study and recitation of the Vedas—
it cannot be said that this realization is purposeless or erroneous,
since it is observed to have the fruit of the cessation of ignorance.

Furthermore, because there is no subsequent sublating cognition, we have already stated that prior to the realization of the oneness of the Self, the entire worldly and Vedic practice involving truth and falsehood remains unimpeded.

Therefore, once the oneness of the Self has been established by the final means of valid knowledge, all previous conventional usage based on duality is sublated; consequently, there is no room for the postulation of a Brahman possessing a manifold nature.

Objection: Is it not understood from the presentation of examples such as clay that Brahman is intended by the scripture to be subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), for in the world, objects such as clay are known to be transformative? Reply: No, it is said.
"Verily, this great person is the Self—ageless, immortal, deathless, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25);
"This is that Self described as 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26);
"Neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
Because of these and other scriptural passages prohibiting all modification, Brahman is understood to be immutable (*kūṭastha*).
For it is impossible to maintain that the one Brahman possesses both the quality of undergoing transformation and being devoid of it.
If it is argued that this could be like the case of standing and moving, we say no.
Because of the qualification "of the immutable" (kūṭasthasya). For it is not possible for the immutable Brahman to be the substratum of multiple attributes such as staying and moving;
and we have already stated that Brahman is eternally immutable because all modifications are denied of it.

Furthermore, unlike the realization of the oneness of the Self with Brahman, which is indeed a means to liberation, the realization that [Brahman] undergoes transformation into the form of the world is not intended as an independent means for any result whatsoever,
because there is no authoritative evidence for such a claim.

For the scripture demonstrates that the fruit arises solely from the knowledge of the immutable Brahman-Self, beginning with "This Self is 'not this, not this'" and concluding, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).
Such is the nature of this [argument].

In this regard, the following is established: since the attainment of the fruit is accomplished simply through the vision of Brahman—which is devoid of all specific attributes—as taught in the context of Brahman, whatever is heard there that lacks a fruit of its own, such as Brahman’s transformation into the form of the world, is employed solely as a means for the vision of Brahman.
Just as it is said that "that which is fruitless in the proximity of something fruitful is a subordinate part [of it]," it cannot be imagined as being independent for the sake of a result.
For it is not logical to say that the result of the Self's possessing transformation would be its possessing transformation [itself].
If it is argued that because liberation is immutable and eternal,

and because for one who maintains the doctrine of the Self as the immutable Brahman there is the absolute oneness [of all things], there would be an absence of both a ruler and that which is to be ruled— thus contradicting the proposition that the Lord is the cause— [we reply: No,
for omniscience depends upon the manifestation of the seeds of name and form, which consist of ignorance.

From such scriptural passages as, "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), this meaning has been proposed: that the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of the world proceed from the Lord—who is omniscient and omnipotent, and whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free—rather than from the non-conscious Pradhāna or any other cause; as stated in the aphorism: "That from which the origin and so forth of this [world proceed]."
That proposition remains exactly as it was; no meaning contrary to it is stated here again.
How could it not be so stated, given that [the text] declares the absolute oneness and non-duality of the Self?
Listen to how it is not so stated: name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),

which are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*), which are as if constitutive of the omniscient Lord (*īśvara*), which are indefinable as being either identical to or different from reality, and which serve as the seed for the manifold world of transmigration (*saṃsāra-prapañca*)— these are designated in the Śruti and Smṛti as the "illusory power" (*māyā-śakti*) and the "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) of the omniscient Lord.

The Omniscient Lord is distinct from those two, according to the Śruti: "That which is called space is indeed the evolver of name and form; that within which these two are contained is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1);
and "I shall manifest name and form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), and "Having fashioned all forms and made names, the Wise One remains designating them" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).
And from such scriptural passages as, "He who makes the one seed manifold" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.12),
the Lord becomes subject to the limiting adjuncts of name and form created by ignorance.
Like the ether, it conforms to limiting adjuncts such as jars and water-pots.

And that [Supreme Self] grants the name "individual soul" (*jīva*)—referring to the cognitional selves (*vijñānātman*) who conform to the aggregate of effects and instruments (the body) produced by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) presented by ignorance—to those very selves that are its own nature, yet occupy the position of the ether within a jar, for the sake of empirical usage.
Thus, the Lord’s status as Lord, his omniscience, and his omnipotence depend entirely upon the delimitation caused by limiting adjuncts consisting of ignorance.

Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), conventional designations such as "ruler" and "the ruled," or "omniscience" and so forth, are not tenable with respect to the Self whose essential nature has discarded all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Thus it has been said: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (*bhūmā*)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1);
and, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
And by such passages as these, all the Vedāntas declare that in the state of ultimate reality (paramārtha), there is an absence of all conventional discourse (vyavahāra).
Likewise, in the Īśvaragītā it is said: "The Lord does not create the agency nor the actions of the world."
There is no connection between action and its fruit; rather, it is intrinsic nature that proceeds.
"The Lord does not take on the sin of anyone, nor indeed their merit;
knowledge is veiled by ignorance, and by that, living beings are deluded" (Gītā 5.14–15).
Thus, it is demonstrated that in the state of ultimate reality, there is an absence of the conventional distinctions between the ruler and the ruled, and so forth.

However, even in the Śruti, the conventional usage of terms such as "Lord" (*īśvara*) is stated in the context of worldly discourse: "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Sustainer, so that these worlds may not be confounded" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).
Likewise, it is said in the *Īśvaragītā*: "The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna."
"Causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine by means of Māyā" (Gītā 18.61).
The author of the Sūtras also states "their difference from that" with the intention of referring to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
However, with the intention of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), he says "it may be as in the world," thereby describing Brahman as being like the great ocean.

Without even rejecting the manifold of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) and resorting to the process of transformation (*pariṇāmaprakriyā*), [the author] relies on it because it will be useful for the meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*).

[Note: The connection is as follows: that which is "seen" means empirical; "perished" means impermanent; and since its own nature is "inexpressible" in that form—being devoid of existence and manifestation—it is "non-different.
Here, "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); that which is produced by it is "natural" (*svābhāvika*).
The absolute state of oneness is isolation (*kaivalya*). [If it were otherwise,] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be contradicted; truth consists in the absence of sublation (*bādhā*).
The sublation consists in the ascertainment of falsity.
It is well known that, due to the error of perceiving lines as the letter *a* and so forth, the real letters *a* and others are cognized.
And because [the object] is perceived when it exists. (BBs 2.1.15)
For this reason as well, the effect is non-different from the cause:
because the effect of a cause is perceived only when the cause exists, not when it is absent.
For example, a jar is perceived when clay exists, and a cloth when threads exist.

Furthermore, it is not observed that the perception of one thing necessarily occurs only when another thing is present; for a horse, though distinct from a cow, is not perceived only when the cow is present,
nor is a jar perceived only when the potter is present.
Even though there exists a relationship between cause and effect, [the two] are distinct.
Now, is it not observed that the perception of one thing is necessarily concomitant with the existence of another, as in the case of smoke when fire exists?
This is not so;
for even when the fire has been extinguished, smoke is still observed coming from things such as cowherds' huts.
Now, one might qualify the smoke by its particular state, saying that "such smoke does not exist in the absence of fire."

Even so, there is no fault whatsoever; for we state that the cause for the non-difference between cause and effect is the intellect (buddhi) being colored by the existence of that [cause]. And this [intellect] does not exist in the case of fire and smoke.
Or, the Sūtra may be read as: "And because it is perceived through its existence."
The meaning is that the non-difference between cause and effect is established not only from scripture, but also because of the existence of direct perception;
for there is indeed direct perception of the non-difference between cause and effect.

For example, in a cloth consisting of a configuration of threads, no effect called "cloth" is perceived apart from the threads; rather, only the threads themselves, possessing lengthwise and crosswise extensions, are perceived through direct perception.
Likewise, in the threads there are fibers, and in those fibers there are their own constituent parts.
From this direct perception of the three colors—red, white, and black—it is to be inferred that there are also [the elements of] mere air and mere space.
Beyond that is Brahman alone, without a second; regarding this, we have stated the finality of all means of valid knowledge. 15. @----------------------

Even in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," there is no absolute non-existence, because of the qualification in the supplementary statement, "It made itself by itself.

Therefore, this designation of the effect as "non-existent" prior to its origination is only with reference to a different attribute. For in the world, an object that has been differentiated by name and form is well known to be worthy of the designation "existent."
Therefore, prior to the differentiation of name and form, it is figuratively described as "it was non-existent" or "it was as if it were. [FN:

The prima facie view is that before [creation] the void existed, and from the void alone the world arose. In the final conclusion (rāddhānta), however, this world prior to creation—because its name and form were undifferentiated and thus equivalent to non-existence—was indeed Brahman itself, which is exceedingly subtle.]
"From that Brahman, the world—whose names and forms were yet to be manifested—was born.
This is known from reasoning and from another scriptural passage.
From reasoning, it is understood that prior to its origination, the effect exists and is non-different from its cause.
And because of other scriptural passages as well.
The reasoning is stated as follows: In the world, those seeking specific objects such as curd, a jar, or a golden ornament are seen to employ specific causes such as milk, clay, or gold.
For instance, those seeking curd do not employ clay, nor do those seeking a jar employ milk; this would not be possible under the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavāda).
For if everything were equally non-existent everywhere prior to its production, why is it that curd arises only from milk and not from clay, and a jar arises only from clay and not from milk?

If it is argued that, although prior non-existence is equal, there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to the curd in milk alone and not in clay, and some excellence belonging to the jar in clay alone and not in milk; [then we reply:]

In that case, because [the cause] possesses an excellence [not present before], the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is abandoned and the doctrine of the existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is established.

Furthermore, the power (*śakti*) of the cause, which is postulated for the purpose of restricting the effect, could not restrict the effect if it were either non-existent or something other [than the cause];
for there would be no distinction in its non-existence and no distinction in its being other.
Therefore, power is the very essence of the cause, and the effect is the very essence of that power.

Furthermore, because there is no cognition of difference—such as one has between a horse and a buffalo—between cause and effect, or between substance and its qualities and so forth, their identity must be accepted.

Even if one postulates inherence (*samavāya*), if a relation between inherence and the inherent entities is admitted, then another relation would have to be postulated for each of those, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And if this were not admitted, it would follow that there is a total severance [of relations].
Now, if inherence (samavāya) is related by itself— without depending on another relation— because its very nature is that of a relation,
then conjunction (saṃyoga) too, being itself of the nature of a relation, would likewise be related without depending on inherence.
Furthermore, because identity (*tādātmya*) is perceived between substance, quality, and so forth, the postulation of inherence (*samavāya*) is purposeless.
Moreover, how does the effect—the composite substance—subsist when residing in its causes, the constituent substances? Does it subsist in all the parts collectively, or in each part individually?
If, first of all, it were to reside in the whole [collection of parts], then the non-perception of the composite would follow,
because it is impossible to bring all the parts into contact simultaneously.
For multiplicity, when residing in a collection of substrates, is not perceived by the perception of individual substrates.

Furthermore, if it were to exist in its constituent parts within all [the parts], then one would have to postulate parts of the whole distinct from the originating parts, by means of which the whole could reside part-by-part within those originating parts; for a sword occupies the sheath by means of parts distinct from the parts of the sheath itself.
Moreover, such a consequence would lead to an infinite regress.
Because it would have to be postulated that other parts exist in order for [the whole] to reside in each of those various parts.
Furthermore, if it were to reside in each part individually, then while it was functioning in one place, it would not be functioning in another;
for Devadatta, while being present in Snuṣṇa on a certain day, cannot be present in Pāṭaliputra on that very same day.
If it were to exist simultaneously in many places, there would be the consequence of its being multiple, like Devadatta and Yajñadatta residing respectively in Srughna and Pāṭaliputra.
If it is argued that there is no fault because it is fully present in each individual instance, as in the case of "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, we say: no.
Likewise, because it does not exist dependently [in each part]:

if the whole were present in its entirety within each individual part, like "cowness" and so forth— for instance, just as cowness is perceived directly in relation to each individual cow, so too the whole would be perceived directly in relation to each individual part—
and yet it is not invariably perceived in this manner.

Furthermore, since the whole (avayavin) is involved in the function of each individual part, and because that whole is a single entity, it would follow that the horn could perform the function of the breast, and the chest could perform the function of the back;
yet this is not observed.
Moreover, if the effect were non-existent prior to its production, then production itself would be without an agent and devoid of essence.
Furthermore, origination is indeed an action,
and it must necessarily have an agent, just like the act of going and so forth.
It would be a contradiction to claim that something is an action and yet lacks an agent.
If the arising of a jar were said not to have the jar as its agent, then it would have to be postulated as having another agent.
Likewise, the arising of the potsherds and so forth, being stated, would also have to be postulated as having other agents.
And that being the case, when it is said "the jar arises," the state of arising would also be perceived for the potter and the others.
Furthermore, because [the state of] having arisen is perceived.
If it is argued that "arising" is simply the connection with the existence of its own cause, and that this is the acquisition of self-nature by the effect,
then it must be explained how that which has not yet acquired self-nature could be connected [to a cause].

For a relationship is possible between two existing things, not between an existent and a non-existent, nor between two non-existents. Furthermore, because non-existence is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), it is untenable to establish a temporal limit (*maryādā*) such as "prior to origination";
for in the world, limits are observed for existing things like fields and houses, but not for non-existence.

For it is not the case that "the son of a barren woman was king prior to the consecration of Pūrṇavarman" is qualified by such a delimitation— namely, "the indefinable son of a barren woman was, is, or will be king prior to the consecration of Pūrṇavarman"— by means of such a causal delimitation.

And if even the son of a barren woman were to exist after the operation of causal factors, then one might also assume that the absence of an effect would likewise exist after the operation of causal factors.

However, we observe that since there is no difference between the son of a barren woman and the absence of an effect in their commonality as non-existents, just as the son of a barren woman will certainly not exist after the operation of causal factors, so too the absence of an effect will not exist after the operation of causal factors.
But if this were the case, it would follow that the activity of the causal factors (*kāraka*) is purposeless.
For just as no one exerts effort to establish the nature of the cause because it is already established beforehand,
so too no one would exert effort to establish the nature of the effect, since it is already established beforehand and is non-different from the cause.
And yet, causal activity does occur.
Therefore, because the operation of the causal factors must be purposeful, we conclude that the effect is non-existent prior to its production.
This is not a fault;
for the operation of the causal agent is rendered purposeful by establishing the cause in the form of the effect.
Furthermore, it has been stated that even this form of the effect is indeed identical with the essence of the cause, because that which is not identical with it cannot be produced.
Nor does the mere perception of a difference entail a change in the substance of the thing;

for Devadatta, though seen with his hands and feet contracted and then with his hands and feet extended, does not undergo a change of substance, because he is recognized as being "that very same person."

Likewise, even though fathers and others assume many different forms day after day, there is no change in their underlying substance, because of the recognition that "this is my father," "this is my brother," or "this is my son.
If it is argued that such [recognition] is appropriate in that case because birth and death do not intervene, but not elsewhere, we say: no.
Since even milk and other substances possess a perceptible configuration in the form of curd and so forth,

the designation "birth" (janman) applies when even invisible things like banyan seeds— having been augmented by other parts of the same kind— come within the range of vision through their transformation into sprouts and the like. Conversely, the designation "cessation" (uccheda) applies when those very same parts, due to their diminution, come to be imperceptible.

In this regard, if it were the case that a non-existent thing attains existence because it is separated by the interruption of such a birth, then it would follow that there is a difference between one dwelling in the womb and one lying on his back;
likewise, it would follow that there is a difference between childhood, youth, and old age, and it would entail the collapse of social conventions such as those concerning fathers and sons.
By this, the doctrine of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda) should be refuted.
Furthermore, for one who holds that the effect is non-existent prior to its production, the operation of causal factors would be without an object;
for it is impossible for a non-entity to serve as an object, just as it is like employing various weapons such as swords for the purpose of striking at empty space.

If it is argued that the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) must have the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) as its object, we say no; for if the operation of the causal factors directed toward one object were to produce something else, it would lead to the absurdity of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that the effect is simply a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) within the inherent cause itself, we say no.
Because it would entail the consequence that the effect already exists [in the cause].

Therefore, substances such as milk themselves, persisting in the form of curds and so forth, receive the designation of "effect"; thus, an effect distinct from its cause cannot be established even in a hundred years.
Likewise, the primal cause itself, like an actor, assumes the status of the locus for all worldly transactions through various forms of effects, starting from the final effect.
Thus, through reasoning, the existence and non-difference from the cause of the effect prior to its production are understood.
This is also understood from another scriptural passage (śabdāntara).

Since in the preceding sūtra a word designating "non-existence" was cited, a word designating "existence" other than that is a "different word" (śabdāntara), such as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," and so forth.

Having introduced the position of non-existence with the words, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," and having refuted it with the words, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent?", the text concludes by determining, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). In this context, because the identity of the effect— denoted by the word "this"— with the cause— denoted by the word "existent"— is heard in scripture prior to its production, its existence and non-difference [from the cause] are established.
If, however, the effect were non-existent prior to its production and, being subsequently produced, were to inhere in a cause, then it would be something other than that cause;
in that case, the proposition "by which the unheard becomes heard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3) would be contradicted.
However, this proposition is established through the realization of the non-difference of the effect from the cause.
[Note: *Atiśaya* refers to a property of the effect or a property of the cause;

"the absence of the effect" means that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production]. The logical connection is that it would have been possible—that is, it would have been logically tenable—[if the effect were different from the cause].]
"Being another entity" means being distinct in the ultimate sense.
By this statement— that the cause persists through all its effects—
the example "like an actor" is given in order to clarify the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*).
And it is like a cloth (paṭavat).
Just as when a cloth is rolled up, it is not clearly perceived whether it is a cloth or some other substance;
yet that very same cloth, when unrolled, is perceived as manifest through the act of unrolling, [realizing] that the substance which was rolled up is indeed a cloth.

Just as at the time of being rolled up, although it is perceived as "cloth," its specific length and breadth are not perceived, yet at the time of being spread out, that very same [cloth] is perceived with its specific length and breadth— and this is not a different cloth distinct from the form in which it was rolled up—

so too, the effect such as cloth, which exists in the state of causes such as threads, being unmanifest, becomes manifest and clearly perceived through the operations of agents such as the shuttle, the loom, and the weaver.
Therefore, the meaning is that the effect is non-different from its cause, precisely according to the analogy of a cloth being rolled up and then spread out. // 19 // [FN:
Length is extension;
and as in the case of the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth. BBs_2,1.20 /

Just as in the world, when the various vital breaths such as prāṇa and apāna are restrained through breath control (prāṇāyāma), they persist in the form of their mere cause, and only the effect of mere life-sustenance is maintained, while other effects such as contraction and expansion do not occur;
yet, when those same vital breaths resume their activity, other effects such as contraction and expansion, in addition to mere life-sustenance, are also accomplished.

Nor is there any difference between the various modifications of the vital breath and the vital breath itself which possesses those modifications, because there is no distinction in their nature as air;
in this same way, the effect is non-different from its cause.

And therefore, because the entire world is an effect of Brahman and is non-different from it, this scriptural proposition is established: "By which, when heard, the unheard becomes heard; when thought, the unthought becomes thought; when known, the unknown becomes known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1).
7. The Section Concerning Designation as the Other (Itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 21–23:
"Because of the designation as the other, there follows the contingency of faults such as not doing what is beneficial" (BBs 2.1.21).
Furthermore, the doctrine of a conscious cause is challenged from another perspective.
For if the process of the world were based on volition (*cetanā*), defects such as the failure to act for the benefit [of others] would follow.
Why?
Because of the designation of the other.
The Śruti declares that the other, the embodied self, has Brahman as its Self, because of the awakening [in the passage]: "That is the Self; thou art That, O Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
Or alternatively:

Moreover, it designates the other Brahman as the embodied self (śārīrātman), for in the passage, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), it is shown that the unmodified Brahman, the creator itself, becomes the embodied self by entering into its own effects.
Likewise: "Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
Thus, the supreme deity, designating the living being by the word "self," shows that the embodied self is not different from Brahman.
Therefore, whatever is the creatorship of Brahman belongs to the embodied self alone.

Consequently, being an independent agent, it would only do what is beneficial and conducive to its own well-being, and not what is harmful—the manifold web of evils such as birth, death, old age, and disease.
For no one who is not dependent on another would build a prison for himself and enter it;
nor would anyone who is himself utterly pure ever accept an utterly impure body as his self.
Furthermore, whatever he has done that causes suffering, he would abandon by his own will.
And he should take up that which brings happiness, and remember: "By me this manifold reflection of the world has been fashioned.
For everyone, having clearly performed an action, remembers: "This was done by me."
Just as a magician effortlessly withdraws by his own will the illusion he himself has projected, so too the embodied soul (śārīra) should be able to withdraw this creation;
yet even his own body, the embodied soul is not able to withdraw without effort.
Thus, because no such beneficial action or similar motive is observed, it is understood that the process of the world is unjust. // 21 //
"But [Brahman is] superior because of the designation of difference.
The word "but" sets aside the previous position.
That Brahman, which is omniscient, omnipotent, and by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free, is superior to—that is, other than—the embodied soul.
We declare that he is the creator of the world;
in him, defects such as failing to act for the benefit [of others] do not apply,
for there is nothing beneficial for him to perform, nor anything harmful to avoid.
Because its nature is eternally liberated,
there is neither any obstruction to its knowledge nor any obstruction to its power anywhere, owing to its omniscience and omnipotence.
But the embodied self is not of such a nature; in its case, faults such as failing to act for the benefit [of others] would necessarily follow.
However, we do not say that it is the creator of the world. Why is this so?
Because there is a teaching of distinction:
"The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5);
and "That is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
Passages such as, "Then, my dear, he becomes united with the Existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1),

and "The embodied self is mounted by the conscious self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35), which indicate distinctions such as agent and object, demonstrate that Brahman is superior to the individual soul (jīva).
But surely, a teaching of non-difference has also been shown, such as "That thou art.
How can difference and non-difference, being contradictory, coexist?
This is not a fault.
For it has been established in various places that both [attributes] can coexist according to the analogy of space and the space within a jar;

moreover, when non-difference is realized through such an instruction of non-difference as "That thou art," then the transmigratory state of the individual soul (jīva) and the creatorship of Brahman vanish,
because the entire conventional usage of difference— which is a manifestation of false knowledge— is sublated by perfect knowledge.
In that case, how could there be creation, or how could there be defects such as the failure to act for the benefit [of others]?

For we have stated more than once that transmigratory existence—characterized by the failure to act for the benefit of others and so forth—is a delusion produced by the non-discrimination of the limiting adjuncts consisting of the aggregate of body and organs, which are themselves constructed from name-and-form presented by ignorance; it does not exist in an ultimate sense, just like the conceit regarding birth, death, cutting, breaking, and so on.

But when the conventional usage of difference is not sublated, the superiority of Brahman—as understood through such designations of difference as "He is to be sought after, He is to be desired to be known"—prevents the occurrence of defects such as the failure to act for the welfare [of beings]. // 22 //
And its impossibility is like that of stones and so forth.

Just as in the world, although stones are all equally possessed of the common property of "stoneness" (pṛthivītva), some are precious gems such as diamonds and lapis lazuli; others are of middling power, such as sun-crystals; and others are discarded stones fit only to be thrown away by dogs and crows—thus there are many varieties.
A variety is observed;

for instance, even among seeds that rely upon the same single earth, a manifold variety of leaves, flowers, fruits, fragrances, tastes, and so forth is perceived in such things as sandalwood and the *kiṃpāka* fruit.
And likewise, from the essence of a single food, various effects arise, such as blood and the like, or hair of the head and body and the like.

Thus, even for a single Brahman, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme knower (prājña), as well as the diversity of effects, is logically possible; therefore, there is no inconsistency in this.
The meaning is that the defects imagined by others do not apply.

Furthermore, this is a supporting argument based on the authority of scripture, the fact that modifications are merely "beginnings of speech" (vācārambhaṇamātra), and the analogy with the diversity of objects seen in a dream. 23.
FN: *Kiṃpāka* is the fruit of the great *tāla* tree. 8.

The Section on the Observation of Appropriation (*Upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇa*). Sūtras 24–25. "If it be said that [the attributes] are not [to be combined] because of the observation of appropriation, we say no; for it is like milk. (BBs 2.1.24)
That which was stated—that conscious Brahman alone, one without a second, is the cause of the world—is not tenable.
Why?
Because we observe the withdrawal [of the world into it].

For in this world, potters and others who are the makers of jars, cloths, and so forth, are seen to perform their respective effects only after having gathered various instruments such as clay, staffs, wheels, and threads;
yet Brahman, according to your view, is intended to be without assistance. In the absence of the gathering of other means, how could its status as a creator be logically established?
Therefore, if it is argued that Brahman is not the cause of the world—
This is not a fault,
because it is established through a specific nature of the substance, like milk.
For just as in the world milk or water transforms itself into the state of curds or ice without depending on external means, so too will it be in this case.

[Objection: But surely even milk and the like, when undergoing transformation into the state of curds and so forth, require external means such as heat; how then can it be said that "it is like milk"?
[Reply: This is not a fault.
For although milk itself undergoes a certain degree of mere transformation, it is only to that extent that it is prepared by heat and other factors for the state of becoming curds.
Furthermore, if it did not possess the inherent nature of becoming curd by itself, it would never attain the state of curd even through the force of heat and other conditions;
for neither wind nor space attains the state of curd through the force of heat and so forth.
And its perfection is brought about by the completeness of the causal complex (*sādhana-sāmagrī*).
But Brahman is of full power;
its fullness is not to be accomplished by anything else.
And there is a scriptural text: "Of it, no effect or cause is found; neither an equal nor a superior is seen."
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and it is innate.
(Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.2).
Therefore, even for the single Brahman, a manifold transformation is logically possible due to its connection with diverse powers, just as in the case of milk and other substances. // 24 // [FN:
The "conjunction" (upasaṃhāra) of causal factors refers to their integration.]
Milk is transformed into the state of curd by heat and other factors;
this is also seen in the world, as in the case of gods and others.
This might be so.

It is observed that non-conscious things such as milk undergo the state of becoming curds even without depending on external means; however, conscious agents such as potters are seen to engage in producing their respective effects only by depending on a collection of instruments. How, then, could the conscious Brahman proceed toward creation without any assistance?
We say: "Like the gods and others.

Just as in the world, beings such as the gods, ancestors, and seers—who possess great power and are conscious—without depending on any external means, by virtue of their particular sovereign power, produce through mere volition many things of various forms out of themselves alone.
Based on the authority of the mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, and purāṇas, we perceive those who fashion embodied beings such as palaces and vehicles like chariots;
furthermore, the spider creates threads from itself alone,
and the crane conceives a fetus even without semen.
Furthermore, a lotus plant proceeds from one lake to another without depending on any external means of transport;
likewise, the conscious Brahman will create the world by itself, without depending on any external instrument.
If he should say: "These examples of the lotus and so forth that have been cited for Brahman are not equal to the subject of the illustration (the dārṣṭāntika), Brahman."
For it is the body alone—insentient—that serves as the material cause for the production of the manifestation of another body and so forth in the case of gods and others, and not the conscious self.
Furthermore, in the case of the spider, saliva becomes solidified by the consumption of very small insects and thus becomes a thread;
and the crane conceives upon hearing the sound of thunder.
And the lotus-pond, though itself insentient, is set in motion by a conscious agent and thus functions toward approaching another lake as if it were sentient;
therefore, these are not [valid] examples for Brahman.
To him, one should say: this is not a fault.
This is because what is intended to be expressed is merely the distinction from the examples of the potter and others.

For just as potters and the like, though they share the same quality of being conscious with gods and other beings, depend upon external means when beginning their work while gods and others do not, so too Brahman, although conscious, will not depend upon external means; this is what we intend to express by citing the example of the gods and others.

Therefore, the intention is that there is no absolute certainty [in the matter], because just as the capacity of one is observed, so too must it be for all; thus, what is seen in one case does not necessarily apply to every case.
[Note: "Loka" is that by which an object is perceived or known—namely, the scriptures such as the Mantras and Arthavādas, as well as the usage of elders.
"Abhidhyāna" means volitional resolve.]
Just as in the *Mahābhārata*, a continuous succession of garments arose for Draupadī by the mere will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, so too does Brahman possess causality even though it is without assistance.
9. The Section on the Implication of Totality (Kṛtsnaprasaktyadhikaraṇa). Sūtras 26–29:
"There would follow the implication of total [dissolution], or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding partlessness. (BBs 2.1.26)

It has been established that Brahman—consciousness alone, without a second—is the cause of the world, transforming itself without depending on external means, like milk or like the gods and so forth. However, for the sake of purifying the meaning of the scripture, he raises an objection once more: "The consequence would be the transformation of the whole; it follows that the entire Brahman would undergo transformation into the form of the effect."
Because it is partless.
If Brahman were possessed of parts like the earth and other elements, then one part of it would have perished and another part would have remained.
However, Brahman is understood from the scriptures to be partless, as it is said: "Without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19).
"For the divine Person is indeed formless, both within and without, and unborn" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2);
"This great being is infinite, boundless, and a mass of consciousness alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12);
"He is this Self, described as 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
This is because of such passages as "neither coarse nor fine" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8), which negate all specific attributes.
Consequently, if the possibility of partial transformation were to lead to the contingency of total transformation, the very root [of the doctrine] would be destroyed.
Furthermore, the instruction that [Brahman] is to be seen would become purposeless, because the effect would be seen without effort;
moreover, since there is no Brahman distinct from that [effect], there would be a contradiction with scriptural passages concerning its being unborn and so forth.
Now, if—wishing to avoid this fault—one were to admit that Brahman indeed possesses parts, even then those scriptural passages cited which establish its partlessness would be contradicted.
"And if it possessed parts, the consequence would be that it is impermanent.
Thus he objects that this position cannot be established in any way whatsoever. (26) [FN:
*paryaṇaṃsyat* means "it would have undergone transformation."]
And one part would remain untransformed and undecayed;
however, because of the scriptural statement, [the conclusion follows] since it has the Word as its source.
The word "however" (*tu*) sets aside the objection.
Indeed, there is no fault whatsoever in our position.
To begin with, the consequence that the whole [would be produced] does not apply.
Why?
Because of scripture.

For just as the origin of the world from Brahman is heard in scripture, so too is the existence of Brahman apart from its modifications heard; for there is a designation of the distinction between the material cause and its modification, as in: "That divinity thought: 'Well, let me enter these three divinities with this living self and differentiate names and forms'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

Thus [it is said], and from such passages as: "Such is his greatness, and the Puruṣa is even greater than that; all beings constitute one quarter of him, while his three quarters are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
This is because of the statement that [Brahman] has the heart as its abode, and because of the statement regarding its union with Being (*sat-sampatti*).

Furthermore, if the entire Brahman were consumed by becoming the effect, then the qualification applied to one who has entered deep sleep— namely, "then, my dear, he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1)— would be untenable.
Because Brahman is eternally endowed with its unmodified nature, and because there is no such thing as a modified Brahman;
furthermore, because the range of the senses is denied of Brahman, whereas it is logically consistent for a modification to fall within the range of the senses.
Therefore, there exists an unmodified Brahman.
Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural statement regarding partlessness, for partlessness itself is indeed accepted precisely because it is heard [in scripture].

Furthermore, Brahman has the Word as its source and the Word as its means of valid cognition; it does not have the senses or other such means of cognition as its authority, and thus it must be accepted exactly as it is stated in the Word.
And the Word (Śabda) establishes both [contradictory attributes] of Brahman: its lack of partial manifestation and its partlessness.

Even among worldly things such as gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs, powers are observed whose effects consist of various contradictory actions due to the diversity of place, time, and causal conditions.

Even these cannot be understood through mere reasoning alone, without the aid of instruction, [in the form]: "This object has this many powers, with such assistance, directed toward such objects, and serving such purposes."
How much more so, then, could the nature of Brahman—which is itself inconceivable—not be defined except through words?
Thus say the authors of the Purāṇas: "One should not apply logical reasoning to those entities that are indeed inconceivable;
and that which is beyond the primary material causes (prakṛti) is the characteristic of the inconceivable."
Thus, the comprehension of the true nature of supersensuous objects is rooted solely in verbal testimony (*śabda*).

But [it may be objected]: even by means of verbal testimony, a contradictory matter cannot be made known—for instance, that Brahman, which is partless, undergoes transformation, yet it does not do so in its entirety.
If Brahman were indeed partless, it could not undergo transformation at all.
Or else, it would have to transform in its entirety;
or, if it were to transform in one form while remaining as it was in another, then by the postulation of such a differentiation of forms, it would necessarily follow that it possesses parts.

For regarding the subject of ritual action, there are injunctions of this kind: "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice" and "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice."
Even when a contradiction is perceived, resorting to an alternative (vikalpa) serves as the means for resolving that contradiction, because the performance [of ritual acts] depends upon the person.

However, in this case, even by resorting to an alternative, the resolution of the contradiction is not possible, because the reality of the thing does not depend upon the person. Therefore, this [position] is difficult to establish.
This is not a fault.
This is because we accept that the distinction of forms is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).
Indeed, a thing does not become possessed of parts merely by means of a distinction of forms imagined through ignorance.
For the moon, though appearing as if it were many to one whose eyes are afflicted by a cataract, does not thereby actually become many.

And through the differentiation of form characterized by name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which is imagined by ignorance (avidyā), consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, and being indefinable as either identical to or different from reality (tattva), Brahman becomes the locus for all worldly transactions such as transformation (pariṇāma) and the like;
yet, in its ultimate (pāramārthika) nature, it remains beyond all worldly transactions and without undergoing transformation.

Furthermore, because the differentiation of name and form imagined through ignorance is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), the partless nature of Brahman is not contradicted. Nor is this scriptural passage concerning transformation intended to establish actual transformation,
for no fruit is perceived in the realization of such a transformation.

This [scriptural teaching], however, is for the purpose of establishing the nature of the Self as Brahman, which is devoid of all empirical transactions, because one realizes that very [nature] through its reflection.
Having begun with, "This Self is 'not this, not this'," [the text] says: "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).
Therefore, in our position, there is no possibility of any fault whatsoever. // 27 //
And likewise in the Self, for they are indeed manifold.
Furthermore, one should not dispute here as to how a creation of many forms could occur within a single Brahman without the destruction of its own nature;
because even in the case of a single Self who is a dreamer, a creation of many forms is recorded as occurring without the destruction of its own nature: "Not..."

In this regard, [the scripture] states: "There are no chariots there, nor the yoking of chariots, nor roads; yet he creates chariots, the yoking of chariots, and roads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10), and so forth.
Even in the world, among gods and others, as well as among magicians and the like, various creations of elephants, horses, and so on are observed precisely without the destruction of the dream-form.
In the same way, even within a single Brahman, a creation of manifold forms will occur without any destruction of its own essential nature. // 28 //
And because of the defect in their own position:
this same defect in one's own position applies equally to others as well.

For even for the proponent of *pradhāna*, his own position is that *pradhāna*—which is partless, unlimited, and devoid of sound and other qualities—is the cause of an effect that possesses parts, is limited, and has sound and other qualities.

In that case as well, it follows that either the entire *pradhāna* would be involved [in the creation], because the *pradhāna* is partless, or else there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine of its partlessness.
Now, it might be argued that they do not indeed accept the *pradhāna* to be partless;

rather, the three qualities (*guṇas*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are eternal, and their state of equilibrium is the *pradhāna*. Thus, by virtue of those very qualities as its parts, the *pradhāna* is possessed of parts.
The fault under discussion cannot be avoided by means of such a [doctrine of] having parts;
for even among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, each one individually possesses the same partlessness (*niravayavatva*).

And since each one, when assisted by the other two, serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for its own class of manifold effects (*prapañca*), the consequence of the fault in our own position remains equal.
If it is argued that because reasoning lacks a firm foundation, [the world] must necessarily possess parts, then even so, the fault of impermanence and other defects would follow.
Alternatively, if the intention is that "parts" are merely powers (śakti) indicated by the diversity of effects, [then the following applies].
But those [opponents] who propound Brahman remain as well;

likewise, even for those who propound atoms, when one atom joins with another atom, if it were to join in its entirety because it lacks parts, then, since expansion would be impossible, there would be the undesirable consequence that it remains a mere atom.
If, on the other hand, it were to join by way of a single part, then the admission of its being partless would be contradicted. Thus, this same defect applies equally to their own position as well.

And because they are equal, it is not appropriate to propose [this objection] against only one of the two positions; thus, the fault in his own position has been refuted by the proponent of Brahman. (29) [Note:
For according to the Vaiśeṣikas, a single dyad is produced by the conjunction of two atoms.]
The process is as follows: one *tryaṇuka* (triad) is produced from those three *dyaṇukas* (dyads).
10. The section on "Endowed with All" (*sarvopetādhikaraṇa*). Sūtras 30–31:
"And [the Lord] is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen [in scripture]. (BBs 2.1.30)
It has been stated that the manifold expansion of transformations is possible for even a single Brahman due to its possession of diverse powers;
however, how is it understood that this is the Supreme Brahman?
To that, it is said:
And because of seeing that [divinity], it must be accepted that the supreme deity is endowed with all [qualities] and possessed of all powers. Why?
Because that is seen;

for scripture demonstrates the possession of all powers by the supreme deity: "He whose work is all, whose desire is all, who possesses all odors, who possesses all tastes, who has pervaded all this, who is without speech and without regard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4).
"He whose desire is truth and whose resolve is truth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1);
"He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9);
"By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9).
Such are the types [of statements]. (30) [Note:
*abhyāttaḥ* means completely pervaded;
*avākī* means devoid of the faculty of speech.]
Disregard means being free from desire.
If it is argued that [the Self] is not [the object of knowledge] because it is devoid of organs, that has already been answered.
It might be argued: "The scripture teaches that the supreme deity is devoid of organs, stating: 'It is without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
Such is the nature of this [objection].
How could that [Primal Nature], even though endowed with all powers, be capable of producing an effect?

For gods and others, though they are conscious and endowed with all powers, are known to be capable of their respective effects only when equipped with internal instruments of action (ādhyātmika-kārya-karaṇa).
If it be asked how the possession of all powers can be possible for a deity from whom all distinctions have been negated by the statement "not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26),
that which must be said on this point has already been stated previously.
This Brahman, being exceedingly profound, is to be fathomed through scripture alone and not through logic;
nor is there a rule that because the capacity of one thing is observed, another must necessarily possess that same capacity.

Furthermore, it has already been stated—by introducing the distinction of forms imagined through ignorance—that even for Brahman, from which all specific attributes have been negated, the possession of all powers is possible.
And so the scripture says: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19).
This demonstrates that Brahman, though devoid of organs, is endowed with all capacities. // 31 //
11. The Section on Having a Purpose. Sūtras 32–33:
"Not [so], because it has a purpose" (BBs 2.1.32).
Otherwise, the fact that the world has an intelligent creator is again called into question.
Indeed, the conscious Supreme Self cannot possibly fashion this reflection of the universe.
Why?
Because all activities are motivated by a purpose.

For in the world, a conscious person acting with prior intelligence, when engaging in activity, is never observed to undertake even a slight effort that does not serve his own purpose, much less one involving great exertion. And there is a scriptural text that echoes this worldly consensus: "Verily, it is not for the sake of all that everything is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that everything is dear" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
Thus, this activity—namely, the fashioning of the cosmic form of the world with its manifold variety—is exceedingly strenuous.
If this activity were postulated as serving some purpose for the conscious Supreme Self, then the scriptural teaching of the Supreme Self’s absolute contentment would be contradicted;
or, in the absence of a purpose, there would likewise be an absence of activity.
If it were argued that even though he is conscious, the Supreme Self might act like one who is insane— acting without regard for his own purpose due to a lapse of intellect—
then the omniscience of the Supreme Self as taught in scripture would be contradicted.
Therefore, creation from a conscious being is untenable.
Note: "Error of the intellect" means the absence of discrimination.
"But as in the world, it is mere sport" (BBs 2.1.33).
With the word "but," he refutes the objection.

Just as in the world, for someone whose desires have been fulfilled, there may occur activities in the form of mere play during sports and diversions, undertaken with no other purpose in view; and just as inhalation, exhalation, and so forth occur by their very nature without aiming at any external purpose,
so too the activity of the Lord will be in the form of mere play, occurring by His very nature without depending on any other purpose.
Indeed, no other purpose for the Lord can be established either through reason or through scripture;
nor can his inherent nature be questioned.
Although this construction of the world-image appears to us as involving a very great effort, it is nevertheless nothing but the mere sport (*līlā*) of the Supreme Lord.
Because its power is immeasurable.
Even if some subtle purpose could be imagined for even His divine play (*līlā*) in the world, nevertheless, no purpose whatsoever can be imagined here [in this case],
because of the scriptural statement that He has attained all desires.
Nor is there non-activity or activity like that of a madman, because of the scriptural testimony regarding creation and the scriptural testimony regarding omniscience.

Furthermore, one must not forget this: this scriptural teaching on creation does not have the ultimate reality (paramārtha) as its object, because it pertains to the sphere of conventional usage involving names and forms imagined through ignorance (avidyā), and because its primary purpose is to establish the identity of Brahman and the Self. // 33 // [FN:
"Distinct" means distinct from mere play.]
The distinction is that the scriptural account of creation does not imply a lack of agency [on the part of the Lord], nor does the scriptural account of His omniscience imply madness.
This concludes the section on partiality and cruelty (Sūtras 34–36).
"Inequality and cruelty [cannot be attributed to God] because He has regard [for karma]; for thus [the scripture] shows.

Furthermore, the status of God as the cause of the birth of the world and so forth is challenged once more, according to the maxim of "firmly planting a pillar," in order to strengthen the point already asserted:
that it is not logical for God to be the cause of the world.
Why?
Because it would entail the consequence of partiality and cruelty;
for [if he were the creator], he would make some, such as the gods and others, partakers of extreme happiness, [while making others suffer].

For one who fashions such a diverse creation— some, like animals and others, partaking of extreme suffering, and some, like humans and others, partaking of moderate enjoyment— the occurrence of passion and hatred would follow, just as it does for an ordinary person; consequently,
the destruction of the Lord’s essential nature, such as purity, as established by the Śruti and Smṛti, would result.

Likewise, even by base people, mercilessness and extreme cruelty would be censured; these would follow [if God were the cause] because of the infliction of suffering upon beings and the destruction of all creatures. Therefore, since it would entail the consequence of partiality and mercilessness, the Lord cannot be the cause. To this objection, we reply: partiality and mercilessness do not apply to the Lord.
Why?
Because [the Lord] is dependent.
For if the Lord were independent and created a diverse world by himself alone, these two faults—partiality and cruelty—would indeed follow;
however, there is no such thing as the independent creatorship of one who is not dependent.
For God creates this unequal world in dependence upon something.
If it is asked what He depends upon,
we reply that He depends upon merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Therefore, since the diverse creation depends upon the merit and demerit of the living beings being created, this is not the fault of the Lord;
rather, the Lord is to be regarded as like the rain-cloud.
For just as the rain-cloud is the common cause for the production of rice, barley, and other crops, [so too is the Lord].
However, regarding the diversity between rice, barley, and so forth, the causes are the specific, non-common potencies residing in their respective seeds;
likewise, God acts as the common cause in the creation of gods, humans, and others.

But regarding the diversity among gods, humans, and so forth, the causes are indeed the specific karmas residing in those respective individual souls. Thus, because He is dependent [on these factors], God is not tainted by partiality or cruelty.
But how is it understood that the Lord creates the low, middling, and superior cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) with dependence [on other factors]?

For the Śruti demonstrates this: "For He alone makes him perform good action whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; and He indeed makes him perform evil action whom He wishes to lead down" (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 3.8).
And [it is said]: "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13).

Smṛti as well shows that the Lord's quality of being a bestower of grace depends precisely upon the specific actions of living beings—for instance, in such passages as: "In whatever way they approach me, in that same way do I reward them" (Bhagavad Gītā 4.11). 34.
FN: An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is a commoner.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "He who desires to lift up—that is, to lead upward—a person, this Lord (*īśvara*) causes that person to perform good deeds.
If it is argued [that this is not so] because there is no distinction in karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness (*anāditva*). (BBs 2.1.35)
"O Somya, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
Since this establishes the state of non-differentiation prior to creation, there is no karma depending upon which a diverse creation could occur;
for karma depends on the differentiation of bodies and so forth, which exists only after the time of creation.
Furthermore, since the differentiation of bodies and so forth would depend upon karma, a mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) would result.

Therefore, let it be granted that after the initial separation, the Lord acts in dependence on karma; however, prior to that separation, since karma—which is the cause of diversity—does not exist, it follows that the first creation must be uniform. If this is argued:
This is not a fault, because saṃsāra is beginningless.
This fault would arise only if saṃsāra had a beginning.

However, in the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), the operation of karma and the diversity of creation proceeds through a causal relationship, like that between a seed and a sprout; thus, it is not contradictory. // 35 //
But how is it understood that this saṃsāra is beginningless? To this, he recites the following answer:
"It is both logically established and empirically observed. (BBs 2.1.36)
Furthermore, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is established;

for if saṃsāra had a beginning, it would follow that it arises spontaneously, which would entail the recurrence of saṃsāra even for those who are liberated, as well as the consequence of encountering the results of actions not performed.
Because the inequality of pleasure, pain, and so forth cannot be without a cause; and it has already been stated that Īśvara is not the cause of this inequality;
nor is ignorance alone the cause of inequality.
Because it is of a single uniform nature;
however, ignorance (*avidyā*), depending upon karma projected by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions such as passion (*rāga*), would produce inequality.
And yet, a body cannot come into being without karma.
Furthermore, since action is not possible without a body, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence;
however, if [the series] is beginningless, it is established by the analogy of the seed and the sprout, and thus no fault arises.
Moreover, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is perceived in both Śruti and Smṛti.

In the Śruti, first of all, in the passage "by this living self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2), at the beginning of creation, the embodied self is designated by the word *jīva* on the basis of its sustaining the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); this shows that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless.

For if it had a beginning, how could the self—which prior to that time had not yet acquired the vital breaths—be designated at the start of creation by the word *jīva*, which is based on the sustaining of the vital breaths?
Nor can it be said that [the past] will maintain [the connection],
because the past connection is stronger than the future one,
owing to its having already been established.
And the wording of the mantra, "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as before" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3), demonstrates the existence of previous kalpas.
Furthermore, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is found in the Smṛti: "Neither its form is perceived here in such a way, nor its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation" (Gītā 15.3).
And it is established in the Purāṇa that there is no limit to the conceptualization of past and future [kalpas]. // 36 //
13. The Section on the Arising of All Dharmas. Sūtra 37:
"And because all dharmas are possible.

Having determined that the meaning of the Veda is that conscious Brahman is the cause and the material source (prakṛti) of the world, the Teacher has refuted the defects such as "having different characteristics" (vilakṣaṇatva) and others put forward by opponents.
Now, intending to commence a treatise primarily concerned with the refutation of opposing views, he concludes the treatise primarily concerned with the acceptance of his own position:

Since all the attributes of a cause are logically consistent when this Brahman is accepted as the cause—in the manner already demonstrated—namely, that "Brahman is omniscient, omnipotent, and possessed of great illusory power (māyā)," therefore this Upaniṣadic philosophy is not to be doubted. // 37 //

Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka-Mīmāṃsā, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda. And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, there is no inference [of a creator]. (BS 2.2.1)

Although this treatise has been undertaken to determine the purport (*aidaṃparya*) of the Vedānta passages, and not— like a school of logic (*tarka-śāstra*)— to establish or refute some philosophical tenet through divine arguments, nevertheless,

the subsequent quarter (*pāda*) proceeds for the purpose that those who explain the Vedānta passages must also refute the Sāṃkhya and other systems which stand as adversaries to right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

Since the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta has the purpose of perfect realization (*samyagdarśana*), the establishment of one's own position was performed first through that determination; for that is more worthy than the refutation of the positions of others.

Now, it may be argued: "For those seeking liberation, it is proper to perform only the establishment of one's own position in order to define perfect realization as the means to liberation; what is the use of refuting the positions of others, which causes hatred toward others?
[The author replies: "Certainly so."
