Nevertheless, observing that the great systems such as Sāṃkhya and others—which are embraced by the masses and proceed under the pretext of teaching right vision—are being perceived [by some], there might arise in certain dull-witted persons the expectation that these too should be taught for the sake of right vision; and since there is the possibility of their being profound and logical, as well as being spoken by an omniscient one, faith in them may also arise. Therefore, an effort is made to demonstrate their lack of essence. Now, [it was argued] that "because of seeing, that which is not based on scripture [is not Brahman]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5).

Furthermore, the refutation of the Sāṃkhya and other positions was already established previously in the passages: "And because of [the nature of] desire, there is no need for inference" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.18), and "By this, all [other views] have been explained, they have been explained" (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.28).
But what is the point of further elaboration?
It is said in response: the Sāṃkhyas and others, in order to establish their own positions, even cite Vedānta passages and explain them by interpreting them solely in accordance with their own views;
that such an explanation of theirs is a mere semblance of an explanation (*vyākhyānābhāsa*) and not a correct explanation—this much has already been established previously.
However, the distinction here is that an independent refutation of that reasoning is being made, without reliance on scriptural statements.

In this regard, the Sāṃkhyas maintain: "Just as in the world various specific objects such as jars and bowls, when analyzed as being permeated by the nature of clay, are seen to be preceded by a commonality consisting of clay;

likewise, all external and internal specific objects, when analyzed as being permeated by the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, must necessarily be preceded by a commonality consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion."

That which is the universal characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion is the Pradhāna, consisting of the three guṇas; like clay, it is insentient, yet it evolves by its own diverse nature into the form of modifications in order to accomplish the purpose of the sentient Puruṣa.
Thus, one infers that very Pradhāna through such marks as transformation (pariṇāma) and the rest.

To this we reply: if this were to be determined solely by the force of analogies, then nothing insentient in the world is ever seen to independently fashion transformations capable of accomplishing specific human purposes without being presided over by a sentient being.

For in the world, houses, palaces, beds, seats, pleasure grounds, and so forth, are seen to be constructed by wise artisans at the appropriate time, designed to facilitate the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering.
Likewise, this entire world— both the external, such as the earth and so forth, which is fit for the enjoyment of the fruits of various karmas,

and the internal, such as the body and so forth, which is endowed with various species, possesses a specific arrangement of parts, and serves as the locus for experiencing the fruits of manifold karmas—
is seen to be something that cannot even be conceived by the mind of the most highly skilled craftsmen among the wise.
How could the insentient *pradhāna* fashion [the world]? For such a thing is not observed in the case of clods of earth, stones, and the like.

Furthermore, even in the case of clay and other materials, a specific arrangement is seen only when they are presided over by a potter or similar agent; likewise, it would follow that the *pradhāna* must also be presided over by another sentient being.

Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule that the root cause must be determined solely by relying on the properties of the material cause (upādāna), such as clay, and not by relying on external factors such as the potter;
for if this were so, nothing would be contradicted, and on the contrary, the Śruti would be supported by its presentation of an intelligent cause.
Therefore, for the reason that "the formation [of the world] is impossible," it cannot be inferred that the non-conscious is the cause of the world.
By the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and because of the impossibility of [positive] concomitance and so forth," he combines the lack of proof for the reason.
For indeed, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of external and internal diversities with the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is not tenable.
Furthermore, pleasure and the like are perceived as being internal,
whereas sound and the like are perceived as not having that nature; moreover, they are perceived as being the causes of those [pleasures and so forth].
Furthermore, even when there is no difference in sound and so forth, a distinction in pleasure and other experiences is perceived due to a distinction in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Likewise, having observed that limited particulars such as roots and sprouts are preceded by a combination [of causes], one who infers that external and internal particulars must also be preceded by a combination because they are limited, would face the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are themselves preceded by a combination.
Because of the specific quality of being limited [in size].

However, since the relationship of cause and effect is observed in the case of beds, seats, and so forth, which are produced with foresight and deliberation, it is not possible to postulate that external and internal diverse entities are preceded by something insentient on the basis of their causal relationship. // 1 //
FN: By means of a pretext—that is, by way of a disguise—and because of [the Buddha's] activity;
let this composition stand for now.

The activity directed toward the accomplishment of that [purushartha], which consists in the displacement from the state of equilibrium, the assumption of the relationship of subordinate and principal among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and the orientation toward specific effects— that too is not possible for the insentient *pradhāna* acting independently,
because it is not observed in the case of clay and the like, nor in the case of chariots and the like.

For clay and the like, or chariots and the like, being themselves insentient, are never seen to engage in activity directed toward a specific effect without being presided over by sentient agents such as potters or horses; and since the unobserved is established on the basis of what is observed, for this reason—that activity would otherwise be inexplicable—an insentient cause of the world must not be inferred.
[Objection: But even in the case of a sentient being, activity is never seen in isolation.
This is true;
nevertheless, it is observed that inanimate objects such as chariots and the like, when conjoined with a conscious agent, possess activity,
but it is never observed that a conscious being possesses activity when conjoined with an inanimate object.
What, then, is logical here? Is it that the stream belongs to that in which activity is observed, or that the stream belongs to that with which it is seen to be conjoined?
Surely it is logical that the stream belongs to that very thing in which the activity is observed, because both are perceptible.
However, the conscious being (*cetana*) is not perceived as such by itself, like a chariot or similar objects, merely by virtue of being the substratum of activity.

Rather, the existence of the conscious being is established only when it is conjoined with the body and so forth, which are the substrata of activity; for it is observed that the living body differs from purely insentient things like chariots.
For this very reason, the Materialists (*Lokāyatikas*) have concluded that consciousness belongs to the body alone, because it is seen when the body is present and not seen when it is absent.
Therefore, it follows that activity belongs only to that which is insentient.
To this, it is replied: we do not say that activity does not belong to that insentient thing in which activity is observed;
let it indeed belong to that very thing.
We say, however, that it arises from volition (*cetanā*), because it exists when that [volition] exists and it does not exist when that [volition] is absent.

Just as the transformation characterized by burning and illumination—though dependent on wood and other materials—is produced solely from the fire itself even when the fire is not perceived in isolation; so too is this case.

Because [the body] is seen when there is conjunction with that [consciousness] and not seen when there is disjunction from it, just like that [consciousness], even for the Lokāyatikas, the conscious body alone is observed to be the initiator of insentient things such as chariots; thus, the initiating power of the conscious being is not contradicted. If it is argued that this initiating power is untenable because, for you, even though the Self is conjoined with the body and so forth, activity is impossible apart from the mere nature of consciousness itself, we say: no.
For it is logically possible for that which is devoid of activity to be an instigator, just like a magnet or like visible forms and other objects.

Just as a magnet, though itself devoid of activity, becomes the instigator of iron, or just as objects such as visible forms, though themselves devoid of activity, become the instigators of the eye and other senses.
Thus, it is logically consistent that the Lord—even though devoid of activity—being omnipresent, the self of all, omniscient, and omnipotent, could set everything in motion.
If it is argued that because He is one, there is no object to be set in motion, and therefore His status as a mover is untenable;
we say no, for this has been answered more than once by the fact that He acts through the power of the influence of the illusion of name-and-form (nāmarūpa-māyā) presented by ignorance (avidyā).
Therefore, activity is possible when the cause is omniscient, but not when the cause is insentient. (2) [FN:
Of both the activity and its substratum. If it is argued that it is like milk or water, then in that case as well—BBs_2.2.3.
It might be argued as follows:
"Just as insentient milk proceeds by its very nature for the sake of the growth of the calf,

and just as insentient water flows by its very nature for the benefit of the world, so too will the insentient *pradhāna* proceed by its very nature for the accomplishment of the purpose of the *puruṣa*."
This is not well said;
for we infer that even in those cases, the activity of water and milk occurs only when presided over by a conscious being,
because activity is never observed in an insentient object alone, such as a chariot, which is admitted by both parties.

And the scripture— such as "He who dwells in the waters, yet is within the waters, and controls them" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.4), and "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9)— declares that the entire movement of the world is presided over by the Lord.
Therefore, because it is included within the category of the probandum (*sādhya-pakṣa*), the example "like milk and water" is not a valid instance;
for it is possible that the conscious cow causes the milk to flow through her desire for affection,
and because the milk is drawn forth by the sucking of the calf.
Nor is there absolute independence from water,
since flowing depends upon low ground and other such factors;
however, dependence upon a conscious agent has been demonstrated in all cases.

Regarding the sūtra, "If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the cause] because we see the need for external instruments, we say no, for it is like milk" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.24), it is shown from the perspective of worldly observation that an effect can arise residing within its own substrate even without depending on external instrumental causes.
However, from the perspective of the scripture, the fact that everything everywhere depends upon the Lord is never negated. // 3 //

FN: Because it is equal to the subject (*pakṣa*) in its possession of the probandum (*sādhyavat*), it is not presented [as a separate example] and is not a ground for investigation; and because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established, it is independent [of such an example]. (BBs 2.2.4)
For the Sāṃkhyas, the three *guṇas* abiding in a state of equilibrium constitute *pradhāna*.
There exists nothing external to it that stands as either an instigator or a restrainer of *pradhāna*.
Furthermore, the *puruṣa* is indifferent, being neither an instigator nor a restrainer; therefore, *pradhāna* is independent.
Furthermore, because [the Pradhāna] is independent, the claim that it sometimes transforms into the form of the Mahat and so forth, while at other times it does not transform, is illogical.
In the case of Īśvara, however, both activity and non-activity are not contradictory, owing to his omniscience, omnipotence, and possession of great illusory power (māyā). // 4 //
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the transformation] is not like that of grass and so forth.
It might be argued:

"Just as grass, twigs, water, and so on transform into the form of milk and the like by their very nature, independent of other causes, so too will the *pradhāna* transform into the form of the *mahat* and the rest."
And how is it understood that grass and so forth do not depend on any other cause? Because no other cause is perceived.
For if we were to perceive some other cause, then we could, at our will, produce milk by taking up that grass and so forth.
"But we do not establish that [conclusion].
Therefore, just as the transformation of grass and the like is inherent, so too would the transformation of the Pradhāna be inherent.
To this it is replied: The transformation of the Pradhāna would indeed be inherent, like that of grass and the like, if the transformation of grass and the like were admitted to be inherent.
It is not accepted [that it is the same], because another cause is perceived.
How is another cause perceived?
Because it does not occur elsewhere.
For grass and the like become milk only when consumed by a cow, and not when discarded or consumed by an ox or other animals.
If this transformation were without a specific cause, then grass and the like would turn into milk even when unrelated to the body of a cow.
Nor does it become causeless merely because it cannot be accomplished by humans according to their own will;
for some effects are to be accomplished by humans while others are to be accomplished by fate.
Humans, too, are indeed able to produce milk by employing appropriate means, such as gathering grass and other materials.
For those desiring abundant milk cause the cow to graze on abundant fodder, and from that they obtain abundant milk.
Therefore, the transformation of the Pradhāna is not natural (svābhāvika) in the same way as grass and such. // 5 //
FN: "Abandoned" means destroyed.
Even if it were admitted [to exist], it would lack functional efficacy (*arthābhāva*).
It has been established that the activity of *pradhāna* does not proceed by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikī*).
Moreover, even if, out of deference to your faith, we were to accept that the activity of the Pradhāna is indeed inherent, the fault would still persist.
Why?
Because of the absence of a purpose.

If it is asserted that the activity of the Pradhāna is inherent and does not depend on anything else here, then just as it does not depend on any auxiliary cause, it likewise will not depend on any purpose; consequently, the proposition that the Pradhāna acts in order to accomplish the goal of the Puruṣa would be abandoned.

If he should say that it requires only the auxiliary cause and not even a purpose, even so, the purpose of the primary cause's activity must be distinguished: would it be experience (*bhoga*), liberation (*apavarga*), or both? If it were experience, what kind of experience could there be for a *puruṣa* in whom no excellence (*atiśaya*) can be produced?
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of no liberation; for if liberation were already established even prior to activity, then activity would be purposeless.
Moreover, there would be the consequence that sound and other objects could not be perceived.

Even if one accepts that both [creation and dissolution] serve a purpose, since the primary constituents (*pradhāna*) to be experienced are infinite, there would still be the consequence of no liberation.
Nor is activity for the sake of the cessation of longing;
for longing is not possible for the *pradhāna*, which is insentient,
nor for the *puruṣa*, who is stainless and partless.

If it is argued that the activity [of primordial matter] proceeds out of fear that the power of vision and the power of creation would otherwise be rendered useless, then—just as the power of vision is never severed—the power of creation can never be severed either; consequently, because saṃsāra would never cease, the result would be the impossibility of liberation.

Therefore, the claim that the activity of the *pradhāna* is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is untenable. (6) [Note: "Because of the absence of purpose" means because it would follow that there is no purpose for the person.]
[This refers to] that which is devoid of any excellence consisting in the attainment of pleasure or the avoidance of pain.
"Mātrās" are enjoyments, so called because they are measured (*mīyante*) or experienced (*bhujyante*).
Even if it is argued that [the relationship between the Self and objects] is like that of a person and a stone, even so: (BBs 2.2.7)
It might be argued as follows:

just as a certain man who possesses the power of vision but lacks the power of action—a cripple—impels another man who possesses the power of action but lacks the power of vision—a blind man—by presiding over him;
or just as a magnet, though not moving by itself, impels iron.
Thus, the objection is raised again by means of an illustrative example, namely that the Puruṣa will set the Pradhāna in motion.
To this it is replied: even so, there is no escape from the fault;
for first of all, the fault of abandoning what has been accepted follows.
This is because it is accepted that the *pradhāna* acts independently, whereas it is not accepted that the *puruṣa* is an instigator; furthermore,
how could the *puruṣa*, being indifferent (*udāsīna*), set the *pradhāna* in motion?
For even a lame man impels a blind man by means of speech and other such means;
however, the Puruṣa possesses no such activity of impelling whatsoever,
because it is devoid of action.
Nor could it set [the mind] in motion by mere proximity, like a magnet;
for since its proximity would be eternal, there would follow the undesirable consequence that activity would also be eternal.
In the case of a magnet, however, its proximity—which is its own operation—is non-eternal.
Furthermore, since this [Self] requires such things as being wiped clean, the analogy of the "man and the stone" is not applicable.
Likewise, because the Pradhāna is insentient and the Puruṣa is indifferent (audāsīnya), and because there is no third entity to connect them, a connection between the two is logically untenable.
Moreover, if the connection were based on a capacity (yogyatā), then because that capacity would never cease, it would follow that liberation is impossible.
As in the previous case, here too the absence of an object [as a cause] is to be considered.
However, there is a distinction: the Supreme Self possesses neutrality based on its own essential nature (svarūpa), whereas its agency is based on Māyā. // 7 //
And because the status of being a principal [factor] is untenable (BBs 2.2.8). For this reason as well, the activity of the *pradhāna* is not admitted.

For that state of the *pradhāna* is its abiding in a state of equilibrium, consisting merely of its own nature, wherein the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* have abandoned their mutual relationship of subordinate and principal.
In that state, since their own natures are independent, it is impossible for them to stand in a relationship of mutual subservience (aṅgāṅgibhāva) for fear of the destruction of their own nature;
and since there is no external agitator, the production of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, which is caused by the inequality of the guṇas, would not occur. // 8 //

And in the case of an inference based on a different [nature], there would be a lack of the capacity for cognition. (BBs 2.2.9) Now, it might be argued: "We shall infer in such a way that this immediately preceding fault does not follow.
For we do not admit that the qualities (*guṇa*) are independent by nature or immutable (*kūṭastha*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a claim."
However, the nature of the *guṇas* is accepted according to their effects;
in whatever way the production of an effect is logically established, in that very way their nature is accepted.
Furthermore, there is the accepted principle that "the functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile."
Therefore, even in the state of equilibrium, the *guṇas* remain capable of undergoing transformation into a state of disequilibrium.
Even so, because the *pradhāna* is devoid of the power of cognition (*jña-śakti*), the previously mentioned defects—such as the impossibility of its creative arrangement—remain exactly as they were.
Furthermore, one who attempts to infer even the power of cognition [in the *pradhāna*] would cease being a true opponent [of our position].
Furthermore, [the Sāṃkhya position] entails the consequence of the doctrine of Brahman, because a single conscious principle (*cetana*) would be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the manifold world.
Moreover, even though the *guṇas* are capable of undergoing inequality, they would never attain inequality in their state of equilibrium due to the absence of a cause;

or, if they were to undergo inequality, they would always remain unequal because the absence of a cause remains constant—thus, this very same fault mentioned immediately above necessarily follows. // 9 //
And it is inconsistent because of contradiction;
for this doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas is mutually contradictory:
in some places they enumerate seven faculties, [while in others they enumerate eleven].
In some places there are eleven;
likewise, in some places they teach the creation of the subtle elements from the Great One (mahat), and in others from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Likewise, in some places they describe three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while in others they describe only one.
Thus, there is indeed a contradiction with the Śruti which teaches that the Lord is the cause, as well as with the Smṛti that follows it.
For this reason also, the Sāṃkhya system is inconsistent.

Here [the opponent] says: "Is it not the case that the view of the followers of the Upaniṣads is likewise inconsistent? For they do not admit a difference in nature between the sufferer and the causer of suffering. Indeed, for those who accept that Brahman alone—which is the self of all—is the cause of the entire phenomenal world, it must be admitted that the sufferer and the causer of suffering are merely specific states of that very same single Self, and not entities belonging to different natures."

Furthermore, if these two—the sufferer and the causer of suffering—were merely specific attributes of a single self, then that self would never be liberated from those two, the sufferer and the causer of suffering; consequently, the scripture which teaches right vision for the sake of pacifying suffering would be rendered useless.
For it is not possible for a lamp, whose nature consists of heat and light, to be liberated from those very qualities while remaining in that same state.

As for the analogy presented regarding water, waves, ripples, foam, and so forth, even there, since the single essence of water remains eternal through the manifestation and disappearance of particularities such as waves, it is the same: the essence of water is not released from its waves and other states.
Furthermore, this difference in nature between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is well known in the world.
For instance: both the seeker and the object are perceived as distinct from one another.

If the object were not inherently other than the seeker, then for whatever object a particular seeker has a desire, that object would be eternally established for him; consequently, he would have no desire for that object.
Just as for a lamp whose nature is light, the object called "illumination" is already eternally established; thus, it has no desire directed toward that object.
For desire belongs to one who seeks an object that has not yet been attained. Likewise, the object itself would likewise lack the status of being an object [of desire].
If it were so, it would have to be for one's own sake alone;
but this is not the case,
for these two words— *artha* and *artha*— are relative terms.
Furthermore, a relationship exists between two related parties, not with only one; therefore, these two— the object and the seeker of the object— are distinct,
as are the non-object and the seeker of the non-object.
For one who desires, the desired object is favorable and the undesired object is unfavorable; both are connected to him in turn.
In that case, because the desired object is minimal and the undesired object is predominant, both the desired and the undesired result in nothing but misfortune; thus, it is called the "tormentor.
The person, however, is the "tormented" one, who alone is connected to both in turn. If there were a single identity between these two—the tormented and the tormentor—liberation would be impossible.
But if there were a difference in nature between them, liberation might possibly occur through the avoidance of the cause of their conjunction.
To this it is replied: No;
because, precisely due to their oneness, the relationship of the sufferer and the causer of suffering is untenable.
This fault would indeed arise if, in a state of oneness, the sufferer and the inflictor were to enter into a relationship of object and subject with one another;
but this is not the case precisely because of their unity.
For fire, being one, does not burn or illuminate itself, even though there exists a difference in its attributes such as heat and light, and even though it is subject to transformation.
How could the relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering possibly exist within the one, immutable Brahman?
Where, then, might this relationship of sufferer and causer of suffering reside?
It is replied: Do you not see that the living body, which is the locus of action, is the sufferer, and the sun is the causer of suffering?
Now, "torment" (tāpa) is indeed suffering, and that belongs to the conscious being, not to the insentient body.
For if torment belonged to the body alone, it would perish of its own accord upon the destruction of the body; thus, no means for its destruction would need to be sought.
It is replied: even in the absence of the body, torment of the pure conscious being alone has never been observed.
Nor is it accepted by you that the modification called "fever" belongs to the pure conscious self alone;
nor is there a combination of the body and consciousness, because that would entail defects such as impurity;
nor do you admit that fever itself possesses fever.
If it is argued that even for you [the Sāṃkhya], there exists the relationship of the afflicted and the afflictor, such that *sattva* is the afflicted and *rajas* is the afflictor—this is not so;
for it is impossible for the conscious principle (*cetana*) to be conjoined with those two.
If it is further argued that the conscious principle also appears as if afflicted because it conforms to *sattva*, [we reply:]...
In that case, it follows from the use of the word "as if" (*iva*) that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), there is no suffering at all.
If it does not suffer, the word "as if" is not a fault;
for a *ḍuṇḍubha* [a type of non-venomous snake] does not become venomous merely by the statement, "It is like a serpent."

Just as a snake or a *ḍuṇḍubha* becomes non-venomous by that much, so too this relationship between the sufferer and the causer of suffering is produced by ignorance and is not ultimate; this must be accepted. This being so, nothing is impaired for me either.
Now, if you admit that the capacity to suffer belongs to the conscious self (*cetana*) in an ultimate sense, then for you, liberation would be even more impossible;
this is because you also admit the eternity of the suffering agent (*tāpaka*).

Even if the powers of being the sufferer and the sufferer were eternal, since they would necessarily depend on a conjunction with a cause, when the non-perception (*adarśana*)—which is the cause of that conjunction—is removed, there would be an absolute cessation of the conjunction.
If it is argued that, consequently, absolute liberation is thereby established, we say no;

for you admit that the darkness of non-perception is eternal, and because the emergence and suppression of the *guṇas* are not fixed, the cessation of the cause of conjunction is likewise not fixed. Since disjunction is therefore also not fixed, the Sāṃkhya would find himself unable to avoid the unavoidable consequence of the absence of liberation.

However, for one who accepts the monistic doctrine of the Self according to the Upaniṣads, since it is impossible for a single entity to stand in the relation of subject and object, and because scripture declares that the distinction between modifications is a mere matter of words (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), no suspicion of non-liberation arises even in a dream. But as for empirical practice, in whatever manner the relationship between the sufferer and the cause of suffering is observed in a given case, it remains exactly so there; thus, it neither needs to be raised as an objection nor refuted. // 10 //
Note: Indeed, according to you, there is only one sense-faculty, the intellect (*buddhi*), which alone is capable of apprehending multiple forms and other objects;
the [other] senses are five, and the mind (*manas*) is the seventh—thus, there are seven sense-faculties.
The five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the mind make eleven;
intellect, ego, and mind make three;
and "one" refers to intellect alone.
2. The Section on the Great and the Long. Sūtra 11: The doctrine that the Pradhāna is the cause has been refuted;
now, the doctrine that atoms are the cause must be refuted.
In this regard, first of all, the objection raised by the proponent of atoms (*aṇuvādin*) against the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*) is being refuted.

Herein is the position of the Vaiśeṣikas: qualities inherent in a causal substance produce another quality of the same genus in the resulting substance, because we observe that from white threads a white cloth is produced, and because we do not observe the opposite.
Therefore, if it is admitted that the conscious Brahman is the cause of the world, then consciousness ought to inhere in its effect, the world as well.
Since this is not observed, the conscious Brahman cannot be the cause of the world.
He refutes this admission by means of their own method of reasoning:
"Or [the great and long arise] from the short and the spherical," as in the case of the great and the long.
This is their theory: atoms, it is said, remain for some time without having initiated an effect, possessing respectively color and other qualities, and the dimension of sphericity (*pārimaṇḍalya*).
Then, preceded by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and others, and aided by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), they initiate the entire range of effects through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.
The qualities of the cause produce another quality in the effect.
When two atoms (paramāṇu) originate a dyad (dvyaṇuka), then the specific qualities such as whiteness and so forth residing in the atoms produce other [qualities] such as whiteness in the dyad.
However, the specific quality of the atom, namely sphericity (pārimāṇḍalya), does not produce another sphericity in the dyad.
Because it is accepted that the dyad possesses a different dimension;
for they describe minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*) as the dimensions residing in the dyad.
Even when two dyads originate a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*), the capacity to originate [the effect] remains the same for the whiteness and other qualities inherent in the dyads.
However, minuteness (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*), even when inhering in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), do not initiate [larger effects],
because it is accepted that a tetrad (*caturaṇuka*) possesses the dimensions of largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*).
Even when many atoms, or many dyads, or an atom together with a dyad initiates an effect, the same reasoning applies.

Thus, just as from a spherical atom (*paramāṇu*) there arises a binary compound (*dvyaṇuka*) that is minute and short, and a tertiary compound (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth that are large and long, yet not spherical;
or just as from a binary compound that is minute and short there arises a tertiary compound that is large and long, yet neither minute nor short— likewise,
if you accept that the insentient world is born from the sentient Brahman, what is lost to you?

Now, you might think: "I accept that in the case of composite substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, the sphericality (*pārimaṇḍalya*) and other qualities residing in their causes do not initiate [their own counterparts] in the effect because the effect-substance is occupied by another, contradictory dimension (*parimāṇāntara*);

however, there is no such occupation of the world by another quality contradictory to consciousness (*cetanā*), on account of which consciousness residing in the cause would not initiate another consciousness in the effect."
For there is no quality called "insentience" that is the opposite of sentience,
because it is merely the negation of sentience.
Therefore, due to its difference from qualities such as atomicity (*pārimāṇḍalya*), it follows that sentience must be a productive cause.
Do not think thus;

for this part [of the argument] is the same: just as spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and other qualities, though existing in their causes, do not initiate [new effects], so it is with consciousness (*caitanya*).
Nor is it the case that spherical dimension and the like fail to initiate [effects] because they have passed into another dimension, since their capacity to initiate is logically established.
For it is accepted that even a substance that has begun to exist remains devoid of qualities for a mere moment prior to the commencement of its own qualities.

Furthermore, the spherical dimensions (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and other such qualities are not occupied in initiating another dimension; therefore, they do not initiate another dimension of their own kind, because it is accepted that another dimension has a different cause.
As stated in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra: "The large [dimension] arises from the plurality of causes, from the largeness of the causes, and from a specific accumulation" (VS 7.1.9).
"An atom is the opposite of that," and "By this,
length and shortness are explained"— these are indeed the aphorisms of the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas).
Nor can it be argued that, due to some specific proximity or multiplicity of causes, only [qualities such as] number and so forth initiate [an effect], while sphericity and the like do not;
for when another substance or another quality is being produced, all causal qualities participate equally because of their specific inherence in their own substratum.
Therefore, the non-initiating nature of sphericity and the like arises solely from their own inherent nature.
The same should be understood to apply to volition as well.
Furthermore, because one observes the production of heterogeneous substances and so forth from conjunction, there is a deviation from the rule that things must arise from those of their own kind.
If it is argued that, since substance is the subject under discussion, providing an example of a quality is inappropriate, we say no.
This is because, by means of the example, what is intended to be expressed is merely the commencement of something of a different character.
Furthermore, there is no reason for any restrictive rule that a substance must be illustrated only by a substance, or a quality only by a quality.

Even your own author of the Sūtras has cited a quality as an illustration of a substance: "Because the conjunction [of the elements]—some of which are perceptible and some of which are imperceptible—is itself imperceptible, the body composed of five elements does not exist" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.2.2).

Just as the conjunction inhering in the perceptible earth and the imperceptible ether is itself imperceptible, so too the body— inhering in the five elements, some of which are perceptible and some imperceptible— would be imperceptible;
yet the body is indeed perceptible.
Therefore, it is not composed of the five elements.
This is what is meant: the body is a substance (dravya) characterized by the quality (guṇa) of conjunction (saṃyoga).
"But it is seen" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.6).
Thus, even here, the arising of something with different characteristics has been explained in detail. [Objection:
But if this is so, is this not already covered by that very [previous discussion]?
[Reply: We say it is not.
That [refutation] was directed against the Sāṃkhya;
this, however, is directed against the Vaiśeṣika.

But has not an extended application (*atideśa*) also been made on the basis of identical reasoning in the passage: "By this, those [systems] not accepted by the learned are also explained" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.12)?
This is true;
however, at the commencement of this Vaiśeṣika system, this elaboration has been made by means of an illustration that conforms to that system. (11) [FN:
An atom is spherical; the dimension residing in it is sphericity (*pārimāṇḍalya*).]
It should be read as "two and two. Section 3: The Topic of the Atom Not Being the Cause of the World. Sūtras 12–17:
In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [world] does not exist. (BBs 2.2.12)

Now he refutes the doctrine of atoms as the cause. That doctrine arises as follows: for in the world, substances possessing parts, such as cloth and the like, are seen to be produced by substances such as threads and so forth—which possess their own constituent parts—aided by conjunction.
By analogy with this, it is understood that whatever possesses parts is all produced by those very substances which possess their own constituent parts, aided by conjunction.
And that point at which this division of part and whole ceases is the atom (*paramāṇu*), having reached the limit of diminution.
Furthermore, this entire world, including the mountains, oceans, and so forth, possesses parts; and because it possesses parts, it has both a beginning and an end.
Since an effect cannot exist without a cause, it is the intention of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika) that atoms are the cause of the world.

Having perceived these four elements—known as earth, water, fire, and air—as possessing parts, four kinds of atoms are postulated; and because they have reached the ultimate limit of reduction, no further division is possible for them when they are being destroyed.
The dissolution of the earth and other elements down to their ultimate atoms constitutes the period of dissolution (*pralaya*).

Then, at the time of creation, an action arises in the atoms of air dependent upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); that action joins its own substrate-atom with another atom. Thereafter, air arises through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth;
likewise fire, likewise water, and likewise earth.
In this very way, the body is endowed with sense faculties;
likewise, this entire world arises from atoms.

The followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that the qualities such as color belonging to dyads and so forth arise from the qualities such as color residing in the atoms, according to the analogy of threads and cloth.

In this regard, the following is stated: First, the conjunction of atoms existing in a state of separation must be admitted as depending upon action, because conjunction is observed in the case of threads and other substances possessed of action.
Furthermore, since action is an effect, some cause for it must also be admitted.

If [such a cause] is not admitted, then due to the absence of a cause, there would be no initial action in the atoms. Even if it were admitted, if one were to assume some cause for the action— such as effort, impact, or whatever else is observed— the initial action in the atoms could not occur at all, because such a cause is impossible.
For in that state, effort as a quality of the self is not possible due to the absence of a body;
for effort, which is a quality of the self, arises when there is contact between the self and the mind established in a body.
By this same reasoning, other perceived causes such as impact (abhighāta) and so forth must also be rejected.
For after the time of creation, it is not possible for all that [subsequent] to be the cause of the first action.

Now, if it were said that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is the cause of the first action, would that [unseen force] be inherent in the self or inherent in the atoms? In either case, an action in the atoms could not be accounted for as having the unseen force as its cause, because the unseen force is insentient.
For it has been stated in the Sāṃkhya system that what is insentient does not function, nor cause others to function, independently when not presided over by a sentient being;
and because the Self, in that state, is insentient since consciousness has not yet arisen in it.
Furthermore, because [the unseen force] is admitted to be inherent in the Self, it could not be the cause of motion in the atoms due to a lack of connection.
If it is argued that there is a connection between atoms and a person who has not seen [the truth],

then because the connection would be constant, it would follow that activity would be constant, as there would be no other regulating factor. Thus, in the absence of some specific cause for action, there could be no initial motion in the atoms.

In the absence of action, conjunction—which is dependent upon it—would not exist. And in the absence of conjunction, the entire range of effects dependent upon it, such as dyads and so forth, would not exist.
Furthermore, the conjunction of one atom with another would have to occur either by way of its entire self or by way of a single part.
If [the atom] were to combine with its entire self, then because accumulation would be impossible, it would follow that it is merely atomic in size, which contradicts what is observed;
for it is observed that a substance possessing spatial divisions (pradeśa) undergoes conjunction with another substance possessing spatial divisions.
If, on the other hand, it were to combine with only one part, it would follow that it possesses parts (sāvayavatva).

If it is argued that the parts of atoms are merely conceptual constructs, then since conceptual constructs lack reality, conjunction itself would be unreal; consequently, it could not serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for a real effect. And in the absence of a non-inherent cause, composite substances such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth would not be produced.

Just as at the initial creation (*ādisarga*), due to the absence of a cause, no action capable of producing conjunction can arise in atoms, so too at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), no action capable of producing disjunction can arise in atoms;

for even there, no fixed visible cause for such action is observed. Nor is the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) intended for the accomplishment of dissolution, since it exists for the sake of accomplishing experience (*bhoga*). Therefore, due to the absence of a cause, no action capable of producing either conjunction or disjunction can belong to the atoms.
Furthermore, due to the absence of conjunction and disjunction, the non-existence of creation and dissolution—which depend upon those two—would follow as a logical consequence.
Therefore, this doctrine that atoms are the cause [of the world] is untenable.
[Note: *svānugataiḥ* means "by their own inherent [qualities]" or "by those connected to themselves."]
Furthermore, the relation [between atoms] is a collection consisting of the supported and the support, which serves as the cause for cognition.

And because of the acceptance of inherence (samavāya), and because of its similarity [to other relations], there would be an infinite regress. Thus, the phrase "and because of the acceptance of inherence, that [relation] does not exist" is connected with the ongoing refutation of the atomic theory.
Furthermore, you maintain that when a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is produced from two atoms (*aṇu*), it inheres in those two atoms while being entirely distinct from them.
However, by maintaining this, you are unable to establish that atoms are the cause [of the dyad].
Why?
Because of the lack of a final resting point due to parity:
for just as the dyad, being absolutely distinct from its two atoms, is connected to them by a relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*),
so too inherence itself, being absolutely distinct from the things that inhere (*samavāyin*), would require yet another relation characterized as inherence.
By means of a relation, it would have to be connected with its inherent substrates because of the complete equality of their difference;
and consequently, since a further mutual relation for each of those would have to be postulated, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would necessarily result.

[Objection: But here, inherence (samavāya), which is apprehended by cognition, is grasped as being eternally connected with its inherent substrates, not as unconnected or as depending on another relation.
And therefore, no other relation should be postulated for it, lest an infinite regress (anavasthā) should result.
To this it is replied: "No.
For if that were the case, conjunction (saṃyoga) as well would be eternally connected with the conjuncts; thus, like inherence (samavāya), it would not require any further relation.
Now, if conjunction, being a distinct entity, were to require another relation,
then inherence too would require another relation because it is likewise a distinct entity.
Nor is it reasonable to say that conjunction requires another relation because it is a quality (guṇa), while inherence does not because it is not a quality.
Because the causal factor of dependence is identical [in all cases],
and because the technical definition of a quality (*guṇa*) is not a restrictive criterion,
therefore, for one who accepts *samavāya* as a distinct entity, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would necessarily follow.
Furthermore, if an infinite regress were to follow, then since one [atom] would be unestablished, all would be unestablished; consequently, a dyad (dvyaṇuka) could not be produced from two atoms.
Therefore, the theory that atoms are the cause is also untenable. // 13 //
And because [the atom] exists eternally.
Furthermore, atoms must be admitted to have either the nature of activity, the nature of non-activity, the nature of both, or the nature of neither, as there is no other alternative;
yet none of these four possibilities is tenable.

If its nature were activity, then because activity would exist eternally, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of dissolution. If its nature were cessation, then because cessation would exist eternally, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of creation.
Furthermore, for it to possess both natures simultaneously is untenable due to contradiction.

If, however, it is admitted that activity and cessation occur due to some cause despite [the atoms] lacking both natures, then because a cause such as *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) would be eternally present, there would follow the consequence of eternal activity.
Alternatively, even if *adṛṣṭa* and so forth were not the governing factor, there would follow the consequence of non-eternal activity.
Therefore, for these reasons as well, the theory that atoms are the cause is untenable. // 14 //
And because they possess form and so forth, the opposite [of the atom's partlessness] follows from observation:
when substances possessing parts are divided according to their parts, that beyond which no further division is possible—
those fourfold atoms possessing form and so forth— are the originators of the fourfold primary elements and derivative matter which possess form and so forth.
Furthermore, that which the Vaiśeṣikas assert—namely, that atoms are eternal—is a thesis entirely devoid of foundation.
This is because, since atoms possess form and other qualities, it would follow that their atomicity and eternity are reversed;
the meaning is that, in relation to the ultimate cause, their grossness and impermanence would result, which is the opposite of what they intend.
Why?
Because it is observed thus in the world.
If, in the world, an entity possessing form and so forth is observed to be gross and impermanent in relation to its own cause; [then how could that which is not so be a cause?]
For example, just as a cloth depends upon its threads and is thus coarse and impermanent, and the threads themselves depend upon their fibers and are thus coarse and impermanent;
so too, these atoms are accepted by them [the opponents] as possessing color and other qualities.
Therefore, they too must have causes, and in relation to those, they would necessarily follow as being coarse and impermanent.
Furthermore, as for the reason they have stated for permanence— namely, "That which exists and is without cause is eternal" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.1)—
that too, this being the case, is not possible in the case of atoms;
for, by the manner already explained, it is established that even atoms possess causes.
As for the second reason stated for permanence— namely, "And because there is no specific negation of the term 'impermanent'" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.4)—
that too does not necessarily prove the permanence of atoms. For if there were no permanent entity whatsoever, the formation of a negative compound with the word "permanent" would be untenable.
Furthermore, it is not the permanence of atoms alone that is required;
for there exists the eternal Brahman as the ultimate cause.
Nor does the establishment of any object occur merely through the conventional usage of words and their meanings.
Because linguistic usage proceeds from words and their meanings as established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the third reason stated for [the world's] eternality—namely, "and non-perception" (*avidyā ca*, Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.5)—if it is explained in this way: that "non-perception" (*avidyā*) is the non-apprehension by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of existing causes whose effects are currently being observed; then...
Consequently, even the duality of atoms (dvyaṇuka) would result in being eternal.

If it were further qualified by the condition "provided it is not a substance" (adravyatve sati), even then, the very fact of "not having a cause" (akāraṇavattva) would be understood as the ground for its eternity.
And since that has already been stated previously, the phrase "and ignorance" (avidyā ca) would be a mere redundancy.

Furthermore, it might be explained that since there is no possibility of a third cause for destruction other than the separation of the constituent causes and the destruction of the constituent causes, this "non-perception" (avidyā) demonstrates the eternity of atoms.
However, there is no necessary rule that a perishing object must perish by means of only these two causes;
for this would only be the case if one were to accept that a distinct substance is produced by multiple substances acting together with conjunction as a concomitant condition.

But when it is accepted that the cause, which is of the nature of a generality (sāmānya) with its specificities discarded, becomes the originator by attaining another state possessing specificities, then destruction is possible even through the dissolution of the state of material form (mūrti), just as the solidity of ghee is dissolved [by heat]. Therefore, because they possess color and other qualities, the opposite of what is intended for the atoms would follow.
For this reason as well, the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] is untenable. // 15 //
And because there would be faults in either case:
gross earth has the qualities of odor, taste, color, and tangibility;
subtle water has the qualities of color, taste, and tangibility.
Fire has the qualities of color and touch and is subtler;

air has the quality of touch alone and is most subtle. Thus, these four elements are observed in the world to possess an increasing or decreasing number of qualities, and to be endowed with a gradation of grossness, subtlety, greater subtlety, and extreme subtlety.
In the same way, one might either conceive of atoms as possessing an increasing or decreasing number of qualities, or not.
In either case, the persistence of a logical fault would be unavoidable.

First, if one assumes that qualities increase or decrease, then for those qualities that have increased, there would follow the consequence of their no longer being atoms due to the increase in their physical dimension (*mūrti*).
Nor can it be said that an increase in quality occurs without an increase in physical dimension.
Because an increase in form is observed when there is an accumulation of qualities in elemental effects;

for if an accumulation or diminution of qualities were not postulated in order to establish the uniformity of atomhood, then, if all atoms were postulated as possessing only a single quality each, there would be no perception of touch in fire,
nor of both color and touch in water.
And on earth, there are taste, color, and touch,
because the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of their cause.
Now, if it were assumed that all [substances] possess exactly four qualities, [this would be inconsistent].
Consequently, there would be the perception of odor even in water;
in fire, the perception of both odor and taste; and in air, the perception of odor, color, and taste.
And it is not observed to be so;
therefore, for this reason as well, the theory that atoms are the cause [of things] is untenable. (16) [FN:
"Due to the increase of form" means due to grossness.]
And because it is not accepted [by the learned], it is utterly disregarded.

(BBs 2.2.17) The doctrine that primordial matter (*pradhāna*) is the cause was formulated even by certain knowers of the Veda, such as Manu and others, with the intention of relying on aspects such as the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*).

However, this doctrine that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the cause has not been accepted in any respect whatsoever by any of the learned; therefore, it must be utterly disregarded by those who follow the Veda.

Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas accept six categories that constitute the meaning of their system— namely, substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence— as being absolutely distinct and possessing distinct characteristics,

just as a human, a horse, and a hare are distinct. Having accepted them as such, they nevertheless accept that the remaining categories are dependent upon substance, which contradicts that very position.
That is not tenable.
How so?
Just as in the world, things such as rabbits, kuśa grass, and palāśa leaves, which exist as absolutely distinct from one another, do not possess a state of mutual dependence.
Thus, because substance (*dravya*) and its qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are absolutely distinct, it is not possible for the qualities to be dependent upon the substance.

Now, if the qualities were indeed dependent upon the substance, then—since they exist when the substance exists and do not exist when the substance does not exist—it would be the substance itself that becomes the object of various words and cognitions due to differences in configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and so on;
just as Devadatta, though being one and the same, becomes the object of various words and cognitions through connection with different states, so too [would the substance].
If that were the case, it would result in the undesirable consequence of adopting the Sāṃkhya doctrine and contradicting one's own established tenet.
[Objection: But surely even smoke, though distinct from fire, is seen to be dependent upon fire.
[Reply: True, it is so seen.
In that case [of fire and smoke], however, their distinctness is determined because they are perceived as separate;

here, however, in instances such as "the blanket is white," "the cow is ruddy," or "the lotus is blue," since it is precisely that very substance which is perceived through those respective qualifiers, there is no perception of a distinction between substance and quality as there is between fire and smoke.
Therefore, the quality (guṇa) has the nature of substance (dravya).
By this, the fact that action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya) have the nature of substance is explained.
As for what might be said—that qualities and so forth are dependent on substance because substance and quality are inseparable (ayutasiddha)—[that is not the case].
Furthermore, this state of being inseparable (*ayutasiddhatva*) must be either non-distinctness of location, non-distinctness of time, or non-distinctness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In every respect, it is untenable.
First, regarding non-distinctness of location, your own accepted doctrine would be contradicted.
How so?
For it is accepted that the location of the cloth is the location of the threads, not the location of the cloth;
however, the qualities of the cloth, such as whiteness and so forth, are accepted as being in the location of the cloth, not in the location of the threads.
And so they have said: "Substances originate another substance, and qualities originate another quality" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.10).

For they maintain that the threads, which are causal substances, originate the cloth, which is the effect-substance; and the qualities such as whiteness residing in the threads originate another quality, such as whiteness, in the cloth, which is the effect-substance.
That admission would be contradicted if the non-separateness of substance and quality were understood as their occupying the same location.
Alternatively, if inseparability (*ayutasiddhatva*) were said to mean non-separateness of time,
then it would follow that even the left and right horns of a cow would be inseparable.
Furthermore, if there is no distinct nature [between substance and quality], then because they are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), a difference in essence between substance and quality is impossible,

since that [difference] is perceived only as identity (*tādātmya*). Their assertion— that the relation between two separable things is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), whereas the relation between two inseparable things is inherence (*samavāya*)— is merely false.
Because it is impossible for a cause that is already established to be inseparably connected (*ayutasiddha*) with its effect;

or, if this admission were made with reference to only one of the two— that is, that inherence (*samavāya*) is the connection of an effect, which is itself inseparably connected, with its cause— even so,
a connection between a cause and an effect that is not yet established and has not yet acquired its own nature is untenable, since a connection depends upon both parties.
If it is argued that [inherence] exists once [the effect] has become established, then,

if the establishment of the effect prior to its connection with the cause is admitted, the statement that "conjunction and disjunction do not exist between cause and effect because they are not separately established" (ayutasiddhi) would be wrongly stated.
This is because, for example, as soon as it is produced, the effect-substance, being devoid of motion, is connected with other all-pervading substances such as space (ākāśa).
If conjunction (*saṃyoga*) alone is admitted [as a relation] and not inherence (*samavāya*), then the connection with a causal substance would likewise be only conjunction and not inherence.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of either conjunction or inherence apart from their being relations.
If it is argued that their existence is established because we observe the words and cognitions "conjunction" and "inherence" distinct from the word and cognition "relation," this is not so.
Even in the case of oneness, because multiple words and cognitions are observed in dependence upon both the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and external forms;
just as Devadatta, though being one, becomes the recipient of multiple words and cognitions in the world in dependence upon his own nature and his relational forms—
such as "man," "brahmin," "learned in the Vedas," "generous," "child," "youth," "old man," "father," "son," "grandson," "brother," and "son-in-law."

Just as a single line, by being placed in different positions, undergoes a variety of verbal cognitions such as "one," "ten," "hundred," or "thousand," so too, it is only the two related entities themselves—apart from the word and cognition of a "relation"—that are capable of receiving the words and cognitions of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) or "inherence" (*samavāya*); this is not due to the existence of a separate entity.
Thus, because that which meets the conditions for perception is not perceived, there is an absence of any other distinct thing.
Nor does it follow that the word and the cognition of "relation" would exist continuously even when the relation is not their object,
for this has already been answered by the fact that they depend on their own specific forms (svarūpa) and other forms.
Likewise, conjunction is not possible between atoms, the self, and the mind, because they lack spatial parts (apradeśatva).
Because we observe that a substance possessing spatial divisions (pradeśavat) enters into conjunction with another substance possessing spatial divisions;

if it is argued that imagined spatial divisions will exist for atoms, the self, and the mind, we say no, because if one imagines objects that do not exist, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of proving every possible object.
There is no restrictive cause for the rule that only this much—whether contradictory or non-contradictory—is to be postulated as an object and nothing more;
for such postulation depends on one's own will and can potentially be carried out extensively.
Furthermore, there is no reason to prevent one from postulating a hundred or a thousand objects beyond the six categories (padārthas) imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas.
Therefore, whatever is pleasing to whomever, that shall be established for them.

A compassionate person might imagine that the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is full of suffering for living beings, should simply not exist; or another, being afflicted by calamity, might imagine that even those who are liberated should be born again.
Who could be the preventer of these two?
Furthermore,
it is impossible for a composite dyad (dvyaṇuka) to have contact with two partless atoms, just as [it is impossible] for space to have contact [with them].
For there is no joining together of space and the elements such as earth like that of lacquer and wood.
If it is argued that "inherence must necessarily be postulated because the relationship of supported and support between cause and effect substances would otherwise be untenable," we say no,
because that would involve mutual dependence.

For if the difference between cause and effect were established, then the relationship of the supported and the support would be established; and if the relationship of the supported and the support were established, then their difference would be established—just as in the case of a bowl and its jujube fruit—resulting in a circular argument (*itaretarāśrayatā*).

Indeed, neither the difference nor the relationship of the supported and the support between cause and effect is accepted by the Vedāntins, because they maintain that the effect is merely the particular configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the cause itself.
Furthermore:

because atoms are delimited, they must possess as many parts as there are directions—whether six, eight, or ten; and since they would thus have parts, they would be impermanent. Consequently, the accepted doctrine that they are eternal and partless would be contradicted.
If you argue that those very parts which you conceive as being differentiated by spatial directions are themselves the atoms (*paramāṇu*), we say no;
for destruction is logically established through a sequence of gradations from grossness to subtlety, down to the ultimate cause.
Just as the earth, though it is a substantial entity, perishes when compared to dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and other subtler forms.
Then, that which is subtle and even subtler than the subtle perishes, being of the same class as earth; after that, the dyad (dvyaṇuka) perishes;
likewise, even the atoms (paramāṇus) would perish because they are of the same class as earth.
If it is argued that even things perishing perish only through the disjunction of their parts,
this is not a fault; for we have already explained that destruction can occur even as in the case of the melting away of the solidity of ghee.

For just as in the case of clarified butter, gold, and the like, even though their parts are not divided, the destruction of their solidity occurs through the attainment of a liquid state due to contact with fire, so too for atoms, the destruction of their form and other qualities will occur through the attainment of the state of the ultimate cause.
Likewise, the commencement of an effect does not occur through the mere conjunction of parts alone.

Because we observe the production of effects such as curds and ice even without a new conjunction of parts—as in the case of milk and water—and because this theory is constructed from extremely weak arguments, contradicts the scriptural texts concerning God as the cause, and has not been accepted by the learned authorities such as Manu and others who are devoted to the Vedas, it follows that seekers of the highest good must absolutely disregard this doctrine of atoms as the cause; this is the completion of the sentence. 17.
FN: "Tathātva" means absolute difference. Here, the Vedāntin is to be understood as the Sāṃkhya;
alternatively, the term "Sāṃkhya" is used because even for the follower of Kapila (the Sāṃkhya), there is the doctrine of identity (*tādātmya*).

Because of the possibility of abundance and the possibility of being limitless, "conjunction" (saṃśleṣa) means "collection" (saṃgraha); the meaning is that it is impossible for there to be a non-extraction of others by means of the extraction of one [atom].
This is the section on the aggregate (samudāyādhikaraṇa), Sūtras 18–27.
Even if both causes were present for the whole, that [result] would not be attained.
It has been stated that the Vaiśeṣika tenet is not to be relied upon because of its connection with faulty reasoning, its contradiction of the Veda, and its non-acceptance by the learned.
Since he is a "partial nihilist" (ardhavaināśika), we shall now demonstrate that the tenets of all nihilists (sarvavaināśika) are even less to be relied upon, due to their commonality as nihilism.
And that [system] is of many kinds, due to differences in practice or differences among those to be trained.

In this regard, there are these three types of proponents: some are proponents of the existence of all things (sarvāstitvavādins), while others are proponents of the mere existence of consciousness (vijñānāstitvamātravādins).
Others, however, are proponents of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatvavādin*).

Among them, those who maintain the existence of everything (*sarvāstitvavādin*) accept both external and internal entities—namely, the primary elements (*bhūta*), the derivative matter (*bhautika*), as well as mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).
We shall first respond to them.
In that regard, the primary elements (*bhūta*) are the earth element and so forth;
the derivative matter (*bhautika*) consists of visible form and so forth, as well as the eye and so forth.

Furthermore, they maintain that within the four [elements], the atoms of earth and the others—which possess the intrinsic natures of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—coalesce to exist in the state of earth and the other [elements].

Likewise, they consider that the five aggregates—known as form, consciousness, feeling, perception, and mental formations—are also aggregated internally by virtue of being the basis for all conventional designations. To this, it is said:
This collection, which is intended by the opponents to be caused by both [internal and external factors] and to be of both kinds, [is untenable].

Even when that aggregate is intended as being caused by both—that is, having the nature of a collection of primary elements (bhūta) and derivative matter (bhautika), and having the nature of the five aggregates (skandha)—there would be a failure to attain it; that is, a failure to attain the aggregate. The meaning is that the existence of the aggregate is logically untenable.
Why?
Because the constituents of the aggregate are insentient,
and because the kindling of the mind is dependent upon the accomplishment of that aggregate.

Furthermore, because no other conscious being—whether as an enjoyer, a ruler, or a stable synthesizer—is admitted; because if one admits activity independent [of a cause], it would follow that such activity never ceases;
because the "intention" (*āśaya*) cannot be defined as either distinct or non-distinct [from the momentary stream];
and because, given the admission of momentariness, activity is untenable due to the absence of any causal operation.
Therefore, the composite whole is untenable;
and if the composite whole is untenable, the worldly course of life which depends upon it would be destroyed. (18) [FN: The external consists of the primary elements and their derivatives.]
The distinction is that mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) belong to the internal [realms] such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Within the fourfold [classification], there are four kinds:
vowels, solids, those belonging to earth, and atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Moisture is the nature of the watery elements;
heat is that of the fiery elements;
and movement or motion is the inherent nature of the airy elements.
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of the sense faculties together with their specific qualities;
the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the stream of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) characterized by the thought "I, I";
and the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) is the experience of pleasure and so forth.
The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is the conceptual cognition characterized by such names as "fair-complexioned" or "horse.
The aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of the factors of passion, hatred, and delusion.
The continuum (*saṃtāna*) is the basis (*āśaya*), so called because passion and the other afflictions reside within it.
If it is argued that [the world-process] is possible because of mutual conditionality (*itaretara-pratyayatva*), we say no, because [these factors] are merely causes for the arising [of one another].

(BBs 2.2.19) Even though no conscious agent—whether an enjoyer or a ruler—is accepted as a permanent synthesizer, the course of worldly existence is nonetheless established through the mutual causality of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors. And since that [course of existence] is thus established, there is no further [cause] to be required.

And these factors beginning with ignorance— namely, ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, existence, birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and mental distress—
are of such a nature that they are mutually causal; in the Buddhist doctrine, they are taught in some places concisely and in others in detail.
If it is argued that this entire complex beginning with ignorance is undeniable for everyone,

and thus, since this complex of ignorance and so forth revolves incessantly like a waterwheel through the mutual relationship of cause and effect, the formation of an aggregate is logically entailed and established—
this is not so.
Why?
Because it is merely the cause of arising.
A composite would be possible if some cause for the composite were perceived.
But this is not understood;

for even if ignorance and the other factors are mutually dependent, while each preceding one might serve as the mere cause for the arising of each subsequent one, no cause whatsoever for the arising of the composite aggregate is possible. [Objection:
But was it not said that the composite aggregate is implied by the very nature of ignorance and the other factors?

To this it is replied: If the intention here is that ignorance and the other factors, being unable to establish themselves without an aggregate, depend upon an aggregate, then the cause of that aggregate must be stated.

And it has already been explained in the *Vaiśeṣika-parīkṣā* that such a cause is not possible, even if one accepts eternal atoms, or if there exist enjoyers who stand in the relation of substratum and dependent.
How much less, then, could it be possible when momentary atoms are accepted as being devoid of an enjoyer or empty of a substratum?
Now, if the intention is that ignorance and the rest alone are the cause of the aggregate,
how could they— being dependent upon that very aggregate for their own existence— be its cause?

Now, if you think that it is only the aggregates (*saṃghāta*) themselves that proceed in a continuum through beginningless *saṃsāra*, and that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors have those as their basis—
then even in that case, when one aggregate arises from another aggregate,
it would necessarily arise either as something strictly similar [to its predecessor] or [as something different].
Alternatively, it might arise as either similar or dissimilar without any restriction.
If one accepts a fixed rule, it would follow that a human person could never attain the state of a god, an animal, or a denizen of hell.
Even if one accepts the absence of such a rule, it would follow that a human person might, in a single moment, become an elephant, a god, or again a human.
Both [positions] are contrary to your own tenets.
Furthermore, it is your tenet that there is no permanent enjoyer for whom this composite [body] exists as an object of enjoyment;
therefore, enjoyment is for the sake of enjoyment alone and should not be sought by anyone else.

Likewise, since liberation is for the sake of liberation alone, one who desires liberation must not be anything other than that [seeker]; if he were to seek both [enjoyment and liberation], he would have to exist throughout the periods of both enjoyment and liberation. If he were to persist [throughout those times], there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
Therefore, even if ignorance and the other factors were to exist merely as causes for their mutual origination, let it be so; however, the formation of a composite aggregate would not be established.
The intended meaning is that this is because of the absence of an enjoyer (bhoktṛ). [19] [Note:
A *pratyaya* is that which moves toward (*ayate*) or goes toward (*gacchati*) an effect; thus, it is a cause.]
Consciousness and the four elements beginning with earth constitute form; these together with the sense-faculties are the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) for that which is born of the faculties.
Through craving, there is the grasping of vocal and bodily activity. Lamentation (*paridevana*) is the wailing such as "O son! or "O father! and so forth.
The phrase beginning with "āśraya" (basis) is a qualification of the enjoyer; it means "in those things which have the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as their basis.
Regarding the statement "because of the prior cessation when there is the arising of the subsequent":
this has already been explained—that since ignorance and the other factors are merely the causes for the arising [of the next moment], there is no establishment of a composite whole (*saṃghāta*).
However, it is now demonstrated that even this [position] cannot possibly maintain that [the preceding moment] is merely the cause for the arising [of the subsequent one].
For the proponent of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin) maintains this thesis: "When the subsequent moment arises, the preceding moment ceases.
Yet, by one who accepts this, it is impossible to establish a causal relationship (hetuphalabhāva) between the preceding and succeeding moments.
Because a preceding moment—whether in the process of ceasing or already ceased—is seized by non-existence, it is impossible for it to serve as the cause of a subsequent moment.
Alternatively, if the intention is that a preceding moment which has become an existent entity in its fully accomplished state is the cause of the subsequent moment, even so, this is not tenable;
for if one further postulates an activity for that which has already become an existent entity, it would entail the consequence of its connection with another moment.

Now, even if the intention is that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is simply the existence (*bhāva*) of the cause itself, this too is not tenable; for it is impossible for an effect to arise if it is not colored by the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of its cause.

Furthermore, if one accepts that there is such coloring by the intrinsic nature, then since the intrinsic nature of the cause would have to persist until the time of the effect, it would follow that one must abandon the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Furthermore, for one who accepts the relation of cause and effect even without the coloring of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be the fallacy of over-extension, as that relation would apply everywhere.
Moreover, what are called "arising" and "cessation" must be either the very essence of the entity itself, another state of it, or a distinct entity altogether;
in every case, this is untenable.
If, first of all, the very nature of the entity were its arising and cessation, then the word "entity" and the words "arising" and "cessation" would become synonyms.
One might think there is some distinction in that the states called "beginning" and "end" of the entity existing in the middle are designated by the terms "arising" and "cessation.
