Even so, because the entity would be connected to three moments—the initial, the final, and the middle—there would be a loss of the accepted doctrine of momentariness.
Furthermore, if arising and cessation were entirely distinct from the entity, like a horse and a buffalo,
then the entity would be unconnected with arising and cessation, which would entail the consequence that the entity is eternal. Moreover,
if seeing and not seeing were the arising and cessation of the entity, [the same fault would follow].
Even so, those two [states] would be properties of the perceiver and not properties of the object; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the object being eternal.
For this reason as well, the Buddhist doctrine is untenable. (20) [Note:
*Nirudhyamānatva* refers to the proximity of a cause of destruction.]
The state of being past is the state of having ceased.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction of the thesis and simultaneity [of cause and effect].
In the doctrine of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda), it has been stated that because the preceding moment is seized by cessation, it does not become the cause of the subsequent moment.
If, on the other hand, one were to assert the arising of an effect even when a cause is non-existent,
then there would be a contradiction of one's own thesis;
for this thesis— that mind and mental factors arise in dependence upon four kinds of causes— would be abandoned.
Furthermore, if arising were without cause, there would be no obstruction, and everything would arise from everything.
If you should say that the preceding moment persists for as long as it takes for the subsequent moment to arise, then there would be simultaneity of cause and effect;
even so, your thesis would still be contradicted.
Otherwise, this proposition that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary" would be contradicted. // 21 //
The non-attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is due to their non-interruption.
Furthermore, the Nihilists (*vaināśika*) imagine that whatever is cognizable by the intellect, other than the three [unconditioned phenomena], is conditioned and momentary;
they also describe that [momentariness] as destruction, analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, and space.
They consider all three of these to be mere non-existence, devoid of any defining characteristic (*nirupākhya*):
namely, that which is called "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), said to be the intentional destruction of entities;
its opposite, "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and space (*ākāśa*), which is merely the absence of obstruction.
He will later refute their [position regarding] space;
now he refutes the two types of cessation:
there is no attainment of analytical and non-analytical cessation.
The meaning is "impossibility.
Why?
Because there is no interruption.

For these two— cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)— must either have the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) as their object or have the entity (*bhāva*) as their object.
First of all, it is not possible for them to have the continuum as their object, because in all continua,
since the relationship of cause and effect among the members of the continuum is uninterrupted, the interruption of the continuum is impossible.
Nor can they both have existence as their objective domain;
for it is impossible for entities to undergo a destruction that is without continuity and devoid of any designation,
since in all states one observes an uninterrupted continuity by virtue of recognition.
Even in states where recognition is indistinct, because an uninterrupted continuity is observed in some instances, it can be inferred in other cases as well.
Therefore, the two types of cessation postulated by others are untenable. (22) [FN:
"Nirupākhyam" means that which is devoid of intrinsic nature.]
*Pratīpā* means contrary or adverse. *Pratisaṃkhyā* is the discernment of the form: "I shall make an existing state non-existent. Cessation by means of that is *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*.
Furthermore, because there are faults in both cases:
regarding this cessation of ignorance and so forth, which is included within *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* as imagined by others—
That [cessation] would arise either from right knowledge together with its auxiliaries, or by itself.

In the former alternative, there follows the undesirable consequence of abandoning the accepted doctrine of the destruction of what is to be removed. In the latter case, however, there follows the undesirable consequence of the uselessness of the instruction on the path.
Thus, since faults follow in both cases, this view is untenable. [Note:
"Parikara" refers to the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth;
the instruction on the path consists of the teaching to cultivate the realization that all suffering is momentary.]
And because there is no distinction regarding space (BBs 2.2.24). Furthermore,
as for their intended claim that the two types of cessation and space are indefinable,
the indefinability of the two cessations has already been refuted above.

Now, space is being refuted. Furthermore, the acceptance of space as being indefinable (nirupākhya) is illogical, because there is no distinction [between it] and the realization of its being a real entity (vastu), just as in the case of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
First, by virtue of the authority of scripture (*āgama*), the reality of space is established through such Vedic texts as, "From the Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
However, for those who hold contrary views, its being inferable from the quality of sound must be stated.
This is because qualities such as odor are observed to have their locus in substances such as earth.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that space is merely the absence of obstruction, it would follow that when one eagle is flying, there would be no room for another eagle wishing to fly up, since the obstruction [of the first] exists [in that location].
If it is argued that the second eagle will fly where there is an absence of obstruction, [the response follows...]

In that case, for the Buddhist who considers space to be a real entity (*vastubhūta*) precisely because its nature as an obstruction is specified, a contradiction with his own tenets would follow. For in the Buddhist tradition, in the course of the following series of replies to the question, "O Blessed One, on what is earth based?"—at the end of the sequence concerning earth and the other elements, there occurs this reply to the question "On what is wind based?": "Wind is based on space."
Therefore, it would not be tenable for space to be a non-entity;
for this reason as well, the non-substantiality of space is incorrect.
Furthermore, it is a contradiction to claim that these three—the two types of cessation and space—are all designated as non-entities (nirupākhya), yet are also eternal.

For neither permanence nor impermanence is possible for a non-entity (*avastu*), because the conventional usage of properties (*dharma*) and their substrata (*dharmin*) is based upon an entity. Indeed, if there were such a relation of property and substratum, it would possess substantiality (*vastutva*) like a jar or similar objects, rather than being a mere indefinable abstraction (*nirupākhya*). // 24 //
FN: "Will fall" means it will move about.
Is it "well-determined" (*saṃniścayā*) because its basis is a correct determination? And because of recollection (*anusmṛti*). BBs 2.25.
Furthermore, the nihilist (vaināśika), while asserting the momentariness of all things, must also accept the momentariness of the perceiver;
yet that is not possible.
For "recollection" (anusmṛti)—that is, memory—is precisely the recollection that arises following a prior experience or perception.
And that [recollection] is possible only when it has a single agent of perception;
for we do not observe recollection in one person regarding an object perceived by another person.
Indeed, how could there be the cognition "I saw that" and "I see this" if there were not a single entity who is both the prior and subsequent seer?

Furthermore, for everyone in the world, there is well-established through direct perception a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding a single agent of both seeing and remembering, expressed as: "I saw this, and now I see it.
For if the agent of these two were different, then one would perceive: "I am remembering, while another saw it.
Yet no one perceives in such a manner.
In cases where such a distinction is perceived, everyone in the world understands that the agent of seeing and the agent of remembering are indeed different, as in:

"I remember that so-and-so saw this. However, in the present case, one understands that the very same single self is the agent of both seeing and remembering, thinking: "I myself saw this. Even though [the self] perishes, it is understood as the sole agent of both seeing and remembering.
Just as one does not deny the perception of oneself by saying "I am not," nor like claiming that fire is cold or lacks luminosity;

so it being thus, when there is a connection between two characteristics—namely, seeing and remembering—for a single [subject], the nihilist (vaināśika) would be unavoidably forced to abandon his admission of momentariness.
Likewise, by recognizing the successive cognitions of the self itself as having a single agent from the present breath until the final exhalation, and also those of the past...

If a proponent of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin) who is a nihilist (vaināśika) were to say, "How can one who links together actions performed by oneself alone from birth onwards [be consistent with this view]?"— if he should reply, "This is accomplished through similarity," one should answer him as follows:
Therefore, because similarity depends upon two things,
for one who maintains the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga), there is no single cognizer to perceive two similar entities; thus,
the claim that "recognition is caused by similarity" would be nothing but a false prattle.

If there were a single grasper of the similarity between the preceding and succeeding moments, then, because that one [grasper] would persist through two moments, the thesis of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would be undermined.
If it is argued that this cognition "this is similar to that" is merely another distinct cognition and not caused by the grasping of both the preceding and succeeding moments, we say: no.
"Because of this, that [is similar]," it is said;
for it takes up distinct referents.
If the cognition itself were to have similarity as its object, then the employment of the sentence "this is similar to that" would be purposeless.
The application [of the term] would result in being merely "similarity.

For when a category of object well-known in the world is not accepted by investigators, then neither the establishment of one's own position nor the refutation of the opponent's position— whatever may be stated— enters the stream of consciousness of the investigators or of oneself as something corresponding to reality.
In this very way, that which is determined to be the meaning of this [text] is precisely what should be stated;
anything else being said would merely demonstrate one's own prolixity.
Furthermore, this conventional usage based on similarity is not logical.
This is because there is the cognition of that [previous] state and the non-cognition of a state similar to it.
In the case of an external object, since deception is possible, there might occasionally arise a doubt as to whether "this is that very same thing" or "this is similar to it.
However, with respect to the perceiver, even such a doubt never arises as to whether "I am that very same person" or "I am similar to him."

Because there is the perception of that very same state with certainty, in the form of "I, who saw this yesterday, am the very same I who remembers it today," the doctrine of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas) is therefore untenable. // 25 //
"Because that which is non-existent has not been observed [to produce anything]. (BBs 2.26) For this reason as well, the doctrine of the Nihilists is untenable;
for those who do not accept a stable, persisting cause, it follows that an entity arises from non-existence.
And they demonstrate the arising of an entity from non-existence, saying: "Because there is no manifestation without having first destroyed [the cause].
For it is said that a sprout arises from a seed that has perished, and likewise curd from milk that has perished.
From a lump of clay comes a jar.
If an effect were to arise from an unchanging cause, then because there would be no distinction, everything could arise from everything.
Therefore, they maintain that an entity arises from non-existence, since sprouts and the like are produced from seeds and so forth which have been swallowed up by non-existence.
Regarding this, it is said: "Not from the non-existent, because it has not been observed.
An entity does not arise from non-existence.
If an entity were to arise from non-existence, then since there would be no distinction in the state of being non-existent, the acceptance of specific causes would be purposeless.

For there is no distinction in the state of non-existence between seeds and the like that have been destroyed and things such as a rabbit’s horn, since they are equally devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). If there were some distinction in their non-existence by which it could be meaningfully accepted that a specific causal difference exists—such that a sprout arises from a seed alone and curd from milk alone—then that would be so. However, if a non-distinctive non-existence is accepted as a cause, then sprouts and the like would arise even from rabbit’s horns and similar things.
But it is not observed to be so.

Furthermore, if a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) were admitted even for non-existence (*abhāva*), just as blueness and so forth are for blue lotuses and the like, then, precisely because it possesses a specific quality, non-existence would result in being an entity (*bhāvatva*), just like a blue lotus and so forth.
Nor could non-existence be the cause of the production of anything.
Precisely because it is non-existent, like the horn of a hare and so forth;
and if an entity were to arise from non-existence, every effect would necessarily be permeated by non-existence.
And it is not observed to be so;
for every entity is perceived as having its own specific form by way of its very nature as an existent thing.
Furthermore, no one accepts that objects such as bowls, which are modifications of threads and the like, are actually permeated by clay.
However, people perceive objects as being composed of clay precisely because they are associated with clay.

As for the claim that the arising of an entity from non-existence must occur— since it is impossible for any immutable substance to function as a cause without undergoing a destruction of its own nature— that is poorly argued.

For it is observed that only those things of a stable nature, such as gold and the like, which are recognized [as being the same], exhibit the relationship of cause and effect in the form of bracelets and other ornaments.
Even in cases such as seeds where the destruction of the original form is perceived, that destroyed prior state is not accepted as the cause of the subsequent state;
rather, it is because the persisting parts of the seed and so forth, which are themselves not destroyed, are accepted as the cause of the sprout and its subsequent effects.

Therefore, since one does not observe the production of an existent from non-existent things such as a hare’s horn, whereas one does observe the production of an existent from existent things such as gold, this admission that an entity arises from non-existence is untenable. Furthermore, by those nihilists who first admit that mind and mental factors arise from the four [great elements], and that a composite consisting of primary elements and elemental derivatives arises from atoms, yet subsequently deny what they have admitted by postulating that an entity arises from non-existence— they are contradicting their own tenets.
The entire world is thrown into confusion. // 26 //
Moreover, in this way, success would accrue even to those who are indifferent.
(BBs 2.27) For if it were admitted that an entity arises from non-existence, then,
such being the case, the desired success would belong even to people who are indifferent and making no effort.
Because non-existence is easily obtained,
there would be the production of crops even for a farmer who does not exert effort in his field-work,
and the production of vessels even for a potter who does not exert effort in the preparation of clay.
Even for a weaver who is not actually weaving threads, there is the acquisition of cloth as if he were weaving;
yet no one would strive for heaven or liberation in such a manner,
nor is this logical or accepted by anyone.
Therefore, this acceptance of the arising of an entity from non-existence is also untenable. [Note:
*anīhamānānām* means "of those who are without effort";
*amatra* means "a vessel such as a jar," etc.]
5. The Section on Non-existence (Abhāvādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 28–32:
"Non-existence [is not possible], because [objects] are perceived" (BBs 2.2.28).

Thus, after the criticisms regarding the non-attainment of the composite whole and so forth have been raised by relying on the doctrine of external objects, the Buddhist Proponent of Consciousness-Only (Vijñānavādin) now comes forward to respond.
It is said that, observing the attachment of some to external objects, this system of the doctrine of external referents (*bāhyārthavāda*) was elucidated in accordance with their inclinations;
it is not the intended meaning of the Sugata.
For his intended view, however, was the doctrine of consciousness alone as the single aggregate (*vijñānaikaskandhavāda*).

And in this doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*), the entire conventional operation of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is established as being internal, by way of forms mounted upon the intellect (*buddhi*).
For even if external objects exist, the conventional operation of means, objects, and results of knowledge does not occur without their being mounted upon the intellect.
But how is it understood that this entire conventional operation is internal alone, and that no external object exists apart from consciousness?
He says that this is because of the impossibility of that [external object].
For if an external object were admitted, it would have to be either atoms or their aggregates, such as pillars and the like.
In that regard, atoms cannot possibly be the objects determined by cognitions of pillars and so forth (because no cognition arises that has the appearance of atoms).
Nor are the aggregates such as pillars [the objects],
because it is impossible to determine whether they are different from or non-different from their atoms. In this same way, one should understand universals (*jāti*) and so forth as well.

Furthermore, since cognition—which by its very nature is common to all objects—arises with this partiality toward each respective object, such that there is "cognition of a pillar," "cognition of a wall," "cognition of a jar," or "cognition of a cloth," this cannot be accounted for without a specific quality residing within the cognition itself;
thus, one must necessarily admit that cognition possesses a form corresponding to its object (*viṣayasārūpya*).
And once that is admitted, since the form of the object is already contained within the cognition itself, the postulation of the existence of an external object is useless.
Furthermore, because they are necessarily perceived together, it follows that there is no difference between the object and its cognition;
for when one of these two is not perceived, the other is never perceived.
And this is not logical if their intrinsic natures were distinct.
Because of the absence of obstructing causes,
for this reason as well there is an absence of external objects;
and this should be understood as being like dreams and so forth.
For just as cognitions such as dreams, illusions, mirages, water in a desert, and cities of the Gandharvas occur in the form of grasped objects and grasping subjects even without an external object,
it is understood that cognitions regarding the waking state, such as those of pillars and so forth, must likewise exist;
because there is no difference in their status as cognitions.
But how, if there is no external object, is the diversity of conditions (pratyaya) possible?
He says: it is due to the diversity of latent impressions (vāsanā).
For in beginningless saṃsāra, just like the relationship between seed and sprout, the diversity of consciousnesses and latent impressions—existing as mutual causes and effects—is not contradicted.
Moreover, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the variety of cognitions has its cause solely in mental impressions (*vāsanā*).
This is because, in cases such as dreams, both of us admit the existence of a variety of cognitions caused by mental impressions even in the absence of external objects;
whereas I do not admit a variety of cognitions caused by external objects in the absence of mental impressions.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no external object.
This being the case, we reply: "There is no non-existence, because [the object] is perceived.
Indeed, it is not possible to determine the non-existence of an external object.
Why?
Because of perception.
For an external object is indeed perceived in each respective cognition as a pillar, a wall, a jar, or a cloth.
Furthermore, it is impossible for that which is being perceived to be non-existent.

For instance, if someone while eating were to say, even while personally experiencing the satisfaction produced by eating, "I am not eating, nor am I satisfied," how could his words be accepted when he says, while himself perceiving an external object through sensory contact, "I do not perceive it, nor does it exist"?
"Is it not the case that I do not say, 'I do not perceive any object at all,' but rather I say, 'I do not perceive anything apart from the perception itself'?
"Certainly you say this, because your mouth is unrestrained;
however, you do not say it with reason."
Therefore, even the distinctness of the object from its apprehension must necessarily be admitted on the basis of that very apprehension;
for no one perceives the apprehension itself as "this is a pillar" or "this is a wall.

Rather, all worldly people perceive pillars, walls, and so forth precisely as objects of apprehension. Even those who deny the external object explain it only by referring to the internal form of the knowable, saying: "That which is an internal form of cognition appears as if it were external."

Thus, even they— who, while experiencing consciousness that is renowned to the whole world and appearing as external, yet desire to reject it— employ the expression "as if external" (*bahirvat*) when speaking of the external object.
For otherwise, why would they say "as if external"?
No one would say that Viṣṇumitra appears like the son of a barren woman;
therefore, for those who accept reality in accordance with experience, it is logical to accept that [the object] appears externally, and not that it appears as if external.
[Objection: But surely, because an external object is impossible, it is determined that it "appears as if external."

This determination is not correct, because the possibility and impossibility of a thing are determined based on the operation or non-operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not conversely, that the operation or non-operation of the means of valid cognition is based on possibility and impossibility.
For whatever is apprehended by even one of the means of valid cognition, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, that is possible;
but whatever is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition whatsoever, that is impossible.

In this case, however, since an external object is apprehended by all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to their respective capacities, how can it be said that it does not exist due to dilemmas such as its being distinct or non-distinct [from cognition], given that it is indeed apprehended?
Furthermore, the destruction of the object does not occur simply because the cognition possesses a form similar to the object;
for if the object were non-existent, it would be impossible for the cognition to possess a form similar to that object.
Furthermore, because the object is perceived externally,

one must admit that even the rule of simultaneous perception between the cognition and its object is caused by their relationship as means and end (*upāya-upeyabhāva*), and not caused by their identity. Moreover,
in the expressions "cognition of a jar" and "cognition of a cloth," the difference lies only in the qualifiers— the jar and the cloth— not in the qualified cognition itself.
Furthermore, the distinction between these two is established by [the former] from one and by [the latter] from both;
therefore, there is a distinction between the object and the cognition.
This same principle should be understood to apply here as well, in the case of "the perception of a jar" and "the recollection of a jar."
For here too, the distinction lies only between the two qualified entities—namely, seeing and remembering—and not in the qualifier, the jar.
Just as in the case of "the smell of milk" or "the taste of milk," the distinction lies only between the two qualified entities, smell and taste, and not in the qualifier, the milk; so it is here.

Furthermore, since the two cognitions occurring at earlier and later times are each exhausted by their own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is logically impossible for them to stand in the relation of the apprehended and the apprehender toward one another.

Furthermore, the propositions regarding the differentiation of consciousness, the propositions regarding properties such as momentariness, and the propositions concerning specific and general characteristics, the relationship between the infused and the infuser, the affliction of ignorance, and the bondage and liberation of existent and non-existent phenomena contained within one's own treatises would all be undermined.
Moreover:
It is logical to maintain that for one who accepts consciousness as "consciousness," an external object of such a nature as a pillar or a wall is not accepted at all.
Now, if it is argued that consciousness, because its nature is luminosity, is experienced by itself like a lamp, whereas an external object is not so,
then you are accepting an action within itself that is utterly contradictory, like saying "fire burns itself."

But you do not accept that which is non-contradictory and well-established in the world—that an external object is experienced by a consciousness distinct from itself; oh, what great "wisdom" has been displayed!
Nor is consciousness, even though it is not distinct from the object, experienced by itself, precisely because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.

Now, it might be argued that if consciousness has as its object something distinct from its own nature, then that [object] must also be grasped by another [consciousness], and that too by yet another, resulting in an infinite regress.

Furthermore, since cognition—like a lamp—is of the nature of illumination, for one who postulates another cognition [to illuminate the first], the distinction between the illuminated and the illuminator is untenable due to their equality; thus, such a postulation is useless.
Both of these arguments are incorrect.
Since the desire to perceive the witness of consciousness does not arise once consciousness itself has been perceived, the suspicion of an infinite regress is untenable;
furthermore, because of the difference in nature between the witness and its object, the relationship of perceiver and perceived is established;
and finally, because the self-evident witness cannot be denied.
Furthermore:

by asserting that consciousness, like a lamp, manifests by itself without depending on another illuminator, one would be saying that consciousness is not accessible through any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇagamya*) and lacks a cognizer,
just like the manifestation of a thousand lamps situated in the midst of a solid rock.

If it is argued: "Certainly so; however, because consciousness is of the nature of experience, the position we desire is being conceded by you," [we reply]: No, because another cognizer, whose instrument is the eye, is seen to manifest lamps and other such objects.
Therefore, since consciousness also does not differ in being an object of manifestation, it is understood that its manifestation occurs only when there is another cognizer, just like a lamp.

If you argue: "By proposing that the cognizer—the Witness—is self-established, you have merely adopted my own position—that consciousness manifests by itself—through a different turn of phrase," we say no.
This is because you admit that consciousness possesses specific attributes such as arising, perishing, and multiplicity.
Therefore, we have established that consciousness, like a lamp, is cognizable as something distinct [from its object]. (28) [Note:
*pakṣapāta* refers to the conventional usage of the distinction between specific objects;
*avidyopaplava* refers to the contact with ignorance.]
"And because of the difference in nature, [the waking state] is not like dreams and so forth" (BBs 2.29).

Regarding what was stated by the one who flees from external objects— that even cognitions of pillars and the like occurring in the domain of the waking state could exist without an external object, because there is no difference in their being cognitions—
that must be answered.
To this it is replied: waking cognitions cannot be like dream-cognitions and the like.
Why?
Because of their difference in nature.
For there is indeed a difference between the states of dreaming and waking.
What, then, is this difference?
We say it is sublation and non-sublation.
For one who has woken up, the object perceived in a dream is sublated by the thought, "I perceived a gathering of a great multitude, but it was false";
[one realizes], "Indeed, there was no gathering of a great multitude for me; rather, my mind was overcome by sleep, and therefore this delusion arose.
In the same way, a similar sublation occurs with respect to illusions and the like.
An object perceived while awake, such as a pillar or the like, is never sublated in any state whatsoever.
Furthermore, that which is the seeing of dreams is memory,
whereas the seeing of what occurs while awake is direct perception.

Furthermore, the difference between memory and perception is personally experienced as consisting in the separation from or union with the object, as in: "I remember my beloved son, but I do not perceive him; I desire to perceive him.
This being so, one who personally experiences the difference between these two cannot rightly say that waking perception is false because it is a form of perception, like dream perception.
Nor is it proper for those who consider themselves wise to deny their own direct experience.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to assert that waking cognitions are inherently without an objective basis (nirālambana) because that would contradict direct experience, one seeks to assert it by means of their similarity to dream cognitions.
However, a property that cannot belong to something inherently does not become possible for it merely through its similarity to another thing;
for fire, though experienced as hot, will not become cold simply because of its similarity to water.

The dissimilarity between dreaming and waking has indeed been demonstrated. [Note: "Afflicted by sleep" is a designation for a defect of the instruments [of cognition]. For a cognition produced solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is recollection (*smṛti*).]
Apprehension is experience born from a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
it is not an existent thing, because it is unapprehendable.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that the variety of cognitions can be accounted for solely through the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) even in the absence of an object—[that is not so].
To that, it must be replied:
here it is said—on your position, the non-existence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) would not be tenable, because external objects are not perceived.
For it is due to the perception of objects that latent impressions arise in various forms corresponding to each respective object.
But if objects are not being perceived, what could be the cause for these various latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?

Even if they were beginningless, it would result in a baseless infinite regress according to the logic of a "blind tradition," which would undermine conventional practice rather than establishing one's intended position.

Furthermore, as for the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) presented by the denier of external objects—who claims that this collection of cognitions is caused solely by latent impressions and not by objects—[they are likewise untenable].
Both of those [arguments] should likewise be understood as refuted,
because the mental impression (*vāsanā*) is impossible without the apprehension of an object.

Furthermore, since they admit the apprehension of an object even without mental impressions, whereas they do not accept the arising of a mental impression without the apprehension of an object, their own positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) actually establish the very existence of the object.
Furthermore, what is called "latency" (*vāsanā*) consists of specific formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
and formative forces cannot be conceived without a substratum,
as this is observed in the world.
And for you, there exists no substratum for the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because none is perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore,
[this is so] because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and because of the nature of existence as arising or being (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, even that which is designated as the *ālayavijñāna*— conceived as the locus of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— cannot serve as the substratum for those impressions, because, by virtue of its admitted momentariness, its nature is unstable, just like the active cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Indeed, this is so unless there exists a single, continuous entity connected to the three times, or an immutable principle that perceives all objects.
The conventional activities of depositing latent impressions (*vāsanā*), recollection, and the reconnection of memory are possible only by depending on place, time, and causal conditions.
However, if the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) were of a permanent nature, the tenets of our system would be abandoned.
Furthermore, since the acceptance of momentariness is common even to the Vijñānavāda, those arguments based on momentariness that apply to the theory of external objects [would likewise apply here].
The refutations previously set forth—beginning with "And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises"—should be applied here as well.
Thus, both these positions of the Nihilists (Vaināśikas)—the position of those who maintain external objects and the position of the Vijñānavādins—have been rejected.
As for the position of the Śūnyavādins, however, since it is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), no further effort is made to refute it.

For this worldly convention, established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be denied without first apprehending another reality, because there is no exception (*apavāda*) to what is established as a general rule (*utsarga*). Furthermore, it is in every way untenable [to deny it]. (BBs 2.2.32)
What need is there for much?
In every way, however this doctrine of annihilation (vaināśika-samaya) is examined for its logical consistency, it simply falls apart like a well dug in sand.
We do not perceive any logical justification for it whatsoever.
Therefore, the conventional practice of the Nihilist school is untenable.

Furthermore, by teaching these three mutually contradictory doctrines—the external object, consciousness, and emptiness—the Sugata has clearly demonstrated his own state of incoherent prattle, or else it was out of malice toward the people, thinking: "May these people be bewildered by the comprehension of contradictory meanings."
The intention is that this system of the Sugata (the Buddha) is in every respect to be disregarded by those who desire their own welfare. // 32 // [Note:
Here, "people" refers to those outside the Veda.
6. The Section on the Impossibility in One [Sūtras 33–36].
Because [the three natures] cannot exist in a single [entity], the Sugata’s system has been refuted. Now,
the system of the Nirgranthas (Jainas) is being refuted.

They maintain that there are seven categories (padārtha) recognized among these: namely, the living being (jīva), the non-living (ajīva), influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), dissociation (nirjarā), bondage (bandha), and liberation (mokṣa).
However, in brief, there are only two categories called the living being and the non-living;
for they believe that, as appropriate, the others are included within those very two.

Regarding these two, they describe this further elaboration known as the five *astikāyas*: the *jīvāstikāya* (the category of souls), the *pudgalāstikāya* (the category of matter), the *dharmāstikāya* (the category of motion), the *adharmāstikāya* (the category of rest), and the *ākāśāstikāya* (the category of space).
They also describe the many kinds of intermediate subdivisions of all these, as imagined within their own system (*svasamaya*).
And in every case, they apply this logic known as the *saptabhaṅgīnaya* (the method of sevenfold predication).
It may exist; it may not exist;
it may both exist and not exist; it may be inexpressible.
It may be that it both exists and is inexpressible; it may be that it does not exist and is inexpressible; and it may be that it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible.
In the same way, they apply this method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*) even to such qualities as unity and permanence.
To this we reply: why is this position not tenable?
Because it is impossible for [contradictory attributes] to coexist in a single [entity].
For it is not possible for contradictory properties, such as existence and non-existence, to coexist simultaneously in a single substratum, just as cold and heat cannot.
These seven categories that have been determined—defined as being exactly this many and of such a nature—must either be exactly so, or they must not be so at all.
Otherwise, if their form were undetermined, such that one might think "they are thus" or "they are not thus," then that cognition would be invalid, just like a doubtful cognition.
[Objection: Surely, since a thing consists of multiple natures, a cognition that arises with a determined form cannot be invalid, just like a cognition of doubt.
[Reply: We say no.

For one who asserts that non-exclusivity (anekāntatva) applies unrestrictedly to all things, even the act of determination itself—because it is a particular instance of a thing—would be subject to the occurrence of conceptual constructions such as "it may be" or "it may not be," and thus its very nature as a determination would be lost.
It might be so;
thus, for the one who determines and for the result of the determination, there would be existence in one case and non-existence in another.

This being the case, how could a teacher who has become an authority (pramāṇabhūta) be able to teach when the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing are themselves undetermined?
Alternatively, how could those who follow his intention proceed toward the object taught by him when its specific form remains undetermined?
For it is only when there is a determination that the fruit is certain that the entire world proceeds toward the performance of its means without confusion; not otherwise.
Therefore, one who composes a treatise whose meaning is undetermined would have speech that is not to be accepted, like that of a drunkard or a madman.

Likewise, when the question is raised whether the number five of the five astikāyas exists or does not exist, it might indeed exist according to one position, but in another position it would not exist; consequently, there would result either a deficiency in number or an excess in number.
Furthermore, the state of being "inexpressible" (avaktavyatva) is not possible for these categories of existence.
If they were inexpressible, they would not be expressed;
yet they are expressed and called "inexpressible"—this is a contradiction.
Furthermore, while being expressed, they are both determined to be so and not determined to be so.

Likewise, if one were to prattle that right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the fruit of such ascertainment, either exists or does not exist, and similarly that its opposite, wrong vision (*asamyagdarśana*), also either exists or does not exist, this would belong to the side of the intoxicated or the insane, not to the side of those who are to be convinced. Furthermore, if heaven and liberation were to exist in one alternative and not exist in another, and likewise if they were eternal in one alternative and non-eternal in another— such a lack of ascertainment would render purposeful action impossible.

Furthermore, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the nature of the soul (*jīva*) and other categories established by their own scriptures— which are held to have existed from beginningless time— would not be as they are determined to be. Thus, since it is impossible for two contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence to reside in a single substratum (*dharmin*) like the soul or other categories,

and since if one property such as existence is present, the other property such as non-existence cannot exist, and likewise if non-existence is present, existence cannot exist, this Jaina doctrine is incoherent.

By this, the various forms of the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*)—such as the acceptance of unity and multiplicity, permanence and impermanence, and being distinct or non-distinct—are to be understood as refuted.

As for the claim that [beings] arise from a collection of atoms designated as *pudgalas*, that has already been refuted by the previous refutation of atomism (*aṇuvāda*); therefore, no separate effort is made to refute it here. // 33 //
FN: The soul (jīva) and the non-soul (ajīva) are the enjoyer and the enjoyed, respectively.
Āsrava is the engagement of the sense organs toward objects;
saṃvara is that which restrains this [engagement], namely restraint (yama), observance (niyama), and so forth.
*Nirjarā* (exhaustion) means that which wears away or destroys impurity; it consists of practices such as ascending heated stones.
*Bandha* (bondage) is karma.
*Mokṣa* (liberation) is the continuous upward movement of one who has entered the space of the non-world (*aloka-ākāśa*) upon the destruction of the fetters of karma.
The term *astikāya* is conventional (*sāṃketika*) and denotes a category of reality (*padārtha*).
The analysis of the compound is: "that which is a living being (*jīva*) and is an *astikāya*.
*Pudgalas* are aggregates of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*); they are called *pudgalas* because they are filled (*pūryante*) and moved (*ganti*), and they are *kāyas*.
The *saptabhaṅgī* is the collection of the seven modes (*bhaṅga*), beginning with "existence" (*asti*). The *naya* is the method (*nyāya*) of that [collection].

And thus, there would be the defect of the soul's non-universality (*akārtsnya*). Just as the impossibility of contradictory attributes in a single substratum (*dharmin*) would result in a fault in the *syādvāda*, so too another fault—the non-universality of the self (*ātman*) or living being (*jīva*)—would necessarily follow.
How so?
For the Ārhatas maintain that the soul (jīva) has the size of the body.

And since the soul possesses the dimensions of the body, it follows that the self is non-omnipresent, not all-pervading, and limited; consequently, the impermanence of the self would result, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects.

Furthermore, because the dimensions of embodied beings are not fixed, a human soul, having been of the dimension of a human body, would not pervade the entire body of an elephant when it attains birth as an elephant due to the ripening of some karma;
likewise, when attaining birth as a gnat, it would not be contained within the entire body of a gnat.

This same fault applies even in a single lifetime, across the stages of childhood, youth, and old age. It might be argued: "The soul consists of parts; therefore, those very parts would contract in a small body and expand in a large one."
Furthermore, it must be stated whether or not the co-location of those infinite constituent parts of the living being (jīva) is obstructed.
If there were obstruction, then infinite parts could not be gathered within a limited space.

If there were no obstruction, then since all the parts would occupy the same location as a single part, their expansion would be impossible, leading to the absurd conclusion that the living being is merely atomic in size.
Furthermore, it is impossible even to imagine an infinity of parts belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) that are restricted solely to the body. [Note:
*Karmavipāka* is the manifestation of the fruits of actions.
Now, if it were argued that when one assumes a large body, certain parts of the soul arrive, and when one assumes a small body, certain others depart, to this also it is replied:
Nor can there be non-contradiction even through succession, because of the objections regarding transformation and so forth.

(BBs 2.2.35) Furthermore, it is not possible to establish that the soul has the same dimension as this body—even by means of succession—through the entering and exiting of parts, without contradiction.
Why?
Because it would entail the fault of undergoing transformation and other defects.
For a living being (jīva) that is constantly being filled and depleted by the addition and removal of constituent parts, its state of being subject to modification is unavoidable;
and if it were subject to modification, it would follow—as with a hide or similar objects—that it is non-eternal.

Furthermore, the accepted doctrine of bondage and liberation would be contradicted; for how could there be an upward movement for a soul enveloped by the eightfold karma and submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, like a gourd, upon the severance of its bonds?
Moreover, because the constituent parts that come and go possess the nature of arrival and departure, the body must be non-self, just like a physical body and so forth.
Consequently, some specific part [of the body] would have to be the self;
yet it is impossible to specify that "this is it" or "that is it.
Furthermore:
It must be explained from where these constituent parts of the living being (*jīva*) emerge when they arrive, and where they dissolve when they depart;
for they cannot emerge from the elements (*bhūta*) nor dissolve into the elements,
because the living being is non-material (*abhautika*).

Nor can any other substratum for the parts of living beings— whether common or uncommon— be established, due to a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, if this were the case, the self (*ātman*) would be of an indeterminate nature.

Because the parts that come and go possess indefinite dimensions, for this reason— and due to the resulting faults such as these— it is not possible to maintain that the coming and going of parts occurs in the self even by way of alternation (*paryāya*). Alternatively, by means of the previous sutra, it was shown that if the self were the size of the body, then upon assuming other bodies that are increased or decreased in size, the consequence of its being non-omnipresent would lead to its impermanence.

Furthermore, if it is urged that even though there is no fixed limit to the measure [of the self] due to its successive transformation, the self would nonetheless be eternal by way of the principle of the permanence of a stream or continuum— just as the followers of the Red Robe (Raktapaṭas) maintain the permanence of the continuum of consciousness despite the instability of individual cognitions, and the same might be argued for us— this Sūtra provides the answer: first of all, if the continuum were not a real entity, it would follow that one is a proponent of non-self (nairātmyavāda).
Even if the self were a real entity (*vastu*), this position is untenable because it would entail defects such as undergoing transformation (*vikāra*). [Note:
Although the dimensions and the self do not remain constant due to the differences in bodies, there is nonetheless a continuous stream even through destruction;
"those who have discarded their clothing" (*visica*) means those who are naked. // 35 //

"And because of the permanence of the final state, and because both [the initial and final states] would be eternal, there would be no distinction. (BBs 2.2.36) Furthermore, since the Jains maintain that the size of the soul (*jīva*) existing in the final state of liberation is eternal, it follows by implication that the sizes of the soul in the two prior states—the state of ignorance and the intermediate state—must also be eternal; thus, there would be no distinction between them.
There would be only the size of a single body, and no attainment of other bodies that are increased or decreased in size.
Alternatively, since the final size of the soul (jīva) is fixed, the soul must likewise have a fixed size even in its two prior states;
consequently, one must admit that the soul is always either atomic or large without distinction, rather than having the size of the body.
Therefore, like that of the Sugata, the doctrine of the Arhats as well is incoherent and must be disregarded. // 36 //

The Section on the Lord (Paty-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 37–41: "On account of the lack of consistency regarding the Lord" (BBs 2.2.37). Now, the doctrine that the Lord is the cause solely as a superintendent is refuted.
How is this understood?

Because at [Brahma Sūtra] 1.4.23–24, "And [the Lord is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples," and "And because of the teaching of His desire," the Teacher himself established that the Lord possesses both natures— that of being the material cause and that of being the presiding agent.

If, on the other hand, the mere doctrine of God as the cause were refuted here without distinction, it would follow that the author of the Sūtras has contradicted himself through inconsistent statements due to internal contradictions between earlier and later passages.

Therefore, this specific position—that God is not the material cause nor the presiding controller, but merely an efficient cause—is strenuously refuted here because it opposes the non-duality of Brahman established by the Vedānta.
Furthermore, this conception of God held by those outside the Vedic fold is of many varieties.

First, some who rely on Sāṃkhya and Yoga postulate that Īśvara is the sole presiding efficient cause of both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, and that *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, and Īśvara are distinct from one another.

However, the Māheśvaras maintain that there are five categories—effect, cause, yoga, rule, and the end of suffering—which were taught by Paśupati, the Lord, for the sake of liberating bound souls (*paśu*) from their fetters; thus, Paśupati, the Lord, is the efficient cause.
They describe [it thus].
Likewise, certain others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas, also describe God as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) in some way according to their own systems.
Therefore, the following answer is stated: "On account of the unreasonableness of [the doctrine of] the Lord" (patyurasāmañjasyāt).
It is not tenable that the Lord (Īśvara) is the cause of the world by virtue of being the presiding director over primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
Why?
Because of the lack of uniformity (asāmañjasyāt).
But what is the inconsistency?

For if Īśvara were to ordain the distinctions among living beings by way of inferior, middling, and superior states, he would be subject to defects such as passion and hatred; consequently, like ourselves and others, he would be liable to the consequence of not being the Lord.
If it is argued that there is no fault because he depends upon the karma of living beings, we say: no.

If karma and the Lord were related as the impelled and the impeller, there would result the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If it is argued that this is not so because of beginninglessness (*anāditva*), we say no; for just as in the present time, the same fault of mutual dependence applies to past times as well, resulting in the fallacy of a "blind tradition" (*andhaparamparā*).
Furthermore, it is the established doctrine of the experts in Nyāya that "faults are characterized by incitement to action" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.18).
For no one is ever observed to act, whether for their own sake or for the sake of another, unless impelled by some fault.
Furthermore, it is inconsistent to claim that all people engage in the welfare of others solely because they are motivated by their own self-interest;

for if God possesses a self-interest, it follows that He would not be the Supreme Lord (anīśvara). Moreover, since you admit that God is a particular kind of person, and since you also admit that a person is characterized by indifference (audāsīnya), there is an inconsistency.
Those who rely on Sāṃkhya and Yoga include Hiraṇyagarbha, Patañjali, and others.
There are four types of Māheśvaras: the Śaivas and the Pāśupatas.
[The schools are] the Karuṇikasiddhāntins and the Kāpālikas. "Paśus" refers to living beings; the meaning is: for the sake of destroying their "pāśa," which is bondage.

And because a relationship is untenable: this [argument] is again even more consistent for us. For there can be no Lord distinct from both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* who is the ruler of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* without a relationship [to them].
First of all, a relationship characterized by conjunction (saṃyoga) is not possible,
because Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara are all-pervading and partless.
Nor is a relationship characterized by inherence (samavāya) possible.
Because the relationship of substrate and superstrate cannot be established,
nor can any other relationship inferable from the effect be postulated, since the very nature of the causal relation remains unproven even now.
If it is asked, "How can this be so for the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādins)? [the answer is] no, because for them, a relationship characterized by identity (tādātmya) is logically possible.

Furthermore, since the proponent of Brahman determines the nature of the cause and so forth on the basis of scripture (āgama), there is no necessary rule that everything must be accepted exactly as it is perceived through the senses.
However, for the opponent who determines the nature of causes and so forth by the force of examples, there is this distinction: everything must be accepted exactly as it is observed.
If it is argued that the opponent’s reliance on scripture is equal because there exists a scripture composed by an omniscient being, we say no;

for this would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the establishment of omniscience would depend upon the authority of scripture, and the establishment of scripture would depend upon the authority of the omniscient one.
Therefore, the conception of God by the proponents of Sāṃkhya and Yoga is untenable.
In this same manner, the inconsistency should be applied, as far as possible, to other conceptions of God found in the Vedas and the Brahmanas. // 38 //
And because of the impossibility of a presiding [agent],
there is for this reason also the impossibility of a Lord (Īśvara) as imagined by the logicians.
For, being so imagined, he would have to set the primordial matter (pradhāna) and other factors into motion by presiding over them, just as a potter works with clay and other materials.
And this is not tenable;
for it is impossible for the Pradhāna—which is imperceptible and devoid of form and other qualities—to be directed by the Lord, because it differs in nature from clay and similar materials. // 39 //
If it is argued that it is like the instruments, we say no, because of experience and so forth.
It might be claimed:

"Just as the Person presides over the collection of instruments such as the eye—which are imperceptible and devoid of form and other qualities—in the same way, the Lord will also preside over the Pradhāna."
Nevertheless, this is not tenable;
for it is from the observation of enjoyment and so forth that the presiding over the collection of instruments is inferred,
yet here no such enjoyments and so forth are observed.

Or, if the equilibrium of the collection of instruments (the body) were admitted [for the Lord], then experiences such as pleasure and pain would necessarily follow for the Lord just as they do for transmigrating beings.

Alternatively, the two sūtras may be explained as follows: "And because of the impossibility of a substratum" (2.2.39). For this reason also, the Lord imagined by the logicians is untenable; for in the world, a king who rules a kingdom is seen to have a substratum—that is, he possesses a body—not to be without a substratum.

And therefore, for one who wishes to postulate an unseen Lord on the strength of that analogy, it would follow that even the Lord must be described as having some kind of body as the locus of his instruments;
yet that cannot be described,
because a body exists only after the creation has occurred, and thus its existence prior to creation is impossible.
Furthermore, if the Lord were without a substratum, his status as a motivator would be untenable, because it is observed thus in the world.
[Objection: "If it is argued that he is like an instrument, [we reply] no, because of [the resulting] experiences and so forth."

Now, if one were to postulate, in accordance with worldly observation, that even for Īśvara there exists some body as the locus of his causal instruments—this too is not tenable. For if he possessed a body, then, like those in saṃsāra, there would follow the consequence of experiences such as pleasure and pain; thus, it would entail that even Īśvara is not truly sovereign (anīśvara). // 40 //
FN: *Bhoga* is the experience of pleasure and pain;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the experience of objects is included.
Because the instruments [of action] exist therein, it is called the "instrumental body" (*karaṇaśarīra*).
Either [the Lord] would be finite or he would be non-omniscient.
For this reason as well, the Lord imagined by the logicians is untenable;
for they admit that he is both omniscient and infinite.
Furthermore, it is accepted that *pradhāna* is infinite and that the *puruṣas* are infinite and mutually distinct.
In that case, would the omniscient Lord determine the measure of *pradhāna*, of the *puruṣas*, and of himself, or would he not determine it? In either case, a logical flaw remains attached.
How so?

First, in the case of the first alternative, because they are delimited by a finite measure (*iyattā*), it necessarily follows that Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara must be finite; for this is observed in the world.

Whatever object in the world is delimited by a finite measure, such as a cloth and the like, is seen to be finite; likewise, the triad consisting of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara would also be finite because they are delimited by a finite measure.
First, numerical quantity is delimited by the three forms of Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara;
likewise, the measurement of their own essential nature contained therein would also be delimited by Īśvara.
And so too is the great number pertaining to the Puruṣas.
Consequently, among those whose number is limited, those transmigrating beings who are liberated from saṃsāra would have a finite saṃsāra and their state of being transmigrators would also be finite.
Likewise, as others are gradually liberated, there would be an end to saṃsāra and to transmigrating beings.

Furthermore, primordial matter (pradhāna), along with its modifications, which is intended by the Lord as the object of His governance for the sake of the Puruṣas and is regarded as the state of saṃsāra—when that is non-existent, what would the Lord govern?
Or in what domain could omniscience and lordship exist?
Furthermore, if the primary cause (pradhāna), the individual soul (puruṣa), and the Lord (īśvara) were thus finite, it would follow that they have a beginning;
and if they have both a beginning and an end, it follows that one falls into the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda).

Now, if the latter alternative were accepted—namely, that "this fault shall not occur" because the Lord does not delimit the number of primary matter (*pradhāna*), individual souls (*puruṣa*), and the Self (*ātman*)—then another fault would follow: the abandonment of the accepted doctrine of the Lord's omniscience. Therefore, the theory of the Lord as the cause (*īśvarakāraṇavāda*) maintained by the logicians (*tārkika*) is also inconsistent. 41.
FN: Number (*saṃkhyā*), measure (*parimāṇa*), or quantity (*iyattā*). 8. The Section on the Impossibility of Origination (Sūtras 42–45). [Sūtra 42: Because origination is impossible. (BBs 2.2.42)

The position of those who maintain that the Lord is not primordial matter (*prakṛti*) but rather the presiding controller and solely an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) has already been refuted. Now, the position of those who maintain that the Lord is both primordial matter and the presiding controller—that is, a cause consisting of both—is being refuted.
But surely, by relying on the sacred scriptures (*śruti*), the Lord was previously determined to be of this very nature: both primordial matter and the presiding controller?
It is an established principle that a Smṛti which conforms to Śruti is authoritative.
For what reason, then, is this position sought to be rejected?

It is said in reply: although such a portion [of the Smṛti] does not fall within the scope of contradiction because it is consistent [with Śruti], there is another portion concerning existence that is a point of contradiction; therefore, an effort is made to reject that.

In this regard, the Bhāgavatas maintain that the Blessed One, Vāsudeva alone, whose nature is stainless knowledge, is the ultimate reality; and he, having divided himself fourfold, is established in the form of the manifestation of Vāsudeva, the manifestation of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the manifestation of Pradyumna, and the manifestation of Aniruddha.
He who is named Vāsudeva is called the Supreme Self (paramātman); he who is named Saṃkarṣaṇa is the individual soul (jīva); he who is named Pradyumna is the mind (manas).
The ego-sense is named Aniruddha;
among them, Vāsudeva is the supreme, the ultimate creative source, while the others, Saṃkarṣaṇa and so forth, are his effects.

Having worshipped this Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, for a hundred years through approaching him, offering materials, ritual sacrifice, recitation of sacred texts, and yoga, one whose afflictions are exhausted attains the Lord himself.

In this regard, as for what might be said—that this Nārāyaṇa, who is well-known as the Supreme Self beyond the unmanifest, the Self of all, remains after having divided himself into many forms—that is not refuted, because [the scripture says]:
"He becomes one-fold; he becomes three-fold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
Since it is understood from such scriptural passages as these that the Supreme Self manifests in manifold ways,
even that worship of the Blessed One characterized by approaching Him and so forth— which is intended to be performed constantly with undivided attention— is not prohibited.
Since devotion to the Lord is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti,
we respond to that which is further asserted— namely, that Saṃkarṣaṇa arises from Vāsudeva, Pradyumna from Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Aniruddha from Pradyumna— as follows:
it is not possible for the individual soul (jīva), designated as Saṃkarṣaṇa, to originate from the Supreme Self, designated as Vāsudeva.
Because it would entail defects such as impermanence;
for if the soul were subject to origination, defects such as impermanence would necessarily follow,
and consequently, its attainment of the Blessed One— liberation— could not occur.
For if the cause were to be attained, it would follow that the effect must dissolve;

moreover, the Teacher will later refute the production of the individual soul in the Sūtra: "The Self is not produced, because it is not heard [to be so] and because of its eternity according to those [scriptural passages]" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.17).
Therefore, this conception is inconsistent.
FN: *Vyūha* means form.
*Abhigamana* is the act of going to the deity's abode preceded by the focused attention of speech, body, and mind;
*upādāna* is the procurement of the materials for worship.
Sacrifice (*ijyā*) means worship; self-study (*svādhyāya*) means the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra and others;
yoga means meditation (*dhyāna*).
Nor is there an instrument produced from the agent.
For this reason as well, this conceptualization is inconsistent;
because in the world, an instrument such as an axe is never seen to arise from an agent such as Devadatta.
And the Bhāgavatas describe that from the agent known as Jīva, the instrument known as Manas (the mind) arises;
and from that which is born of the agent, the ego-sense known as Aniruddha arises.
Yet we are not able to determine this without the aid of an illustrative example.
And we do not find any such scriptural statement.

Or, if they exist as consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that [doctrine]. Furthermore, it might be argued: "These Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others are not intended to be individual souls (jīva) and so on; rather, all these are accepted as being nothing other than the Lord (Īśvara), endowed with the sovereign qualities of knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor."
"All these are indeed Vāsudevas—faultless, without a substratum, and beyond reproach.
Therefore, it follows that this aforementioned defect of the impossibility of origination does not apply.

To this it is replied: even so, there would still be no refutation of that; the impossibility of origination remains unrefuted, for the intention is that the defect of the impossibility of origination occurs by way of another method.

How so? If first of all this is the intended meaning— that these four lords, Vāsudeva and the others, are indeed mutually distinct, possessing identical attributes, and that there is no single selfhood among them—
then the postulation of multiple lords is purposeless.
For the accomplishment of the work of the Lord would be achieved by a single Lord alone; furthermore, this would result in the abandonment of your own tenet,
since you accept that each individual Blessed One, Vāsudeva, is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*).
Now, if the intention is that these four manifestations (vyūhas) of the one Lord alone possess identical attributes, even so, the impossibility of their origination remains exactly as it was;
for the origination of Saṃkarṣaṇa from Vāsudeva is not possible, nor that of Pradyumna from Saṃkarṣaṇa, nor that of Aniruddha from Pradyumna.
Because there is no distinction [between them].
For there must be a distinction between cause and effect, as in the case of clay and a jar;
indeed, in the absence of a distinction, it is not possible to conceive of something as the effect and the other as the cause.

Furthermore, the proponents of the Pañcarātra system do not admit any distinction among Vāsudeva and the others—whether in one or in all of them—based on a gradation of knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth;
for they maintain that all these manifestations (vyūhas) are indeed Vāsudevas, devoid of difference. Nor would these manifestations of the Blessed One be restricted to only four in number.
Because it is understood that the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is a manifestation (*vyūha*) of the Blessed One. [Note:
"Faultless" means devoid of passion and the like;
"without a substrate" means not produced by primordial nature (*prakṛti*).]
"Blameless" means being devoid of destruction and so forth.
And because of contradiction (BBs 2.2.45):
furthermore, various kinds of contradictions are found in this treatise, characterized by the conceptualization of qualities and that which possesses qualities, and so on.
Because of such views as "knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor are the qualities; these blessed ones are indeed Vāsudevas,
who are the Selfs," there would also be a contradiction with the Vedas.

Because we observe the disparagement of the Vedas in such passages as, "Having failed to obtain the highest good in the four Vedas, Śāṇḍilya mastered this scripture," it is established that this [opposing] hypothesis is inconsistent. // 45 //
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Commentary on the Śārīraka Mīmāṃsā composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
Thus ends the second quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, titled "Demonstration of the Fallacious Nature of the Doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and Others.
The third quarter of the second chapter:
In this quarter, the resolution of contradictions regarding the scriptural texts concerning the five great elements, the individual soul (jīva), and so forth.
The Section on Space (Viyad-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1.1.7:
"Space [is not produced], because it is not mentioned [in the scriptures].
In various places within the Vedāntas, scriptural texts concerning origination are found that follow different approaches.
Some maintain that space has an origin, while others do not;
likewise, some maintain that wind has an origin, while others do not;
and the same applies to the soul and the vital breaths.
In this very same way, contradictions based on sequence and other factors are also observed in other Vedic texts.

Since it has been established that the doctrines of others are not to be relied upon because of such contradictions, one might suspect that one's own position is likewise not to be relied upon for the very same reason of contradiction. Therefore, the subsequent section is commenced in order to clarify the meaning of the creation-śrutis found throughout all the Vedāntas.
And when that [text] is rendered pure of meaning, the result is precisely the cessation of the aforementioned doubts.
In this regard, first of all, with reference to space (*ākāśa*), it is considered whether there is an origination of this space or not.
On this point, it is established first: "Space does not originate, because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect]."
Space, indeed, does not arise.
Why?
Because it is not heard [in scripture].
For there is no mention of it in the context of its origin;

for in the Chāndogya, having introduced Brahman denoted by the word "Being" in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chā. 6.2.1), it continues, "It thought" (tadaikṣata).
And in the passage, "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), the origin of the triad of fire, water, and food is taught by taking fire as the middle among the five great elements;
and scripture is our authority for the production of knowledge regarding objects beyond the senses.
Furthermore, there is no scriptural passage here that establishes the origination of space;
therefore, there is no origination of space. // 1 //
But there is [an answer].
The word "but" (tu) is used to adopt an alternative position.
Let it be that, according to the Chāndogya, there is no origination of space; however—
However, there is another scriptural passage;
for the Taittirīyakas record: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and then, having introduced this, they state, "From that very Self, indeed, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Consequently, there is a contradiction between the two scriptural texts: in one case creation begins with fire, while in the other it begins with space.
But surely, a single unified meaning for these two Vedic texts is appropriate?
True;
it is appropriate, but it cannot be understood.
Why?
Because it is impossible for a single creator, mentioned only once in the text "He created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), to be connected with two distinct objects of creation.
"It created fire," and "It created space.
Now, it is observed that even when the agent is mentioned only once, there can be a connection with two separate tasks to be performed.
Just as one might say, "Having cooked the soup, he cooks the rice," so too would I construe it as: "Having created that space, it created that fire.
But this is not a valid construction.
For in the Chāndogya, fire is understood to be the first-born, while in the Taittirīyaka, space is so understood;
and it is not possible for both to be first-born.
By this, the contradiction with the literal words of other scriptural passages is also explained.

In the passage, "From that very Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), it is likewise impossible for the single ablative case and the single act of production, mentioned once, to be simultaneously connected with both space and fire— as in "from that [space] fire was produced"—
given the intervening statement, "From air, fire."
And because they are recorded separately in this manner. // 2 //
Regarding this contradiction, someone says: "Because a secondary sense is impossible;
there is no origination of space precisely because it is not heard [in scripture]."
As for that other scriptural passage cited which asserts the production of space, it must be understood in a figurative sense.
Why?
Because of impossibility.
Indeed, the production of space cannot be conceived as possible while those who follow the view of the venerable Kaṇāda remain alive;
for they deny the production of space on the grounds that the causal totality is impossible.
For it is said that everything being produced arises only from inherent, non-inherent, and instrumental causes.
Furthermore, for a substance, multiple substances of the same class serve as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
However, in the case of space (*ākāśa*), there exists no collection of multiple substances of the same class that could act as an originator;
nor is there an inherent cause in which, together with a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), the conjunction [of causes] could produce space.
But because of that absence [of prior non-existence], the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) which functions to favor it is utterly remote in the case of space.

Furthermore, regarding produced things such as fire and the like, a distinction between their prior and subsequent states is conceivable: before production, the effects such as illumination did not exist, whereas after [production] they do exist.
However, in the case of space, no such distinction between prior and subsequent times can be conceived.
For how could it be determined that prior to its production there existed something without space, without cavities, and without openings?
Furthermore, because of its dissimilarity to earth and other elements, characterized by all-pervasiveness and so forth, the non-produced nature of space is established.
Therefore, just as in common worldly usage one employs figurative expressions such as "making space" or "space was born," [so too is the scriptural description].

And just as the designations of distinctions such as "the space within a jar," "the space within a water-pot," and "the space within a house" are merely figurative (gauṇa) with respect to space itself, which is one, so too in the Veda— in the passage, "They should sacrifice the wild animals in the spaces"—
the scriptural statement regarding origination is likewise to be understood as figurative. // 3 //
And from scripture:
Scripture indeed makes known the unproduced nature of space (*ākāśa*).
For it says: "The wind and the intermediate space—this is immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.3).
For the production of that which is immortal is not possible;

and by stating, "it is all-pervading and eternal like space," the text, by comparing Brahman with space through the two attributes of all-pervasiveness and eternity, indicates that those same two attributes belong to space as well.
And the production of such a thing is not possible.
And there is this illustrative example: "Just as this space is infinite, so the Self is to be known as infinite";
as well as, "Brahman has space as its body" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.6.2), and "Space is the Self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.7.1).
For if space were subject to origination, it could not serve as a distinguishing attribute of Brahman, just as the color blue cannot be an attribute of a lotus [if the lotus itself were produced].
Therefore, it is understood that Brahman is eternal and common to space. // 4 //
And it may belong to one [of two meanings], like the word "Brahman.
This is a sūtra following the preceding term.
It might be argued as follows:

But how can the single word "saṃbhūtaḥ" (originated), occurring in this context—"From that very Self, space originated" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1)—be taken in its primary sense with respect to the subsequent elements such as fire, while being taken in a secondary sense with respect to space?

To this, the following answer is given: Even for a single word like "saṃbhūtaḥ," both secondary and primary usage are possible depending on the specific object, just as in the case of the word "Brahman."

Just as the single word *brahman* has a secondary usage with respect to food and so forth, and a primary usage with respect to bliss, within this context [of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad]: "Seek to know Brahman through austerity; austerity is Brahman" (Taitt. Up. 3.2).

And just as the word "Brahman" is used figuratively for austerity— which is a means to the realization of Brahman— though it applies directly to Brahman as the object to be realized, so it is here. But how, if space is non-produced, is this proposition, "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), maintained?
[Objection: But surely Brahman would then have a second by virtue of space;
and how could it be that "when Brahman is known, everything is known"?
To this it is replied: first of all, the statement "only one" is appropriate with respect to its own effects.
