Just as in the world, someone might observe clay, a staff, a wheel, and so forth in a potter’s workshop on the previous day, and then on the following day observe various kinds of vessels spread out; he might say, "Only the clay alone existed on the previous day. By that restriction, he would intend to imply that the entire collection of effects produced from the clay did not exist on the previous day, but not [that] the staff, the wheel, and so forth did not exist.
In the same way, the scriptural teaching of non-duality excludes any other presiding agent.
Just as a potter is seen to be the presiding agent for clay, which is the material cause of a jar, there is no other presiding authority for Brahman, which is the material cause of the universe.
Nor does it follow that Brahman becomes "with-a-second" (dvitīya) merely because space exists as a second entity.
For diversity is caused by a difference in characteristics;

yet prior to creation, there is no difference in characteristics between Brahman and the ether, because they are as intermingled as milk and water, owing to the commonality of attributes such as all-pervasiveness and incorporeality.
At the time of creation, however, Brahman strives to produce the world, while the other remains as motionless as if it were something else.
By this, their difference is determined;
and thus, from such scriptural passages as "Brahman has space as its body" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.6.2), the establishment of the metaphorical identification of Brahman and space is also proven.
For this very reason, the knowledge of all things is established through the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, every effect, as it arises, arises with a space that is non-different from its own time and place;
and since space itself exists as non-different in time and place from Brahman, [the knowledge of all follows].
Therefore, when Brahman and its effects are known, space is necessarily known along with them.

Just as when a few drops of water are poured into a jar filled with milk, they are grasped simply by grasping the milk; for once the milk is grasped, no separate grasping of the drops of water remains.
Thus, because it does not exist apart from Brahman and its effects in terms of space and time, the ether (*nabhas*) is already included within the apprehension of Brahman;
therefore, the scriptural mention of the "origination" of the ether is merely figurative (*bhākta*).
[Note: *Bhakti* refers to the metaphorical application (*abhedopacāra*) of a term.]
*Kula* means a household;
*amatra* refers to vessels such as jars and the like.
Having reached this point, he said the following:
There is a loss of the thesis because there is no distinction from words:
"By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1);
and "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6).

Thus, in every Vedānta text, a proposition is recognized in such forms as: "O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka 1.1.3), and "There is no knowledge whatsoever external to me.
For that very proposition, there would thus be a great consistency and non-contradiction.
If there were non-difference of the entire aggregate of things from Brahman, which is the object of knowledge,
then this proposition— that by the knowledge of one, everything is known— would be undermined, for that would only be possible if there were difference.
And that very non-difference is established only if the entire aggregate of things originates from the one Brahman.
Furthermore, the fulfillment of the proposition is understood from the words themselves by means of the logic that the cause and its modification are non-different.

For instance, having made the proposition, "By which the unheard becomes heard," this very proposition is supported by examples such as clay, which are intended to demonstrate the non-difference between cause and effect.
And for the sake of proving that very point, the subsequent words state: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

Having thus shown the entire range of effects to have originated from Brahman through such passages as "It thought" and "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), they demonstrate their non-difference [from Him] by saying: "All this has that as its self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
This continues until the end of the chapter.
Thus, if space were not an effect of Brahman, then space would not be understood when Brahman is understood;
consequently, there would be a failure of the initial proposition.

Nor is it proper to render the Veda invalid by abandoning its own thesis. For instance, in every Vedānta text, various words and corresponding illustrations establish that very same thesis: "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6), and "This immortal Brahman alone is before [us]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).
Such are these [objections]. Therefore, like fire and other elements, even space (gagana) is produced.
As for what was stated—that space is not produced because it is not mentioned [in the scripture]—[that is incorrect].
That is incorrect, because another scriptural passage concerning the origination of space has been shown: "From that very Self, indeed, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
True, it has been shown.
But [it might be argued that this is] contradicted by another scriptural passage, "It created fire. No;
for all the scriptures form a single coherent whole.
A single coherent whole exists among those [passages] that are not contradictory.

But here, a contradiction has been stated: because it is impossible for a creator mentioned only once to be connected with two things to be created, and because it is impossible for both to be born first, and because an alternative (vikalpa) is impossible.
This is not a fault.
For in the *Taittirīyaka*, the creation of fire is heard to be the third [step], as it says: "From that very Self, space was produced;
from space, air;
from air, fire" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1).
For this Śruti passage cannot be interpreted otherwise;
however, the Chāndogya Śruti can be interpreted as "having created that ether and air, it created fire.
Indeed, this Śruti, being primarily concerned with the production of fire, is not able to preclude the origination of ether well-established by another Śruti.
Since a single sentence cannot possess two distinct functions,
even a single creator might produce many things to be created sequentially;
thus, when the possibility of interpreting it as a single sentence exists, the scripture should not be discarded on account of its having contradictory meanings.

Nor do we intend to imply that the Creator mentioned by us once is connected with two distinct things to be created, because other things to be created are included on the strength of other scriptural passages.

Just as in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman; from Him it is born, into Him it dissolves, and in Him it breathes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1), the fact that the entire aggregate of existing things is heard to be born directly from Brahman does not preclude the order of creation beginning with fire as prescribed in another section.
In this way, even though the origin of fire from Brahman is heard [in scripture], it cannot set aside the order of creation beginning with ether as prescribed by another scriptural passage.

But is it not the case that this sentence is intended for the injunction of tranquility, given the scriptural statement: "Because it originates from that (tat), dissolves into that (jalān), and breathes in that (an), one should meditate upon it with a tranquil mind"?
This is not a statement regarding creation;
therefore, it cannot override the sequence established in another passage.
"It created fire"—this is the statement regarding creation.
Therefore, one might argue that the sequence should be accepted here exactly as it is heard in the text.
To this we reply: no;
for the entity "space" (viyat), which is well-established in another scriptural passage, must not be discarded merely to conform to the priority of "fire" (tejas).
Because sequence is a property of things (*padārtha*).
Furthermore, in the passage "It emitted fire" (*tat tejo 'sṛjata*), there is no word here that denotes sequence;
rather, sequence is understood from the sense of the matter.
And that [possibility] is precluded by the sequence established in another scriptural passage, namely, "From air, fire.

As for the alternatives of either option or combination regarding ether and fire being the first-born, these are precluded by the impossibility [of such a claim] and by its non-acceptance [by the scriptures].
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the two scriptural passages.

Furthermore, in the Chāndogya, in order to support the proposition heard at the beginning of the passage—"By which the unheard becomes heard"—the ether (*viyat*), though not explicitly mentioned there, must nevertheless be included in the account of its origination;
how much more so, then, should the ether mentioned in the Taittirīyaka not be accepted?

As for what was said—that because space is non-different from all things in terms of place and time, it is already known along with Brahman and its effects, and therefore the proposition is not undermined—[that is refuted as follows].
Nor does this contradict the scriptural statement, "One only, without a second," because the non-distinction between Brahman and space is established, like that of milk and water.
To this, it is replied:
This "knowledge of all through one knowledge" is not to be understood according to the analogy of milk and water;

for, since examples such as clay are provided, it is understood that this "knowledge of all" is to be understood solely by way of the principle of the modification of a primal material cause (*prakṛti-vikāra*).
Furthermore, if the "knowledge of all" were conceived according to the analogy of milk and water, it would not constitute correct knowledge.
For water apprehended through the cognition of milk is not apprehended by a correct cognition;
nor is it possible for the Veda to determine its meaning through illusion, falsehood, deception, and the like, as is the case with human beings.
And this [Vedic determination] is definitive.
If the Śruti text "one only, without a second" were interpreted according to the analogy of milk and water, it would be contradicted.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that this knowledge of all through one, as well as the determination of oneness without a second, refers only to a single part of reality in relation to its own effects;

for since such a thing is possible even in the case of clay and other examples, it would not need to be presented as something unprecedented, as in: "Śvetaketu, that which... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3].

"O gentle one, you are high-minded, thinking yourself well-versed in the Vedas, yet you are arrogant; have you then asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1), and so forth.

Therefore, it should be understood that this knowledge of everything is indeed concerned with all things without exception, and is presented with reference to the fact that everything is an effect of Brahman. // 6 //
As for what was further stated— that the scriptural mention of the origin of the group [of elements] is figurative because it is impossible—
we reply: "But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the world" (BBs 2.3.7).
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of impossibility.
Indeed, one should not entertain a suspicion of impossibility regarding the production of space;

for whatever variety of modifications is seen—whether it be jars, pots, and water-drawing buckets, or bracelets, armlets, and earrings, or needles, arrows, and swords—all that is observed in the world is merely a differentiation [of space].
Nothing unmodified is ever perceived as distinct from anything else;
yet the distinction of space from earth and the other elements is understood. Therefore, space too must be a modification.
By this, the fact that space, time, the internal organ (*manas*), atoms, and so forth are effects is explained.
[Objection: But since the Self (*ātman*) is also distinct from ether and the other elements, it too would follow—like a jar or similar objects—that it is an effect. [Reply: No;
for there is the scriptural statement: "From the Self, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).

For if the Self were also a modification, then since nothing else beyond it has been heard of in scripture, all effects such as space and the rest would be devoid of a Self if the Self were itself an effect;
and in that case, the doctrine of nihilism (śūnyavāda) would follow.
Furthermore, because it is the Self, the suspicion of its being negated is untenable.
For the self is not adventitious to anyone,
because it is established by itself;
indeed, the self is not established by depending upon a means of valid cognition.
For it is for the sake of establishing objects of knowledge not yet established that means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, are employed.
Indeed, no one accepts that categories of entities such as space are self-established or independent of means of valid cognition.
The self, however, being the substratum for the operation of the means of valid cognition and so forth, is established even prior to that operation of the means of valid cognition and the like.
If such [an entity] cannot be refuted,
it is because it is an adventitious thing that is refuted, not its own nature;
for that which is the refuter is itself the very nature of that [refuted thing].

For the heat of fire is not negated by the fire itself. Likewise, [one thinks]: "I myself now know the present object; I myself knew the past and the more distant past; and I myself shall know the future and the more distant future. Thus, although the object of knowledge changes its state according to the conditions of past, future, and present, there is no change in the nature of the knower when it is non-existent [as a separate entity].
Because it always possesses the nature of being present,
even when the body is reduced to ashes, it is impossible to conceive either the annihilation of the self or a change in its nature from its present state.
Thus, precisely because its nature is irrefutable, the self is non-produced (*akārya*), whereas space (*ākāśa*) is produced (*kārya*).

As for what was stated—that there exists no multiple causal substance of the same genus for space—that is answered as follows: first of all, there is no rule that [an effect] must originate only from substances of the same genus and not from those of different genera;
for it is not the case that the threads and their conjunctions possess the same genus.
This is because [the opponent] accepts [them as] substances and qualities.
Furthermore, there is no rule that even instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), such as the shuttle and the loom, must belong to the same genus.
This might be so.
The admission of homogeneity applies only to the case of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and not to other types of causes;
however, that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For it is observed that a single rope is being produced from various heterogeneous materials, such as threads, cow-hair, and fibers.
Likewise, they weave variegated woolen blankets from threads, wool, and so forth; furthermore,
if "belonging to the same genus" were postulated with respect to the substantiality of being a sentient being (*sattva*) and so on, such a restriction would be purposeless,
because everything would be of the same genus as everything else.
Nor is there a fixed rule that [a substance] initiates action only as a plurality and never as a single unit;
for it is accepted that the first motion of atoms and the mind is initiated [by them alone].
Indeed, it is maintained that each individual atom and the mind initiate action, and not by combining with other substances.
If it is argued that there is a rule that only a substance can initiate [another] substance and that this initiation must involve multiple [causes], we say no;
for we accept the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
This rule would hold if one were to maintain that a substance, assisted by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), is the initiator of another distinct substance.
That very substance, however, undergoing a different state characterized by specific qualities, is accepted as being called an "effect.

And that [substance] transforms in some cases into many things, such as clay, seeds, and so forth, into the form of sprouts and the like; in other cases, it transforms as a single thing, such as milk and the like, into the form of curds and the like.
There is no decree of a Lord that a single cause produces only a single effect;
therefore, on the authority of the Śruti, it is determined that the world was born from the one Brahman through the sequence of the production of the great elements, beginning with ether.
Thus it has been said: "If it be argued that [Brahman] cannot be the cause because we see [the need for] an assemblage [of instruments], we say no, for it is like milk" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.14).
As for what was said— that regarding the origination of space, no distinction between the prior and subsequent times can be conceived—

that is incorrect. For by that very distinction by which space, being differentiated from earth and the other elements, is now determined to possess its own nature, it is understood that that same distinction did not exist prior to its origination.

And just as Brahman does not possess a nature characterized by grossness and other qualities such as those of earth and the rest, according to scriptural passages such as, "It is neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
Thus, even by virtue of its nature as space (*ākāśa*), it is understood from scripture that space is not "non-space" in the sense of lacking an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, it is established that prior to creation there was no space.
As for what was also stated—that space is unproduced because it differs in character from earth and the other elements—[that too is refuted].
That too is incorrect;
for when there is a contradiction with scripture, an inference based on the impossibility of origination is shown to be fallacious,
and an inference regarding origination has already been demonstrated.
Furthermore, such formal arguments as "space is impermanent because it is the substratum of impermanent qualities, like a jar," and so forth, are possible.
If it is argued that [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to the self (ātman), we say no;
for from the perspective of the follower of the Upaniṣads (aupaniṣada), it is not established that the self is the substratum of impermanent qualities.
Furthermore, qualities such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and so forth are unestablished for one who maintains that space (*ākāśa*) has an origin.

As for what was stated, "and because of this word," therein the scriptural mention of immortality (*amṛtatva*) should be understood in the same way as the expression, "the gods are immortal in the sky" (*viyati amṛtā divaukasaḥ*).

Because the origination and dissolution [of the world] have already been established, the comparison with space in the statement "and he is all-pervading and eternal like space" is made for the sake of indicating unsurpassed greatness by means of space, which is well-known for its vastness, not for the sake of asserting equality with space.
It is just as when it is said, "the sun runs like an arrow," this is stated for the sake of expressing its swift motion, not because its motion is equal to that of an arrow; so it is here.
By this, the scriptural statement regarding its infinity is explained.
Furthermore, from such scriptural passages as "greater than space" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8), it is established that Brahman possesses a magnitude greater than that of space.
Also: "There is no likeness of Him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.19).
Thus, it demonstrates that Brahman is incomparable; and by the statement, "That which is other than this is afflicted" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2),
it demonstrates that all things other than Brahman, such as space and the rest, are subject to affliction.

The argument that the scriptural mention of the birth of ether (*ākāśa*) is figurative—just as the term "Brahman" is used figuratively for asceticism (*tapas*)—has been refuted by both the direct scriptural statement regarding the origin of ether and by inference.
Therefore, it is established that ether is an effect of Brahman. // 7 // [FN:
By other substances acting as inherent causes.]
The distinction is that [air] has sound as its substratum.
Section on Air (Mātariśvādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 8: By this, air is explained. BBs 2.3.8.
This is an extended application (*atideśa*).
By this same explanation regarding space (*viyat*), the wind (*mātariśvan*)—the air which has space as its substratum—is also explained.
In that case as well, these same positions should be formulated according to their respective applicability.
One position is that air does not originate, because it is not mentioned in the section on origination in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
however, there is another position, namely that there is a mention of its origination in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad in the section on origination: "From space, air" (Tai. 2.1).
Furthermore, when there is a conflict between two scriptural passages (*śruti*), another interpretation holds that the scriptural statement regarding the origin of air is figurative (*gauṇī*),
because its literal impossibility is established by the prohibition of its setting, as in: "This deity, namely air, never sets" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.22).
Furthermore, because of scriptural statements regarding immortality and so forth,

and because the initial proposition (pratijñā) would otherwise be contradicted, as well as because division is admitted for everything that is a product, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that air is produced.
The denial of its setting (astamaya) pertains to the sphere of lower knowledge (aparavidyā) and is relative.
Because, as in the case of fire and other elements, there is no setting (dissolution) for the wind.
Furthermore, there is the scriptural hearing of immortality and so forth as a counter-argument.

Now, one might object: since air and space are similar in that one is heard and the other is not heard within the same context of origination, let a single adhikaraṇa (topic) apply to both subjects; what is the purpose of this extension (atideśa) when there is no difference?
It is said in reply: This is indeed true.
Nevertheless, this extension (atideśa) is made for the purpose of removing doubts based on mere words among those of dull intellect.

For in the Saṃvarga-vidyā and other such contexts, because Vāyu is heard of as being highly exalted as an object of meditation, and because of the prohibition of his setting [at night], some might entertain a doubt regarding his eternity. // 8 //
3. The Section on Non-origination (Asambhavādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 9:
"But non-origination [is established] because it is impossible for that which exists.

Having heard of the origination even of ether and air, whose birth was previously considered impossible, the thought might occur to someone that Brahman also might have originated from something else.

Likewise, having heard that subsequent modifications such as ether and the rest arise precisely from other modifications, someone might think that even ether arises from Brahman, which is itself a modification.
To dispel this doubt, this Sūtra states: "But there is no possibility [of origination].
Indeed, one should not suspect the origination or birth of Brahman, whose nature is Being (sat), from anything else whatsoever.
Why?
Because it is untenable;
for Brahman is pure existence alone.
Its production cannot arise from Being-in-general alone,
because in the absence of some excellence (atiśaya), the relationship between material cause and modification is untenable;
nor can it arise from a particular Being, because that would contradict what is observed.
For particular effects are seen arising from a general cause—such as jars and the like from clay and so forth—but a general cause does not arise from particulars.
Nor can it arise from what is non-existent, because that which is non-existent lacks any essential nature;
as it is said: "How could the existent be born from the non-existent? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2).
This is because such an objection is heard [in scripture];

and furthermore, the passage, "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9), precludes the existence of a progenitor for Brahman.
Furthermore, the re-emergence of ether and air has been demonstrated, but such re-emergence does not exist for Brahman; thus there is a distinction.

Nor can it be argued that because the production of one modification from another modification is observed, Brahman must also be a modification, for if a primal material cause (mūlaprakṛti) were not admitted, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (anavasthā).
That which is admitted as the primal material cause is precisely what we call Brahman; therefore, there is no contradiction. // 9 //
4. The Section on Fire (Tejo 'dhikaraṇa). Sūtra 10: "Fire [originates] from that, for so it says.
(BBs 2.3.10) In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, it is taught that fire has Being (sat) as its root.

In the Taittirīyaka, however, there is the statement that air is the source; thus, since there is a conflict between scriptural passages regarding the origin of fire, the initial position reached is that fire has Brahman as its source.
Why?

Because of the teaching beginning with "Existence alone" and continuing with "It created fire," and because the promise of the knowledge of all is possible only if everything originates from Brahman— as expressed in the phrase "From that, born, by that,
sustained" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

This is because of the scriptural statement of non-distinction, and because another scripture, beginning with "From this, the vital breath is born" (Muṇḍaka 2.1.3), teaches that everything without distinction is born from Brahman;
and also because in the Taittirīyaka, [it says]: "He, having performed austerity..."
"It created all this, whatever exists here" (Tai.
3.6.1), because of this hearing of the statement without qualification.
Therefore, the teaching regarding the sequence in the phrase "from air, fire" should be understood as meaning that fire was produced immediately after air.
This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "Light is born from Mātariśvan (air).
Why?
For it has been said: "From air, fire.
If fire were produced directly from Brahman, or if its production from air did not exist, this scriptural statement, "From air, fire," would be rendered meaningless.
Now, it was argued that this [scripture] must be for the purpose of indicating sequence.

We say: no; because in the preceding passage, "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), the Self is designated as the source of origin by means of the fifth case ending, and because it is that very act of originating which is under discussion here.

Furthermore, since the ablative case is seen in the sense of "origin" in the subsequent passage, "From earth, the herbs" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.1.1), it is understood that in the phrase "From air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*), this too is indeed the ablative case signifying origin. Moreover, while the connection of the word-meaning would have to be postulated as "fire was produced above the air," the connection of the grammatical relation (*kāraka*)— namely, "fire was produced from the air"— is already established.
Therefore, this scriptural passage establishes that fire has air as its source.
But is it not the case that another scriptural passage also establishes that fire has Brahman as its source, namely, "It created fire"? No;
for there is no contradiction even if [fire] is produced through a succession [of causes].
For even when it is conceived that, having created space and air, Brahman— having assumed the state of air— created fire, even then the fact that fire is born from Brahman is not contradicted;
just as in the case of [the statements] "curd is born from her," "buttermilk is born from her," and so forth.
And scripture shows that Brahman exists in the form of its own modification: "It made itself its own self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1).

Likewise, there is a traditional teaching (smaraṇa) concerning the Lord: following the sequence beginning with "Intellect, knowledge, non-delusion" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.4), it says, "The various states of beings arise from Me alone" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.5).

Although cognitions and so forth are seen to arise directly from their own causes, nevertheless, because the entire range of existing things— whether directly or through a mediated process— is dependent upon the lineage of the Lord,
by this [argument] those scriptural passages that speak of a non-sequential creation are explained;
for they are established in every respect.

However, for those who maintain that creation occurs sequentially, [the objection] is otherwise untenable. Furthermore, the proposition (*pratijñā*) requires only that [the world] belong to the same lineage as the Existent (*sat*), not that it be produced immediately [therefrom]; thus, there is no contradiction. [Note:
*Kadarthitā* means "afflicted," "harassed," or "sublated."]
"In that context" means in the context of "origination.
The meaning is that the heated milk of that cow is the direct effect (*sākṣātkārya*), whereas curd and so forth are produced through a succession of stages (*pāramparyaja*).
*Āmikṣā* is thickened milk mixed with curd.
[The term] *praṇāḍyā* means by way of a succession. 5. Topic on the *avadhi*. Sūtra 11.
Water. The phrase "therefore, for thus he said" is understood to carry over.
Therefore, water is born from fire.
Why?
Because it is said: "He created those waters" and "From fire, water"; there is no doubt regarding these statements.
However, having explained the creation of fire, [the author], intending to explain earth, composed the aphorism "water" (*āpaḥ*) so that he would not bypass water. // 11 //
6. The Section Concerning Earth. Sūtra 12:
Earth [is the subject] because of the context, form, and other words.
"Those waters thought: 'May we become many, may we procreate. They created food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.4).
Thus it is heard in scripture.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt: is by this word "food" (anna) rice, barley, and other such edibles like boiled rice that are to be consumed meant, or rather, is the earth meant?
On this point, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that rice, barley, boiled rice, and so forth should be understood.
For the word "food" (anna) is well-known in common usage as referring to that; the remainder of the passage also confirms this meaning:
"Therefore, wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant.
Indeed, it is rice, barley, and so forth that become abundant when it rains, not the earth itself.
This being the case, we reply: it is the earth itself that is intended by the word "food" as that which is produced from water.
Why?
Because of the context, because of the characteristic form, and because of another scriptural statement.
First, regarding the context: the passage "It emitted heat" and "It emitted water" concerns the great elements (mahābhūtas).
In that context, it is not reasonable to bypass the earth element—which follows in the sequence—and suddenly adopt rice and other such things [as the referent].
Likewise, the form mentioned in the supplementary portion of the text is seen to be consistent with the earth: "That which is black belongs to food."
For there is no rule that food such as boiled rice must be black,
nor is there such a rule for rice seeds and the like.
But surely even for earth there is no rule of blackness, since fields are seen to be white as milk and red as charcoal?
This is not a fault,
because it depends on what is predominant;
for the color of earth is mostly black, whereas its white and red colors are not so prevalent.
The authors of the Purāṇas also teach that the night is the shadow of the earth;
and since that [shadow] appears black, it follows that the form of the earth is black.
Furthermore, another scriptural passage of equal authority states: "From water, the earth."
And [the scripture says]: "That which was the solid mass of the waters condensed, that became the earth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.2).
Furthermore, it shows the production of rice and other crops from the earth: "From the earth, plants; from plants, food.
Since there are such passages establishing the earth as the subject matter and so forth, how can rice and other such things be understood [as the primary source]?
Even common usage is set aside by considerations such as the context of the subject matter (*adhikāra*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*)—by stating that food is "earthy" (*pārthivatva*)—indicates through that very fact that the earth alone originates from water.
Therefore, this word "food" refers to the earth. // 12 //

FN: At that time, during the process of creation, that which was the solidification of the waters—like the thickening of curdled milk—was indeed struck together; it became a firm mass. 7. This is the section concerning the contemplation of that [earth]. Sūtra 13:
But by the contemplation of that alone [the earth arises], because of its characteristic mark. (BBs 2.3.13)

Is it that these elements, beginning with space (*viyat*), create their own transformations by themselves, or rather that the Supreme Lord alone, abiding in those respective forms and intending [to create], creates each transformation? When this doubt arises, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they create by themselves. Why? Because...
Because of scriptural statements regarding their independence, such as "From space comes air; from air, fire," and so forth.
[Objection: But the independent activity of insentient things has been refuted.
[Reply: This is not a fault.
"And because of the scriptural hearing of consciousness even in the elements, in the passage: 'That fire thought; those waters thought' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.4).
This being the position reached, it is replied: It is that very Supreme Lord who, abiding in various forms and intending [to create], produces each respective modification.
Why?
Because of its characteristic marks (*liṅga*).

For thus says the scripture: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3).
Thus, this kind of passage shows that the activity of the elements occurs only when they possess a presiding intelligence.

Likewise, having introduced [the topic] with "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" [it continues]: "It became the existent and the non-existent; It made itself by itself" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1).
And thus [the text] shows that he alone possesses the nature of all things.

As for the seeing and hearing of water and fire, these must be understood as occurring solely through the influence of the penetration (*āveśa*) of the Supreme Lord, because of the prohibition of any other seer in the passage: "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).

And because the Existent who is the Seer is the subject under discussion in the passage, "It thought: May I be many, may I grow forth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3). [This concludes] the section on the reversal [of the argument], Sūtra 14. *Note:

The connection is the entry of the Supreme Lord into beings by way of being their inner controller (antaryāmin); it is by virtue of this that perception and hearing are attributed to beings. However, this does not imply that they possess consciousness or independence.* 8. The Section on Reversal (Viparyayādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 14.
But by the reverse order, the sequence is established;
for the sequence of the arising of the elements has been considered,
and now the sequence of their dissolution is considered.
Is this dissolution through an indefinite order, or through the order of origination, or perhaps the reverse?
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that the three—origination, subsistence, and dissolution—of all beings are dependent upon Brahman: "From which indeed these beings are born;
by which, once born, they live; and into which they enter when they depart" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
In this regard, the initial position is that there is no fixed rule, because there is no specific distinction;
or rather, since the sequence of origination is explicitly stated in scripture, that same sequence should apply to dissolution as well, for dissolution likewise requires a sequence.
Having reached this conclusion, we reply: on the contrary, the sequence of dissolution must be the reverse of the sequence of origination.
For it is observed in the world that one descends by the reverse order of the same sequence by which one ascended a staircase.

Moreover, it is seen that a jar, a bowl, or other such objects born from clay return to the state of clay at the time of their dissolution; and things born from water, such as frost and hailstones, likewise return to the state of water. Therefore, this [doctrine] is logically established.

It should be understood that when the earth, having arisen from water, passes beyond its period of duration, it dissolves into water; and when water, having arisen from fire, dissolves, it dissolves into fire.
In this manner, having dissolved each successive cause—becoming progressively subtler and subtler—the entire collection of effects dissolves into Brahman, the ultimate cause and the supremely subtle.
For it is not logical for an effect to dissolve into the cause of its cause by bypassing its own immediate cause.

Even in the *Smṛti*, the order of dissolution is shown in various places to be exactly the reverse of the order of origination—as in such passages as: "O divine sage, the earth, the foundation of the world, dissolves into water; water dissolves into light; light dissolves into air.
However, the order of origination, because it is heard [in scripture] only in relation to origination itself, cannot apply to dissolution.
Nor is that [cause] expected to perish due to its unsuitability;
for while the effect persists, the perishing of the cause is not logical, because it is impossible for the effect to remain once the cause has perished.
However, the persistence of the cause when the effect perishes is logical, as this is observed in the case of clay and other such materials. // 14 //

FN: "In succession" means by way of a continuous sequence. 9. The section concerning intermediate consciousness. Sūtra 15: If it be argued that consciousness and mind exist in succession because there are signs of them [in the interval], we say no, because there is no distinction [between them]. BBs 2.3.15.
It has been stated that the origination and dissolution of the elements occur through the direct and reverse orders respectively;
it has also been stated that origination begins with the Self and dissolution ends with the Self.
Furthermore, the existence of the mind together with the senses and of the intellect is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.
This is known from such indicative marks as: "Know the intellect to be the charioteer, and the mind indeed as the reins; they call the senses the horses" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.3).
Furthermore, the sequential origination and dissolution of those two must also be included within some intermediate stage,
because it is accepted that the entire aggregate of entities originates from Brahman.
Moreover, in the section on origination in the Atharvaṇa [Upaniṣad], the organs are enumerated between the elements and the Self.
If it is argued that this [statement], "From this are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs;

ether, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3), results in the subversion of the previously stated order of the origination and dissolution of the elements, we say: no.
Because there is no distinction.

If the instruments (karaṇas) are indeed composed of the elements (bhautika), then their production and dissolution occur precisely through the production and dissolution of the elements; thus, no other sequence need be sought for these two.
Furthermore, there exists evidence that the instruments are elemental in nature.
"Mind, my dear, consists of food; breath is the essence of herbs; speech is the essence of fire"—such passages as these [should be understood accordingly].
Furthermore, the occasional mention of the elements and the organs together must be interpreted according to the maxim of the "Brahmins and the wandering mendicants" (brāhmaṇaparivrājaka-nyāya).

But even if the instruments (karaṇas) are non-material (abhautika), nevertheless the order of the origin of the elements (bhūtas) is not differentiated by the instruments— namely, that the instruments arise first and the elements last,
or that the elements arise first and the instruments last.
In the Atharvaṇa, however, there is merely a traditional sequence (samāmnāya-krama) of the instruments and the elements.
The stage of origination (*utpatti-krama*) is not taught there;

likewise, elsewhere as well, the sequence of the instruments (*karaṇa-krama*) is handed down separately from the sequence of the elements (*bhūta-krama*), beginning with: "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this [world]. He looked upon himself. He created the mind (*manas*). That was indeed the mind. It looked upon itself. It created speech (*vāk*)," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the sequence of the arising of the elements. (15) [FN:
Words that have another meaning are called "lingas. Prior to this gross [creation], Prajāpati existed as the Sūtrātman.]

10. The Section Concerning the Dependence on the Moving and the Non-moving. Sūtra 16: But the designation [of birth and death] with respect to the moving and the non-moving must be figurative, because it occurs when that [the body] exists.
(BBs 2.3.16) Birth and dissolution also belong to the individual soul (jīva).

Someone might have the misconception that the individual soul (jīva) undergoes birth and dissolution, based on common worldly designations such as "Devadatta is born" or "Devadatta has died," and because of the injunctions for sacramental rites (saṃskāra) such as the birth-ceremony (jātakarman). To dispel that [misconception], we state: there is no birth or dissolution of the soul, because the connection between the scripture and its fruit is logically established [only if the soul is eternal].

For if the individual soul (*jīva*) were to perish along with the body, then the injunctions and prohibitions intended for the attainment of the desirable and the avoidance of the undesirable by one who has reached the end of the body would be purposeless.
Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "Verily, this [body] dies when abandoned by the *jīva*; the *jīva* does not die" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.11.3).
But was it not shown that the worldly designation of birth and death applies to the *jīva*?
It is true that [birth and death] have been shown;
however, this designation of birth and death for the individual soul (jīva) is figurative (bhākta).
But what is the basis for this primary [usage], in relation to which this [usage regarding the soul] is figurative?
It is said: "Based on the moving and the non-moving.
The words "birth" and "death" have as their objects the bodies of the stationary and the moving.

For since living beings—both stationary and moving—are born and die, the words "birth" and "death," being primary with respect to those [bodies], are applied metaphorically to the individual self (jīvātman) residing within them.
Because it exists only when that [body] exists;
for the terms "birth" and "death" apply only when there is the manifestation and disappearance of a body, not when there is none.
Indeed, apart from connection with a body, no one perceives the living being as being born or dead.

Furthermore, the passage, "This person, indeed, when being born, attains a body; when departing, he dies" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.8), shows that the words "birth" and "death" have as their cause only the conjunction with and separation from the body.
Even the injunctions for birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and so forth should be understood as referring solely to the manifestation of the body.
Because there is no manifestation of a living being (*jīva*).
Whether or not the birth of a living being from the Supreme Self exists—just as [the birth] of ether and so forth does—he will explain this in the subsequent Sūtra.
By this present Sūtra, he has stated that the gross birth and dissolution of a living being, which depend upon a body, do not exist. 16. @----------------------

FN: "Deprived of life" means this body has been abandoned by the living principle (jīva). 11. The Soul is the Substratum. Sūtra 17: The Self [is eternal], because of scripture and because of its eternity according to those [scriptures]. BBs 2.3.17.
There exists a self called the *jīva*, the presiding lord over the cage of the body and senses, who is connected to the fruits of action.

Regarding this self, there is a point of doubt due to conflicting scriptural statements (*śrutivipratipatti*): does it arise from Brahman like sparks from fire and so forth, or does it not arise at all, just like Brahman itself?
In certain scriptural passages, the arising of the individual self (*jīvātman*) from the supreme Brahman is recorded through illustrations such as sparks from a fire.

In some [passages], it is understood that the individual soul (jīva) is merely the Supreme Brahman, which is unmodified, assuming the state of a soul by entering into its effects; its origination is not taught [there].
In this regard, the initial position reached is that the soul is indeed produced.
Why?
Precisely because of the non-contradiction of the proposition:
"When one is known, all this is known. This proposition would not be contradicted if the entire range of entities originates from Brahman;
however, if the individual soul were a different reality, this proposition would be contradicted.
Nor can it be understood that the unmodified Supreme Self alone is the individual soul (jīva), because of the difference in their characteristics;
for the Supreme Self possesses attributes such as being free from sin and so forth.
For the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the opposite of that [Brahman].
Furthermore, its status as a modification (vikāra) is established by its being divided;
for whatever is divided, such as space and so forth, all that is a modification, and the origination of that space and so forth has been understood.

The individual soul (jīvātman) as well, being endowed with meritorious and non-meritorious karma and possessed of pleasure and pain, is distinct in each body; therefore, its origination must also occur at the time of the creation of the phenomenal world (prapañca).

Furthermore, after teaching the creation of the objects of enjoyment such as the vital breaths (prāṇa) in the passage, "Just as small sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all the vital breaths [fly forth]," the text teaches the separate creation of the individual souls who are the enjoyers in the words, "All these very selves fly forth."

And [the scripture] states the origination and dissolution of the individual selves (*jīvātman*): "Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks of the same nature fly forth by the thousands, even so, O gentle one, various beings are born from the Imperishable (*akṣara*) and into it they also merge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1).
Because of the statement regarding "having the same form," for the individual selves indeed possess the same form as the supreme self due to their connection with consciousness;
and the non-mention of something in one place cannot preclude what has been heard elsewhere.
Since even additional points found in other scriptural passages that are not contradictory must be integrated everywhere,
the scriptural text concerning "entering" must likewise be explained as referring to the attainment of the state of being a modification (vikāra),
just as in the passage, "He made himself his own self," and so forth.
"Therefore, the living being (jīva) is produced.
This being the position reached, we reply: the self, the living being, is not produced.
Why?
Because it is not heard.
For there is no mention of this [breath] in the section concerning its origin in many places.
But was it not said that the non-mention of something in one place does not preclude its being mentioned elsewhere?
True, it has been said;
however, we maintain that its very arising is impossible.
Why?
And because of its eternity, and from those [scriptural passages]—
the word "and" implying also because of its unbornness and so forth.

For its eternity is understood from the Śruti texts, as well as its being unborn, its immutability, and the fact that it exists as the individual soul (jīvātman) while remaining unmodified Brahman itself, and as existing with Brahman as its self.
And the arising of such a nature is not tenable.
What are those scriptural passages?
"The living being does not die" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.11.3).
"Verily, this great unborn Self is ageless, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22);
"The wise one is neither born nor does he die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18);
"Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient is this [Self]" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18).
"Having created that, He entered into it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1);
"Entering by means of this living self, let me manifest names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2);
"This very one has entered here, even to the tips of the fingernails" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).
"Thou art That" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7),
"I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10),
and "This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
Thus, these and other such passages asserting eternity preclude the production of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Now, it was argued that because it is divided, it is a modification (*vikāra*), and because it is a modification, it is produced.
To this it is replied: its division does not exist inherently (*svataḥ*).
This is according to the Śruti: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).

However, His appearance as divided is caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect (buddhi), just as the appearance of space is divided due to its connection with jars and other objects.

And so says the Śāstra: "That very Self here is Brahman—consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, and consisting of hearing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5).
This and other such passages demonstrate that even though Brahman alone exists as the one, unchanging reality, it appears as consisting of the manifold—such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.

This "consisting of that" (*tanmayatvam*) should be understood as its nature being colored by those [attributes] due to the non-manifestation of its distinct essential form, just as in the expression "the fool consists of women" (*strīmayo jālmaḥ*).

Furthermore, whatever scriptural mention there may be of its origination and dissolution in certain places, that too must be interpreted as resulting precisely from its connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Its arising occurs through the arising of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and its dissolution occurs through their dissolution.
Thus it is shown: "Being a mass of pure consciousness, having arisen from these elements, it perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

Likewise, this is merely the dissolution of the limiting adjuncts and not the dissolution of the Self; this too is stated in this very same passage: "Venerable sir, do not lead me into the depths of delusion... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14).
Or, [the text] establishes this through a series of questions: "Or rather, I know this: there is no consciousness after death," to which it replies:

"Indeed, I do not speak delusion; for this Self, O Maitreyī, is indestructible and of a nature that does not perish; however, its association with the elements (mātrās) occurs" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14).
There is no contradiction of the initial proposition either, because it is precisely Brahman, in its unmodified state, that is admitted to exist in the condition of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Furthermore, the difference in characteristics between these two is caused solely by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
As it is said: "Henceforth, speak only for the sake of liberation" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15).

And because, by means of the rejection of all transmigratory attributes, it is the very self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) under discussion that is established as having the nature of the supreme Self;
therefore, the Self is neither produced nor dissolved. (17) [FN:
*uparodha* means sublation.]
The word *sarūpa* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*); this is the remainder [of the sense].
A *jālma* is one who is dull-witted due to desire;
he is designated as being dependent on women and consisting of women.

Having arisen—that is, having been produced—by way of equilibrium from these elements that have transformed into the form of the body, [the self] perishes subsequently, following after those very elements as they dissolve.
"Moha" means a statement that causes delusion.
(Jñādhikaraṇa, Sūtra 18)
"From this very fact, [the self] is a knower.

(BBs 2.3.18) Regarding this, there is doubt due to the conflicting views of the disputants: is it like that of the followers of Kaṇāda, such that consciousness is adventitious and the self is inherently insentient; or is it like that of the Sāṃkhyas, such that its very nature is eternal consciousness?
What, then, is the prima facie position?
It follows that the consciousness of the self is adventitious, produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind, like the quality of heat produced by the conjunction of fire and a jar.
For if consciousness were eternal, then even those who are asleep, unconscious, or possessed by spirits would possess consciousness.
Yet, when questioned, they declare, "We were not conscious of anything," and they are seen to be conscious only when they have recovered their normal state.
Therefore, because consciousness occurs only occasionally, the self (ātman) possesses adventitious consciousness.

This being the position reached, it is replied: this self is a knower and possesses eternal consciousness for that very reason, since it is not produced; rather, it is the supreme Brahman itself which, through contact with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), exists in the state of a living soul (jīva).
For the Supreme Brahman is traditionally taught to have consciousness as its very nature: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28),
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and "Without interior or exterior, entirely a mass of pure consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

In such scriptural passages as these, it is understood that if the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed that supreme Brahman, then the soul’s nature is also eternally conscious, just like the heat and light of fire.

Furthermore, there are scriptural texts in the section concerning the "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), such as: "Though asleep, he gazes upon those who sleep" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.11).
"Here this person becomes his own light" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9),
and "For there is no departure of the knower from its nature as a knower" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30)—
such are the [scriptural passages].

Furthermore, from the statement, "Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.4), its nature as such is established because it synthesizes through the cognition, "I know this, I know this," by means of all the instruments [of perception].
If it is argued that if the Self were eternal consciousness by nature, the sense organs such as the nose would be useless, we say: no.
This is because [the senses] have the purpose of discerning specific objects such as odors and so forth;
for thus the scripture shows: "The nose is for the sake of odor," and so on.
As for the objection that those who are asleep and the like do not perceive, the refutation of that has already been stated by the scripture itself.

Concerning deep sleep, [the scripture] states: "Verily, when there he does not see, yet he is indeed seeing, though he does not see; for there is no loss of the seer's power of seeing, because of its imperishability. But there is then no second thing, nothing else separate from him, that he might see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23), and so forth.
What is meant by this is that this state of being non-conscious arises from the absence of objects, and not from the absence of consciousness itself.
Just as light, which has space as its locus, is unmanifest due to the absence of objects to be illuminated and not due to an absence of its own nature, so it is in this case.
Furthermore, the reasoning of the Vaiśeṣikas and others becomes fallacious when it contradicts the Śruti.
Therefore, we conclude that the Self is indeed of the nature of eternal consciousness. // 18 //
FN: The Self, being itself never asleep and appearing as luminous, looks upon—that is, beholds—the sleeping speech and other organs whose activities have ceased.
"Determination" (pariccheda) refers to a mental modification (vṛtti). "For the sake of smell" means for the sake of the internal organ's modification directed toward that object.
13. The Section on Departure and Movement (Utkrānti-gati-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 19–32:
Concerning Departure, Movement, and Return.
BBs 2.3.19: Now, however, it is considered what the size of the individual soul (jīva) is.
Is it of atomic dimension, or of intermediate dimension, or perhaps of great dimension?
But has it not been stated that the self is not produced and is eternal consciousness?
Therefore, it follows that the supreme self itself is the living being (jīva).
Furthermore, it is taught in scripture that the Supreme Self is non-different from the individual self; how then can there be any occasion for considering the size of the individual soul?
It is replied: this is true.
However, the scriptural passages concerning the soul's departure [from the body], its movement [to another world], and its journey through the veins imply its limited nature;
moreover, its atomic dimension is directly stated by its own specific term in certain places.
This present undertaking is begun in order to establish that all of this is free from contradiction.
In this regard, it is first established that the individual soul (*jīva*) is of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), because of the scriptural mention of its departure, going, and returning.
As for its departure: "When he departs from this body, he departs together with all these" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3).
Its going is also mentioned: "Whoever indeed departs from this world, they all go to the moon alone" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.2).
There is also the mention of its return: "From that world, he returns again to this world for the sake of action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.6).
Since these—departure, going, and returning—are heard [in scripture], it follows that the individual soul (jīva) must be limited;
for motion is not possible for that which is all-pervading.
And since spatial limitation has been refuted in the *Arhatparīkṣā* on the grounds that [the soul] possesses the same dimensions as the body, it follows that the self is atomic. // 19 //
And by its own nature, it is so for the latter two [stages].
Departure might be possible even for one who does not move, through the cessation of ownership of the body—just as there is the cessation of being a village headman—due to the exhaustion of karma.
However, the subsequent two, going and returning, are not possible for one who does not move.
For their connection occurs through their own selves, since the action of "going" resides in the agent;
moreover, going and returning are possible for that which is neither of medium nor infinite size only when it possesses atomic dimension (*aṇutva*).
And from the mention of going and coming, it is understood that "departure" (utkrānti) is indeed the same as "slipping away" (apasṛpti) from the body;
for going and coming would not be possible without first slipping away from the body.
Furthermore, this is because the regions of the body are spoken of as the point of departure (apādāna) in the act of departing.
"Either from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).
"Taking these particles of light, he descends into the heart itself" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1);
"Having taken the subtle essence, he returns again to his place" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.11).
And thus, even in the case of a subsequent body, the going and coming of the self with respect to that body occur.
Therefore, for this reason as well, its atomicity is established. (20) [FN:
Apādānatva means the state of being a limit or point of departure.]
"If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of the scriptural statement to that effect, we say no, because of the context concerning the other.
(BBs 2.3.21) Now, it might be thought: "This self is not atomic. Why?"
"Because of the scriptural statement to the contrary"; that is to say, because of the hearing of a dimension opposite to atomicity.
"Verily, this great unborn Self is that which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12).

If it is argued that scriptural passages of this kind— such as "And [the Self] is omnipresent and eternal like space" and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1)— would be contradicted if the Self were atomic; then [we reply]:
This is not a fault. Why?
Because of the context of the other.
For this scriptural mention of another dimension pertains to the Supreme Self,
because it is the Supreme Self alone that is the primary subject under discussion in the Vedāntas as that which is to be known;
and because, in various passages such as "The stainless [Self] is higher than the ether," it is specifically the Supreme Self that is the subject of those particular contexts.

But is it not the case that in the passage, "This one which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), the embodied self alone is being referred to by way of its connection with greatness?
This designation, however, should be understood as being from the perspective of the scripture's vision, like that of Vāmadeva.

Therefore, because [the soul] is the object of the wise, and because of the hearing of another measurement [of size], the atomicity of the individual soul (jīva) is contradicted. // 21 // [FN: Because of the context of the other [i.e., Brahman]; and because of its own word and its measurement. BBs_2.3.22.

For this reason also the Self is atomic, since a word directly expressing its atomicity is heard: "This atomic Self is to be known by the mind, into which the fivefold vital breath has entered" (Muṇḍaka 3.1.9). Furthermore, from its connection with the vital breaths, it is understood that this atomic being referred to is indeed the individual soul (jīva). Likewise, the measurement [of the soul] also leads to the understanding of the soul's atomic nature: "Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred parts... (Śvetāśvatara 5.9).

"The individual soul (jīva) is to be known as a part" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.8); and "for even the smallest [atom] is seen to be no larger than the tip of an awl" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.8)—this is another scriptural statement regarding its measurement. // 22 //
But surely, if [the self] were atomic, it would be contradictory for that which occupies only one location to experience sensations throughout the entire body;
yet we observe that those submerged in the waters of the Ganges experience coolness in all their limbs, and during the summer heat, experience a burning sensation throughout the whole body. (Note:
*Uddhriyamāna* means being lifted up; *unmāna* means measurement.)
"Bāla" means hair. That living being (jīva) whose measure or size is equal to the tip of a hair or the tip of an iron needle pierced by a shuttle—that is how it is.
To this, he recites the following:
There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood.

For just as a drop of yellow sandalwood, though connected to only one part of the body, produces a refreshing sensation pervading the entire body, so too the self will produce a perception that pervades the entire body from its location in a single part of the body.
Furthermore, because of its connection with the skin, sensation throughout the entire body is not contradicted;
for the connection between the skin and the self resides in the whole of the skin, and the skin pervades the entire body. // 23 //
If it is argued that [the difference arises] from a distinction in state (*avasthitivaiśeṣya*), we say no, because it is admitted [only] in the case of the heart.

Regarding this, an objection is raised: as for what was stated—that there is no contradiction, just as in the case of sandalwood—that is incorrect, because the example and the subject of the illustration are not comparable.

For the analogy of sandalwood applies only if it were established that the self resides in one part of the body. Indeed, in the case of sandalwood, its specific mode of existence is directly perceived: namely, its localization in one place and its refreshing of the entire body. In the case of the self, however, what is directly perceived is merely the perception throughout the entire body; its residence in one specific part is not perceived.
Even if it were said that "that [self] is the object of inference," inference is not possible here.

Is the sensation experienced throughout the entire body due to a self that pervades the whole body like the sense of touch? Or is it due to one that is all-pervading like space? Or rather, is it due to one that occupies a single location and is minute like a drop of sandalwood paste?
"Because doubt has not been transcended.
To this it is replied: This is not a fault.
Why?
Because it is accepted.
For it is indeed accepted that the self, like sandalwood, has a specific mode of existence consisting in residing in only one part of the body.
How so? It is explained as follows:
For this Self is taught in the Vedāntas as being in the heart:
"This Self is indeed in the heart" (Praśna 3.6); "That very Self is in the heart" (Chāndogya 8.3.3).
This is because of such teachings as: "What is the Self? It is this person consisting of consciousness, who is among the vital breaths, the light within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).

Therefore, since there is no disparity between the illustration and the thing illustrated, this [comparison] is indeed appropriate, and there is no contradiction with the example of sandalwood. // 24 //
Or [it is so] because of its quality, as in the world (guṇādvā lokavat).
Because the quality of consciousness pervades it, there is no contradiction in the fact that the individual soul (jīva), though atomic, performs an action that pervades the entire body.
Just as in the world, the light of gems, lamps, and the like, although located in only one part of a room, pervades the entire room and performs its function throughout the whole room; so it is here.

One might object: "In the case of sandalwood, because it possesses parts, it may refresh the entire body through the diffusion of its subtle parts; however, the atomic jīva has no such parts by which it could spread throughout the entire body. Anticipating this doubt, it is stated: "Or [the soul's perception of the whole body occurs] through its qualities, as in the world. (25)
Furthermore, how could a quality exist elsewhere apart from the possessor of that quality?
For the white quality of a cloth is never seen existing elsewhere apart from the cloth.
If it is argued that this might be like the case of a lamp, we say no.
For that [light] is also admitted to be a substance;
for a lamp is a fiery substance with closely packed constituent parts,
whereas radiance is simply a fiery substance with widely spaced constituent parts.
To this, he recites the following:
"There is a distinction, as in the case of odor" (BBs 2.3.26).
Just as odor, although it is a quality, exists as something distinct from the substance that possesses the odor.
Since the fragrance of flowers and other odoriferous substances is perceived even when those substances have not been reached [by the sense organ],

so too there will be a separation of the quality of consciousness from the soul (jīva), even though it is atomic. Therefore, the argument that "because it is a quality, its separation from its substratum is impossible— just like color and so forth"— is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
If it is argued that, since we observe the separation of a quality from its substrate even while the quality itself persists,
odor likewise must be separated from its substrate, we say no;
for this would entail the destruction of the substance once it has been separated from its original material basis.
Even though it is not being diminished, it is understood to remain in its prior state;
otherwise, it would be deprived of its prior qualities such as heaviness and so forth.
This might be the case.
If it is argued that although a distinction exists, it is not perceived because the parts of the odor-bases have become separated and are minute—

that subtle odor-atoms, having dispersed in all directions, produce the cognition of odor upon entering the nostrils— this is not so; for atoms are beyond the senses, and moreover, a distinct odor is clearly perceived in things such as the *nāgakesara* flower.
Furthermore, there is no common worldly recognition that "the substance possessing fragrance has been smelled";
rather, worldly people recognize that "the fragrance itself has been smelled.

If it is argued that since fragrance is not perceived as separate from its substratum in the case of visible form and other qualities, it is likewise incorrect for fragrance to be separate from its substratum, we say: no.

Because [the object] is directly perceived, inference does not apply. Therefore, whatever is seen in the world in a certain way must be accepted exactly as it is by those who investigate, and not otherwise. For one cannot establish the restriction that because the quality of taste is apprehended by the tongue, other qualities such as color and so forth must likewise be apprehended by the tongue alone. // 26 //
FN: The separation of a quality from its substance is the dissociation from its substratum.

And so he demonstrates this: having stated that the self has the heart as its abode and possesses an atomic dimension, [the scripture] says of that very same self, "From the hair to the tips of the nails" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.8.1).
Thus, by means of the quality of consciousness, he demonstrates its pervasiveness throughout the entire body. // 27 //
Because of the separate teaching [of the two].

From the statement, "Having mounted the body by means of wisdom" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.6), the self and wisdom are taught separately as agent and instrument; therefore, it is understood that the pervasiveness of this [self] throughout the body is due solely to its quality of consciousness.

Furthermore, the teaching that the consciousness of the agent is distinct from the bodily self—expressed in the passage, "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of [his own] consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17)—strengthens this very intention.
Therefore, the Self is atomic. // 28 //
FN: The meaning is that [the self] lies having taken up the cognitive power of the senses through consciousness, which is the quality of sentience.
This being the case, we reply:
"But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by them, as in the case of the Intelligent One (Prājña). (BBs 2.3.29)
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that the self is an atom;

for since no origin [of the self] is heard of, whereas the entry of the supreme Brahman itself is heard of, and because of the teaching of identity, it has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the supreme Brahman.
If the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the supreme Brahman, then the soul must be as extensive as the supreme Brahman;
and since the all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) of the supreme Brahman is declared in the scriptures,
the soul is therefore all-pervasive.

And thus, scriptural and traditional declarations concerning the all-pervasiveness of the individual soul (jīva), such as "This great unborn Self, which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), are rendered consistent. Furthermore, for an atomic soul, the experience of sensations throughout the entire body would not be possible.
If it is argued that [the sensation] would occur because of its connection with the skin, we say no;
for even upon being pricked by a thorn, it would follow that the sensation would be experienced throughout the entire body.
This is because the contact between the skin and the thorn occurs within the whole of the skin, and the skin pervades the entire body.
However, it is only when the sole of the foot is pierced by a thorn that one experiences pain;
moreover, the pervasion of an atom by its qualities is not tenable, because a quality must reside in the locus of the qualified substance.
For the very nature of a quality would be lost if it were to exist without depending upon a substratum possessing that quality.
Furthermore, the fact that the light of a lamp is a distinct substance has already been explained.
Moreover, since odor is admitted to be a quality, it must necessarily move while remaining supported by a substrate.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of losing its status as a quality (*guṇatva*).

Thus it has been said by Dvaipāyana: "If some unskilled people, perceiving fragrance in water, were to say [it belongs there], one should know that it resides in earth alone, having resorted to the water and the air."
Furthermore, if consciousness were to pervade the entire body of the individual soul, the soul would not be atomic;
for consciousness alone is its very nature, just as heat and light are the nature of fire.
Since no distinction between quality and the possessor of the quality exists here, the theory that the soul is equal in size to the body is also refuted.
By process of elimination, the individual self (jīva) is all-pervading.
If so, how is it that there are designations such as "atomic" (aṇu) and so forth? To this, he says: "But because its essence consists of the qualities of that [intellect], it is designated as such.

The qualities of that intellect are its "qualities" (tad-guṇāḥ), such as desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, and so on. That self for which these qualities constitute its "essence" (sāra)—meaning its primary factor—insofar as it is subject to transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva), is "one whose essence consists of those qualities" (tad-guṇasāra). It is of that [self]...
Existence [in this context] consists in having those qualities as its essence. For the pure Self, devoid of the qualities of the intellect (buddhi), does not possess the state of transmigratoriness.

Indeed, the state of transmigratoriness—characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth—is caused by the superimposition of attributes upon the intellect as its limiting adjunct (upādhi); it does not belong to the Self, which is actually a non-agent, a non-enjoyer, non-transmigratory, and eternally liberated.
Therefore, because its essence consists of those qualities (the buddhi), it is designated by the dimensions of that intellect;
and because of its departure and so forth, it is designated as departing and so forth, but not by itself.
And thus it is said: "Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred parts..."
"The individual soul (jīva) is to be known as a portion [of that], and it is capable of infinity" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9).
Having thus stated the atomicity (aṇutva) of the soul, the text then declares its very infinity.
And this would be consistent only if the atomicity of the soul were figurative and its infinity were ultimate (pāramārthika).
For it is not possible for both [the primary and the secondary meanings] to be primary;
nor can it be understood that infinity is merely figurative,
because in all the Upanishads it is intended to be established that Brahman is the very self of the individual.

Likewise, regarding the other measurement as well, [the scripture] teaches that even the smallest [self] is seen to be the size of the tip of an awl only through its connection with the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*), and not by its own nature, in the passage: "By the quality of the intellect and by the quality of the self, it is indeed seen to be the size of the tip of an awl" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8). Also, "This subtle self is to be known by the mind" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.9).
Thus, even here, the atomic dimension of the individual soul (jīva) is not established;
for it is the Supreme Self alone that is the subject under discussion, being characterized by its ungraspability by the eyes and other senses and its accessibility through the clarity of knowledge.
Furthermore, an actual atomic dimension is logically untenable for the individual soul as well.
Therefore, this statement regarding its atomicity should be understood as intended to convey its difficult-to-know nature, or else as referring to its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Likewise, in cases of instruction regarding difference such as "having mounted the body by means of intelligence" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.6), one should interpret it thus: the individual soul (*jīva*) mounts the body by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), which serves as its limiting adjunct.
Or it is a mere designation,
as he said, "the body of a stone statue";
for it has been stated that even the distinction between quality and qualified does not exist here.
The statement regarding the heart being its abode also refers to the intellect alone, because that is its abode.

Likewise, he shows that even the departure [from the body] and so forth are dependent on limiting adjuncts: "In whom, when I have departed, shall I have departed? Or in whom established, shall I be established? (Praśna 6.3), and "He created the vital breath" (Praśna 6.4).
