For in the absence of departure, the absence of going and coming is also understood;
indeed, going and coming could not belong to one who has not moved out from the body.
Thus, because the soul (jīva) has the qualities of its limiting adjuncts as its essence, it is designated as atomic and so forth, just like the Supreme Lord (prājña).

Just as for the wise one, the Supreme Self, there is the designation of minuteness and so forth in meditations on the qualified [Brahman] because the qualities of the limiting adjuncts constitute its essence— such as "smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3) and "consisting of mind, having breath for a body, possessing all fragrances, possessing all tastes, whose desires are true, whose resolves are true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2)— so it is in this case as well.

It might be argued: "If the transmigratory state of the Self were imagined on the grounds that its essence consists of the qualities of the intellect (buddhi), then, since the intellect and the Self are distinct, their separation must necessarily come to an end. Consequently, when there is disjunction from the intellect, the isolated Self would be imperceptible, which would entail either its non-existence or its non-transmigratory state.
To this, he recites the following reply:
"And because it is as pervasive as the self, there is no fault in seeing it.
This aforementioned fault that was just described need not be suspected.
Why? Because [it is as pervasive as the self].
Because the conjunction with the intellect persists as long as the self exists;
for as long as this self remains a transmigrating being,
and as long as its state of transmigration is not terminated by right vision (samyagdarśana), [the conjunction continues].

The conjunction of this [Self] with the intellect does not cease until that very connection with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect ceases; and as long as this connection with the limiting adjunct of the intellect persists, so long does the individual soul (jīva) possess its status as a soul and its state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāritva).
In ultimate reality, however, there is no such thing as a "soul" apart from the nature imagined through the connection with the limiting adjunct of the intellect.
Indeed, in the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta, no second conscious principle other than the Lord—who is omniscient and whose nature is eternally free—is found;

for it is said: "There is no other seer, hearer, thinker, or knower than He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23), and "There is nothing else that sees, hears, thinks, or knows apart from this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
This is known from such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.6) and "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).
How, then, is it understood that the conjunction with consciousness persists as long as the self exists?
He says: "Because that is seen.

For the scripture shows this: "This person, consisting of consciousness, who is the light within the heart among the vital breaths—he, being common to both, wanders through both worlds; he meditates, as it were, and he moves, as it were."
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.4), and so forth.
In that context, "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) means "consisting of intellect" (*buddhimaya*).

This is because, in another passage—"consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing"—the term *vijñānamaya* is recited together with the mind and the other faculties.
And its being "consisting of intelligence" (buddhimayatva) is intended precisely as having intelligence as its essential quality (tadguṇasāratva).
Just as in the world one says "Devadatta consists of women," meaning he is dominated by passion for women and so forth, so it is here.
Furthermore, the passage, "Being the same [as the intellect], he wanders through both worlds," shows that there is no separation from the intellect even when traveling to other worlds.
It is understood that it appears as if possessing intelligence because of its proximity to that very [intellect];
and this he shows by saying, "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).
This is what is meant: it does not meditate by itself.
Nor does it move;
for when the intellect is meditating, the Self seems to meditate, and when the intellect moves, it seems to move.
Furthermore, this connection of the Self with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect is preceded by false knowledge.

Furthermore, since false knowledge does not cease except through right knowledge, the connection with the limiting adjunct of the intellect (*buddhy-upādhi*) does not subside as long as the non-realization of the identity with Brahman persists.
And the scripture shows this: "I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness;
only by knowing Him does one pass over death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8). // 30 //
FN: Consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), it abounds in intellect;
having the color of the sun, it is self-luminous;
beyond darkness, it is untouched by ignorance.
"With the Existent," that is, with the Supreme Self.
But surely, one cannot admit a connection of the self with the intellect during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, as it is said:
"Then, my dear, he becomes united with the Existent; he has gone to his own" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
Because of this statement,
and because the dissolution of all modifications is admitted,
how then can it be said that the connection with the intellect persists as long as the self exists? To this, it is replied:
"But because it exists, its manifestation is possible, just like virility and so forth" (BBs 2.3.31).

Just as in the world, virility and other such qualities exist in the form of seeds during childhood and other stages, yet being unperceived they are regarded as non-existent; these qualities then manifest in youth and other stages.
They do not arise from what was previously non-existent, for if they did, it would follow that even eunuchs and the like could produce them.
In this same way, this connection with the intellect, existing indeed in the form of a potentiality during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, manifests again upon awakening and creation;
for it is only thus that this is logically consistent,
since the spontaneous origination of anything is impossible.
Because that would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].

Furthermore, the scripture demonstrates that the emergence from deep sleep is brought about by the existence of the seed consisting of ignorance, through such passages as: "Having reached the Being, they do not know that they have reached the Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2), and "These [beings] here become a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf," and so forth (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.3).
Therefore, it is established that the connection with limiting adjuncts such as intellect and the rest persists as long as the self exists. // 31 //
Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either its being eternally perceived or never perceived at all, or else a restriction to one or the other.
Furthermore, that internal organ which serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the Self is designated in various ways in different contexts as *manas*, *buddhi*, *vijñāna*, or *citta*.
And in some instances, according to the distinction of its functions, it is called *manas* when its function consists of doubt and so forth.
Buddhi is that which functions as ascertainment and so forth.
It must necessarily be admitted that such an internal organ exists;
for otherwise, if it were not admitted, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception.
If there were constant perception whenever the self, the sense organs, and the objects—the means for apprehension—are in proximity, it would follow that perception occurs eternally.
Alternatively, if the effect were absent despite the presence of the causes, it would follow that non-perception occurs eternally.
Yet, this is not what is observed.
Alternatively, an obstruction of the power of either the self or the sense organ must be admitted;
however, an obstruction of the power of the self is not possible,
because it is changeless (*avikriya*).
Nor does it belong to the sense faculty;
for if its power were unimpeded in both preceding and succeeding moments, its power could not suddenly be obstructed.
Therefore, that which experiences perception and non-perception through attention and non-attention is the mind (*manas*).

And so says the Śruti: "When my mind was elsewhere, I did not perceive; when my mind was elsewhere, I did not hear" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3); and "For it is by the mind alone that one sees, and by the mind that one hears" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).

Furthermore, it shows that desire and the rest are its modifications: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, fear—all this is indeed the mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
Therefore, this is correct:
"The designation [of the Self] is according to that, because its essence consists of those qualities. // 32 //
14. The Section on the Agent (Kartr-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 33–40: "The agent [is the Self], because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. (BBs 2.3.33).
Under the heading of "having those qualities as its essence," another attribute of the individual soul (jīva) is further elaborated.
Moreover, this individual soul (jīva) would be the agent.
Why?
Because it is the subject matter of the scripture.
And thus, injunctions such as "one should sacrifice," "one should offer oblations," and "one should give" become meaningful;
otherwise, they would be purposeless.
For such [injunctions] teach a specific duty to one who exists as an agent.
And this would not be possible if agency did not exist;
likewise, this scripture also becomes meaningful: "For he is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the agent—the Puruṣa whose nature is consciousness" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.9). // 33 //
Because of the teaching regarding its movement [vihāra].
For this reason as well, the soul possesses agency:
because in the section concerning the soul, it teaches its movement in the intermediate state, stating, "Being immortal, he goes wherever he desires" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12).
Thus [it is said], and also: "He moves about at will within his own body" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.18). [FN:
*Saṃdhye sthāne* refers to the intermediate state, the condition of dreaming; *īyate* means he goes.]
Because of appropriation (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, its status as an agent is established by the fact that, in the very process concerning the living soul (*jīva*), it mentions the appropriation of the instruments: "Having taken the cognition of these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by means of cognition" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17).

Thus [it is said], "having taken up the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.18). And: "Because of the designation regarding the action; for if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the reference. (BS 2.3.36) [The commentary on this sūtra: The construction is as follows: during deep sleep, the individual soul (jīva) goes to the heart, having taken up—by means of the intellect (vijñāna)—the "vijñāna," that is, the grasping power of the vital breaths, which are the sense organs (indriya). Furthermore, because there is a designation regarding the action [of going], if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the grammatical reference.

Furthermore, the soul possesses agency, since the scripture designates its agency in both worldly and Vedic actions: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice, and it also performs ritual acts" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1).
Now, it may be argued that the word *vijñāna* is understood to refer to the intellect (*buddhi*).
How is the agency of the individual soul (jīva) indicated by this?
It is said: "No";
for this is a designation of the soul itself, not of the intellect (buddhi).
If it were not the soul (*jīva*), there would be a reversal in the designation;
[the text] would have designated it as "by means of consciousness" (*vijñānena*).

For elsewhere, when the intention is to express the intellect (*buddhi*), the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is seen used with an instrumental case-ending, as in: "Having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of consciousness" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.1.17).

But here, because of the grammatical coreferentiality with the agent in the statement, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.5.1), the agency of the Self as distinct from the intellect is indicated; thus, there is no fault. // 36 //

To this it is said: If the living being (*jīva*), distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*), were the agent, then being independent, he would invariably accomplish what is pleasant and beneficial for himself, and not the opposite.
Yet, he is observed accomplishing even the opposite;
and such an irregular activity is not possible for an independent self.
To this, he recites the following:
"As in the case of perception, there is no restriction" (BBs 2.3.37).

Just as this self, although independent with respect to perception, perceives both the desirable and the undesirable without restriction, so too it will bring about both the desirable and the undesirable without restriction.
If it is argued that even in perception there is no independence because one perceives the appropriation of the causes of perception, we say no;
for the purpose of the causes of perception is merely the conceptualization of objects,
whereas in the act of perception itself, the self has no dependence on anything else due to its association with consciousness (*caitanya*).

Moreover, even with respect to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the self does not possess absolute independence, because it depends upon specific conditions of place, time, and causal factors (*nimitta*).
Nor does the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) cease for an agent who requires assistance;
for indeed, one who cooks remains a cook even while depending on fuel, water, and so forth.
Furthermore, due to the diversity of auxiliary causes, the soul's engagement in the performance of desired or undesired purposeful actions without restriction is not contradictory. // 37 //
Because of the reversal of capacity (śaktiviparyaya). For this reason as well, the living being (jīva) must be the agent distinct from consciousness (vijñāna).
If, on the other hand, the intellect (buddhi)—which is denoted by the term "consciousness"—were itself the agent, then a reversal of capacity would occur.

The instrumental capacity of the intellect would be lost, and it would incur the status of being an agent. And since the intellect possesses this capacity for agency, it must be admitted that the intellect itself is the object of the notion of "I," because it is observed everywhere that activity is preceded by the sense of "I."
"I go," "I come," "I eat," and "I drink"—
for that [self] which is endowed with the power of agency, another instrument must be postulated as the performer of all these actions;
for even a capable agent is seen to engage in activities only by employing an instrument.
Consequently, there would be a dispute over mere terminology, but no difference in the actual entity,
because the status of being an agent is admitted for that which is distinct from the instruments.
And because of the absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

That meditative concentration which is taught in the Vedāntas for the purpose of realizing the Self according to the Upaniṣads—namely, "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon; it is to be sought after, it is to be desired to be known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5)—[is also absent].
Furthermore, such [injunctions] as "Meditate on the Self as 'I am the Self'" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.6) would not be possible if the Self were not an agent.
Therefore, for this reason as well, its status as an agent is established. // 39 //
15. The Section on the Carpenter (Takṣādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 40:
"And as the carpenter is in both ways" (BBs 2.3.40).
Thus far, agency has been demonstrated for the embodied soul by means of reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures.
Furthermore, it is considered whether that agency is innate or caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
In this regard, by these very reasons—such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures—it is argued that agency is innate because there is no cause for its negation.
This being the position reached, we reply:
Intrinsic agency of the self is not possible,
because it would entail the consequence of no liberation;
for if agency were the very nature of the self, liberation from that agency would be impossible.
It is like heat from fire.
Furthermore, for one who is not liberated from agency, there is no accomplishment of the human goal (puruṣārtha),
because agency is of the nature of suffering.
[Objection: Even though the power of agency remains present, the human goal will be accomplished by avoiding the activity of agency;
and that avoidance results from avoiding the instrumental causes, just as fire, despite possessing the power of burning, lacks the effect of burning when separated from wood. [Reply: No.
For it is impossible to completely avoid even the signs (nimitta), since they are connected by a relationship characterized as "power" (śakti).
[Objection: But surely liberation will be accomplished through the prescription of the means for liberation. [Reply: No; because that which depends on a means is impermanent.
Furthermore, the attainment of liberation is intended through the teaching of the Self as eternally pure, enlightened, and free;
and such a teaching of the Self would not be possible if agency were inherent to it.
Therefore, the agency of the Self arises solely through the superimposition of the attributes of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and is not inherent.
And thus says the Śruti: "It meditates, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7);
and "The wise say that the Self, when joined with the body, senses, and mind, is the enjoyer" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.4).
These passages demonstrate that the Self acquires specific attributes such as being an enjoyer only when associated with limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
For those who possess discrimination, there exists no so-called individual soul (jīva) other than the Supreme who is either an agent or an enjoyer;
this is because of scriptural declarations such as, "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.23).
In that case, it would follow that the transmigrating being is the agent and the enjoyer only in relation to the Supreme;

for if the conscious individual soul (*jīva*) were other than the Supreme, it could not exist as an agent distinct from the aggregate of the intellect and so forth. This is not so, because agency and enjoyership are presented by ignorance (*avidyā*).

And thus the scripture, having shown agency and enjoyership in the state of ignorance with the words, "For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14), precludes those very same agency and enjoyership in the state of knowledge with the words, "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14).

Likewise, having made known the exhaustion caused by contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in both the dreaming and waking states— just like that of a hawk flying about in the sky— the text makes known the absence of such exhaustion in deep sleep for one who is embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña-ātman*): "Now, this is his state where desires have been attained, which is the self-desiring, desireless form, free from sorrow" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21).

Starting from this point, the conclusion is reached in the passage: "This is his supreme goal, this is his supreme attainment, this is his supreme world, this is his supreme bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32).
Regarding this, the Teacher says: "And as the carpenter, in both ways."
And this *ca* is read here in the sense of "but.
One should not think that the agency of the self is inherent, like the heat of fire;
rather, it is just as in the world where a carpenter, with an axe and other tools in his hand, becomes an agent and suffers, yet upon reaching his own home, [he is no longer so].

Having set aside the instruments such as the body and so forth, being established in himself, withdrawn from activity, and free from exertion, he becomes happy; in this same way, the Self, when joined with the duality presented by ignorance, becomes an agent and suffers in the states of dreaming and waking.

To dispel that weariness, he enters his own Self, which is the Supreme Brahman, and having become liberated from the aggregate of the body and organs, he becomes a non-agent and happy in the state of profound serenity (*saṃprasāda*).
Likewise, even in the state of liberation, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge (*vidyā*), the Self alone remains, free from activity and becomes happy.
The analogy of the carpenter is to be understood in this respect:
for a carpenter becomes an agent only by depending upon specific instruments such as an adze (*vāsī*) in relation to particular activities like carving.
But by its own body, it is indeed a non-agent.
Thus, this self becomes an agent only by depending upon the instruments such as the mind in all activities; by its own nature, however, it is a non-agent.

Just as a carpenter does not possess limbs such as hands with which he might take up or set down tools like axes, so too the Self does not possess instruments such as the mind with which it could employ or discard them.
As for the argument that the Self’s agency is inherent because of reasons such as the meaningfulness of the scriptures—
that is not the case.
The injunction-scripture (vidhi-śāstra), taking for granted the agency as it is already established, teaches specific duties; it does not establish the self's agency.
Nor is this agency inherent, as we have already stated on the basis of the teaching that Brahman is the Self.
Therefore, the injunction-scripture proceeds by taking for granted an agency produced by ignorance (avidyā).

Even scriptural passages of this kind, such as "The agent is the person whose nature is consciousness," will merely restate the agency created by ignorance, since they are of the nature of restatement (anuvāda) and thus conform to what is already established.
By this, the [scriptural texts concerning] the "wandering" and the "taking up" of the body are also refuted,
for those two are likewise of the nature of restatement.

Objection: Is it not the case that the "wandering" (vihāra) taught in the state of dream—wherein "when the organs have fallen asleep, he moves about at will within his own body"—implies the agency of the self alone?

Likewise, regarding the act of taking [the organs], in the passage "having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of consciousness," the hearing of the accusative and instrumental case-endings for the organs suggests that the agency belongs to the self alone.
To this, it is replied: First of all, in the state of dream, there is no absolute cessation of the self's instruments.
"Having become a dreamer endowed with intelligence (*sadhīḥ*), he transcends this world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7);
for even there, the connection with intelligence (*dhī*) is heard. And so they [the traditional authorities] remember: "If the mind is not ceased when the senses have ceased..."

"One should know that the very pursuit of sense objects is the vision of a dream," and "Desire and the like are the functions of the mind"— so says the Śruti. And these [functions] are seen in a dream.
Therefore, one indeed roams about in the dream state while still possessing the body (*samanā*).
Furthermore, even that roaming there consists solely of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*) and does not exist in an ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*).

Thus, the Śruti describes the activity of dreaming as being bound to forms, just like waking experience: "As if rejoicing with women, as if laughing, and as if seeing terrors" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.13).
Even worldly people speak of dreams in the same way, saying, "I climbed as it were a mountain peak," or "I saw as it were a row of forests.

Likewise, even though in the case of grasping (*upādāna*) there is an indication of the instrumental and objective case endings regarding the instruments [of action], nevertheless, the agency should be understood as belonging only to the self (*ātman*) as conjoined with those [instruments];
for it has already been shown that agency is impossible for the [self] alone.

Furthermore, there are various ways of intending to speak in the world, such as "the warriors fight" or "the king fights with the warriors. Moreover, in this particular usage, one intends to express merely the cessation of the operation of the instruments (karaṇas), and not the independence of any agent, since the cessation of the operation of the instruments is observed even in sleep, which is not preceded by conscious intention. As for this designation that was shown—namely, "consciousness performs the sacrifice"—it is intended to show the predominance of consciousness over the other instruments. This is because it is seen that when the instrument is absent, the result does not arise; whereas when consciousness is present, the result does arise, even if the other instruments are absent. Therefore, it is said: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice. It is not, however, intended to deny the existence of the agent, for that would contradict the scriptural statement: "He who dwells in the self, whom the self does not know, whose body the self is, and who controls the self from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22). Nor is it intended to deny the existence of the instruments, for that would contradict the scriptural statement: "The earth is the sacrificial vessel" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.1.4). Rather, it is intended to show the predominance of consciousness over the other instruments. Just as in the world, although a king is the sovereign lord of all his subjects, he is nevertheless called "the warrior" when he personally engages in battle, so too here, although the Self is the master of all the instruments, it is designated as "consciousness" because it is predominant in the act of knowing. Thus, there is no contradiction with the scripture that establishes the existence of the agent. Furthermore, the scripture declares the non-existence of the agent only in relation to the true nature of the Self, as in: "It thinks, as it were; it moves, as it were" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7). But this does not mean that the Self lacks the capacity for agency altogether, for that would contradict the scripture: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3). Therefore, it is established that the Self is both the agent and the enjoyer. And thus, the Smṛti also says: "The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious, who, though one, fulfills the desires of many" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13). Hence, the conclusion is that the Self is the agent and the enjoyer. ||| End of Section 32 ||| Now begins the section concerning the soul's departure and its destination. In the scripture, it is stated: "When a person departs from this world, he goes to the wind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.10.1). It establishes that agency belongs to cognition alone,
because the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) is well-known in that sense,
and because it is recited immediately after the mind (manas).
And because of the mention of faith and so forth as the limbs of the self consisting of knowledge in the passage, "Faith indeed is its head" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4),
and because it is well known that faith and the rest are attributes of the intellect (buddhi).
And because of the supplementary statement: "All the gods worship consciousness as the eldest Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1);
for its status as the "eldest" is well-known in common understanding as being born first.

Furthermore, because another scriptural passage— “This sacrifice is indeed the successive progression of speech and mind”— determines that the sacrifice is accomplished by means of speech and the intellect;
nor does a reversal of the capacities of the instruments occur when agency is attributed to them,
since it is necessarily the case that all causal factors possess agency with respect to their own respective functions.
The status of these instruments as instruments, however, is dependent upon apprehension,
and that [apprehension] belongs to the self;
yet even with respect to that, the self possesses no agency.
Because its essential nature is eternal perception (*nityopalabdhi*),
agency— even when preceded by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)— cannot belong to the perceiver;
for the ego-sense itself is also something perceived.
And this being the case, there is no consequence of having to postulate another instrument,
because the intellect (buddhi) is admitted to be the instrument.
Furthermore, the absence of meditative absorption (samādhi) is refuted precisely by its being the very purpose of the treatise.

Because meditative concentration (samādhi) is established by taking agency exactly as it is attained [by the adjuncts], it is therefore established that the agency of the self is likewise caused solely by its limiting adjuncts (upādhi). // 40 // [Note:

the world is the pleasure to be enjoyed.

16. The section concerning dependence on another. Sūtra 41–42: But [the soul is] dependent on the Supreme, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. (BBs 2.3.41)

Regarding this agency of the individual soul (jīva) which has been described as being based on grasping during the state of ignorance—does that occur independently of the Lord (īśvara), or does it depend upon the Lord? Such is the inquiry.
On this point, the initial position is that the jīva does not depend upon the Lord for its agency.
Why?
Because there is no need for dependence [on another agent].
For this living being (jīva), being itself impelled by defects such as attachment and aversion and endowed with the collection of other causal factors, is capable of experiencing agency on its own.
What could Īśvara do for him?
Furthermore, there is no common consensus in the world that in activities such as agriculture, another being like Īśvara must be depended upon, as one would depend upon oxen and the like.
Moreover, if Īśvara were to create living beings through an agency consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), it would entail the consequence of his being merciless (*nairghṛṇya*).
Furthermore, if He were to ordain their agency, there would be the fault of partiality due to the resulting unequal fruits.
But has it not been stated that "partiality and cruelty do not apply because [the Lord] has regard for [other factors]" (Brahma Sūtra 1.4.17)?
True, this was stated provided that the possibility of the Lord having such regard exists.
Furthermore, dependence on God is possible only if the merit and demerit of living beings exist, and their existence is possible only if the soul possesses agency.
If that very agency itself were dependent on God, then with respect to what object could God’s dependence be said to exist?
Moreover, in that case, the soul would incur the consequence of receiving the fruits of actions it did not perform.
Therefore, [the opponent claims] that its agency belongs to it by itself. Refuting this conclusion with the word "but" (tu), he asserts: "from another" (parāt).

For the individual soul (jīva) in the state of ignorance—who perceives no distinction from the aggregate of causes and effects and who is blinded by the darkness of nescience—[agency arises from another].

From another Self— the overseer of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious Lord— there arises, by His permission, the accomplishment of transmigratory existence characterized by agency and enjoyership; and it is only through the knowledge caused by His grace that the accomplishment of liberation is possible.
Why?
Because of the scriptural statement to that effect.
Even though the individual soul (jīva) is impelled by defects and possesses the full complement of causal factors, [it does not act independently].

And although in the world the causality of God is not commonly recognized in activities such as agriculture, nevertheless, it is determined from scripture that in all undertakings God is the causal agent.
For thus says the scripture: "For He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He leads up from these worlds."

"For it is he indeed who causes one to perform evil action, whom he wishes to lead downward" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8), and "He who, dwelling within the self, controls the self from within"—passages of this kind [establish this]. (41)
[Objection: But if God is thus the cause of action, there would result partiality and cruelty on His part, and for the individual soul (jīva), there would be the arrival of what was not earned.
[Reply: No; it is said in reply:
"But [God] has regard for the effort performed [by the soul], because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth" (Brahma Sūtra 2.3.42).
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of excluding the faults previously raised.
The Lord causes this [being] to act only with regard to that effort made by the individual soul, characterized as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Consequently, these aforementioned faults do not apply.

It is only with regard to the inequalities of dharma and adharma performed by living beings that the Lord, like a rain-cloud, distributes their respective fruits unequally, acting merely as a causal agent (*nimitta*).

Just as in the world, for various kinds of shrubs, bushes, and so forth, as well as for rice, barley, and the like—which arise from their own specific, non-common seeds—the rain-cloud serves as a common cause;
for in the absence of rain, the inequality of their sap, flowers, leaves, and so on would not come into being.
Nor [is it logical] that [the fruit arises] when their respective seeds are non-existent;
thus, it does not follow that God, depending upon the effort made by the individual soul (jīva), would ordain its good and evil [results].
But surely, this very dependence on the effort made by the soul is untenable if the soul's agency is dependent on another.
This is not a fault;
for even though agency is dependent on another, the individual soul (jīva) indeed acts,
since the Lord causes him who is acting to act.

Furthermore, [the objection that God acts arbitrarily] is without fault because the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is beginningless: He causes [an effect] now in dependence upon a prior effort, and He caused [it] previously in dependence upon an even earlier effort.
But how is it understood that God depends upon past actions?
He says: "Because otherwise the prescribed and the prohibited would be rendered meaningless," and so forth.
For in this way, there is no pointlessness of such prescribed and prohibited injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "a Brahmin must not be killed";
otherwise, they would be meaningless.
The Lord alone would be subject to injunctions and prohibitions,
because the individual soul is entirely dependent;
thus, He might bring about misfortune even for one who performs what is enjoined, and prosperity even for one who performs what is prohibited.

Consequently, the authority of the Veda would vanish; and if God were entirely independent, human effort—even that of worldly beings—would be rendered useless, as would the factors of place, time, and causal conditions, leading to the aforementioned defects. By the use of the word "etcetera" (ādigrahaṇena), he indicates such a collection of faults. 42.
17. The Section on the Part (Aṃśādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 43–53. Sūtra 43:
"He is a part [of the Lord], because of the declarations of manifoldness, and also because otherwise; moreover, some record that he possesses the nature of a fisherman, a hunter, and so forth.
The relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) has been stated.

Moreover, in the world, such a relationship is observed only between two things that are connected, as in the case of a master and a servant, or as in the case of fire and its sparks. Consequently, since one must admit a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), a doubt arises as to whether their connection is like that of a master and a servant or like that of fire and its sparks; thus, it would follow that there is no fixed rule [regarding this].
Alternatively, since the relationship between the ruler and the ruled is well-established only in the manner of master and servant, it follows that the connection must be of that same kind.
Therefore, he says "a part" (aṃśa):
the individual soul (jīva) ought to be a part of the Lord (īśvara).
Just as a spark from a fire, a part is like a portion; for a part in the primary sense cannot exist for that which is without parts.
But why, on account of being without parts, is it not that very same thing?
Because of various designations:
"He is to be sought, He is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1);
"Only by knowing Him does one become a sage"; and "He who, dwelling in the self, controls the self from within"—such designations of difference are not possible if there were no actual difference.
Now, one might object that this distinction between different designations is all the more appropriate when there is a similarity between master and servant; to this, he says: "And otherwise also.
It is not from the mere fact of the distinction between different designations alone that the status of being a part is established.
Rather, there is also another way of designation which establishes non-difference.

For instance, some followers of the Vedic branches declare that Brahman possesses the nature of fishermen, slaves, and gamblers; the Atharvaṇikas, in the *Brahmasūkta*, state: "The fishermen are Brahman, the slaves are Brahman, even these gamblers are indeed Brahman," and so forth.
Here, "fishermen" refers to those well-known as fishermen (*kaivartas*), and "slaves" refers to those who exhaust themselves for their masters.

And by using the example of "those others who are gamblers and players at dice—all these are indeed Brahman," [the text] declares the Brahman-nature of all individual souls (*jīvas*) who have entered into the aggregate of name, form, and the collection of effects and instruments;

likewise, in another passage within the very context of Brahman, this same meaning is elaborated: "You are female, you are male, you are a youth, or even a maiden; you are an old man tottering with a staff; you are born, facing every direction" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.3).

And from such scriptural passages as, "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made their names, sits calling them by those names," and "There is no other seer than He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23), this meaning is established.
And consciousness is undifferentiated in both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), just as heat is in a fire and its sparks;
therefore, from the understanding of both difference and non-difference, the understanding of being a part [of the whole] follows. // 43 //
And from what [source] is the understanding of being a part derived?
From the wording of a mantra as well (BBs 2.3.44).
And the wording of a mantra makes this meaning known: "Such is his greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that."
"One foot of this are all beings; its three feet are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
Here, by the word *bhūta*, he indicates the stationary and moving entities in which the individual soul (*jīva*) predominates, as seen in the usage:
"not harming any beings, except at the sacred sites" (tīrthas).
"Part," "quarter," and "portion" are synonymous;
therefore, from this as well, there is the understanding of being a part. // 44 //
And from what [source] is the understanding of its being a part derived?
Furthermore, it is recorded in traditional scripture (*smṛti*).

Even in the *Īśvaragītās*, the fact that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part of the Lord is recorded: "In the world of living beings, my very own eternal part has become the individual soul" (BhG 15.7).
Therefore, there is also the understanding of being a part.
As for what was said— that in the world the relationship of ruler and ruled is well-known only in cases such as master and servant—
even though this is well-known in the world, nevertheless, from the scripture (śāstra), the relationship of part and whole and the relationship of ruler and ruled are determined here.
And since the Lord, endowed with unsurpassed limiting adjuncts, governs the individual souls who are endowed with inferior limiting adjuncts, nothing at all is contradicted. // 45 //

Here it is objected: "If it is admitted that the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of the Lord (īśvara), then by virtue of the individual soul's experience of the suffering of saṃsāra, the Lord as the whole (aṃśin) would also become subject to suffering.
Just as in the world, Devadatta, the possessor of limbs, becomes subject to suffering through pain occurring in any one of his limbs such as the hand or foot, so it would be here.
Consequently, those who have attained that [state of liberation] would incur even greater suffering."

"Therefore, it would follow that right vision is useless, as one might as well let cyclic existence remain in its prior state. To this it is replied: "The Supreme is not like this, just as light and so forth [are not]. (BBs 2.3.46)
We maintain that the individual soul (jīva) experiences the suffering of saṃsāra, whereas the Supreme Lord does not experience it in such a way.

For the individual soul, under the influence of the onset of ignorance (avidyā), having as it were attained the state of identifying with the body and so forth, imagines itself to be suffering through the pain produced by those [identifications], thinking "I am suffering"—thus it falsely conceives of the experience of suffering created by ignorance.
The Supreme Lord, however, possesses neither identification with the body and so forth nor the conceit of suffering in this manner.

For the individual soul (*jīva*) as well, the conceit of suffering is caused solely by the delusion of non-discrimination from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—such as the body and the senses—which are produced by name and form (*nāmarūpa*) created by ignorance (*avidyā*); it does not exist in an ultimate sense.

Just as one experiences suffering caused by burning, cutting, and so forth occurring in one’s own body through the delusion of identifying with it, so too one experiences suffering pertaining to sons, friends, and others through that very same delusion of identification, thinking, "I am the son," "I am [the friend]," and so on.

Thus, by means of affection, one becomes attached to sons, friends, and so forth, thinking "this is a friend. From this, it is understood with certainty that the experience of suffering is caused solely by the delusion of false conceit.
This is also understood through the observation of negative instances (vyatireka).

For instance, when many people— both those who possess sons, friends, and so forth, and others who do not, yet all of whom harbor the conceit of being related to them— are gathered together, and it is proclaimed that "a son has died" or "a friend has died," grief arises for that cause only in those who possess the conceit of having sons, friends, and so on, and not in those devoid of such conceit, such as wandering mendicants (parivrājaka).
Therefore, since even for an ordinary worldly person the efficacy of right vision is observed,
how much more so for one who perceives no other object apart from the Self— which is devoid of objective referents and whose nature is solely eternal consciousness?
Consequently, there is no contingency of right vision being purposeless.
The phrase "like light, etc. is an introduction of an illustration.

Just as sunlight or moonlight, while pervading space, assumes—as it were—the states of straightness, curvature, and so forth in relation to limiting adjuncts such as a finger when those adjuncts assume those states, yet in reality does not actually assume those states; so too is the case here.

Just as space, although appearing to move when jars and other objects move, does not move in the ultimate sense; and just as the sun, though its reflection in a water-bowl trembles due to the shaking of the bowl, the sun itself—the possessor of the reflection—does not tremble;

so too, although the portion called the individual soul (*jīva*), which is presented by ignorance and conditioned by the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors, experiences suffering, the Lord (*īśvara*), who possesses that portion, does not suffer.
Furthermore, it has been stated that even the soul's attainment of suffering is caused solely by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, by removing the state of being a soul—which is caused by ignorance—the Vedāntas establish the very nature of Brahman for the soul through such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).
Therefore, there is no possibility of the Supreme Self becoming subject to suffering on account of the suffering of the individual soul. // 46 //
FN: In others who are devoid of egoism;
and they remember:
Vyāsa and others remember that the Supreme Self does not suffer because of the suffering of the individual soul (jīva).
In that regard, the Supreme Self is indeed remembered as eternal and devoid of qualities;
it is not smeared by fruits of action, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. But the other, the Active Self, is joined with both liberation and bondage.
"He is joined again with the group of seventeen";
the word "ca" (and) implies that they recite [this] as well, which is the remainder of the sentence:
"One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6).
And also: "In the same way, the one inner Self of all beings, being external [to them], is not tainted by the suffering of the world" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 5.11). // 47 //
Here it is asked: "If, then, there were only one inner self for all beings, how could there be worldly and Vedic injunctions and prohibitions?
But has it not been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part of the Lord?
And because of the distinction between them, injunctions and prohibitions based upon them are logically possible as non-confused entities; so what is the point of this objection?"
It is said: this is not so;

for even the partlessness of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by the scriptures that proclaim non-duality, such as: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), and "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
"He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19);
"That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7); "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
Such are the types [of arguments].
Now, was it not stated that being a part (aṃśatva) is established through the cognition of both difference and non-difference?
This would indeed be so if both difference and non-difference were intended to be propounded.
However, it is non-difference alone that is intended to be established here, since the attainment of the human goal occurs through the realization of Brahman as the Self.
Difference, which is obtained by its very nature, is merely restated;
and it has already been stated that the individual soul cannot be a literal part of the partless Brahman.

Therefore, since the one Supreme alone is the inner self (antarātman) of all beings, existing in the form of the individual soul (jīva), the logical consistency of injunctions and prohibitions must be explained on this basis. [In this context, between the individual soul and the Supreme,
the "karmic self" is the individual soul which is the locus of action.]
The group consisting of seventeen—namely, the ten organs of perception, the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*), mind (*manas*), and intellect (*buddhi*)—is the subtle body (*liṅga*).

"From death to death": the meaning is that he who perceives this universe, composed of sentient and insentient beings, as if possessed of a manifold diversity within Brahman, attains after death a further death—that is, the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) in the form of a succession of births and deaths.
We reply to that:
"Permission and prohibition [apply] due to connection with the body, as in the case of light and so forth.
[The Vedic injunction] "One should approach one's wife during her season" is a permission.
"One should not approach the wife of a teacher" is a prohibition;
likewise, "one should immolate the animal for Agni and Soma" is an injunction;
and "one should not harm any living beings" is a prohibition.

Thus, even in the world, there is permission that "a friend should be served" and avoidance that "an enemy should be shunned. Such permissions and avoidances would exist even though the self is one, due to its connection with the body.
The connection with bodies is "dehasambandha.
But what, then, is this connection with bodies?
It is the arising of a perverted cognition within the self, [thinking], "I am indeed this aggregate consisting of the body and so forth."
And that [notion] has been observed among all living beings, consisting of such thoughts as: "I go," "I come," "I am blind," "I am not blind," "I am deluded," and "I am not deluded.
Indeed, there is nothing other than right vision (*samyagdarśana*) that can prevent this;
prior to right vision, this error persists among all creatures.

Thus, even while accepting the non-duality of the Self, permissions and prohibitions are possible due to the distinctions created by the connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as the body, which have ignorance as their cause.
[Objection: In that case, permissions and prohibitions would become meaningless for one who possesses right vision (samyagdarśin). [Reply: No;
because such a person has already achieved their goal, it is impossible for them to be subject to injunctions.
For it is only with respect to what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is to be accepted (*upādeya*) that one who is to be enjoined (*niyojya*) can be directed by an enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*).
But how could one be enjoined if one does not perceive any object—whether to be abandoned or to be accepted—as distinct from oneself?
Nor, indeed, could the self be enjoined by the self alone.
If it is argued that only one who perceives the self as distinct from the body can be a subject of injunction (*niyojyatva*), we say no;
for there is the conceit of being conjoined with it.

It is true that the status of being a subject of injunction belongs to one who perceives distinction; nevertheless, the conceit of the self being a subject of injunction occurs only in one who, like space and so forth, does not perceive the self as non-conjoined with the body and its adjuncts.
Indeed, an injunction is never observed for anyone who perceives the body and so forth as not being a composite whole;
how much less so for one who perceives the identity of the Self?
Nor does the absence of an injunction lead to the consequence of unrestrained behavior on the part of one who possesses right vision.
Since it is precisely conceit (*abhimāna*) that causes activity everywhere, and since the one who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśin*) is devoid of conceit,
therefore, both permission and prohibition pertain only to the connection with the body,
as in the case of light and so forth.
Just as light, though it is one, is avoided in the case of fire that consumes raw flesh but not in other cases;
and just as the light of the sun, though it is one, is avoided when connected with an impure place but not when situated upon pure ground;
and just as certain earthly regions, such as those containing diamonds and lapis lazuli, are sought after.
Even those things that are terrestrial, such as the corpses of hell-beings and the like, are avoided;
just as cow urine is accepted as pure, yet that very same substance is shunned when it belongs to another species—it is the same in this case. (48) [FN:
*Pratatā* means continuous.]
"Viśeṣa" means difference. A "kravyād" is a flesh-eater, namely the cremation fire. And because [the series] is not continuous, there is no confusion [of karmic results]. (BBs 2.3.49)
It may be granted that permission and avoidance could belong even to a single self due to its connection with different bodies;
however, if one were to accept a single self, the connection with the fruits of one's own karma would become confused because the ownership [of those fruits] would be identical.
To this we say: it is not so.
Because there is no continuity;
for there is no continuous connection of a self that is both agent and enjoyer with all bodies.
For it has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Furthermore, because there is no continuum of a soul due to the absence of a continuum of a self, there will be neither a confusion of karma nor a confusion of its results. // 49 //
And it is merely a reflection.
This individual soul (jīva) is to be understood as a mere reflection of the Supreme Self, like the sun reflected in water and so forth;
it is not the Self itself directly.
Nor is it a different entity. Therefore, just as when one reflection of the sun in water trembles, another reflection of the sun in water does not tremble,
so too, when one living being is connected with the fruit of karma, another living being is not connected with it.
Thus, there is indeed no confusion between action and its fruit;
and since the appearance is produced by ignorance, it is logically established that the transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) which has that appearance as its basis is also produced by ignorance.
Consequently, by means of the removal of that [ignorance], the teaching of the ultimate reality—the identity of Brahman and the Self—is logically established.
However, for those who maintain that there are many selves and that all of them are omnipresent, this very confusion necessarily follows.
How so?

The Sāṃkhyas hold that there are many, all-pervading selves whose nature consists solely of consciousness, who are devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and without distinction; for their sake, there exists a common primordial matter (pradhāna), and by means of it, the accomplishment of their experience (bhoga) and liberation (apavarga) occurs.

In their plurality and omnipresence, they are of the same nature as jars, walls, and so forth; being merely substantial entities, they are inherently insentient. Likewise, the selves (*ātman*) and the atoms of the mind (*manas*), which serve as their instruments, are insentient. Therein, through the conjunction of the substances of the selves and the substances of the minds, the specific qualities of the self, such as desire and the rest, arise.
These [qualities] inhere individually in each self without distinction; that is *saṃsāra*.
The followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that liberation is the absolute non-arising of these nine qualities of the self.

In that regard, first for the Sāṃkhyas, since all selves consist of the nature of consciousness and there is no distinction in their proximity [to the intellect], it would follow that when one self is connected with pleasure and pain, all selves would be connected with pleasure and pain.
This might be argued.
The established order will exist because the activity of Pradhāna has as its purpose the isolation (kaivalya) of the individual soul (puruṣa).
For otherwise, the activity of Pradhāna would be for the sake of manifesting its own power;
and in that case, the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation.
This is not the essence;
for a systematic arrangement based on the attainment of one's desired ends cannot be understood [as valid].
Rather, a systematic arrangement might be stated by means of some logical justification (*upapatti*).
Furthermore, if rebirth were non-existent, even if the desired isolation of the self (*puruṣakaivalya*) were not to occur,
a confusion of experiences would nonetheless result due to the absence of a determining factor for their distribution.
Even for the followers of Kaṇāda, when the mind is conjoined with one self, it would necessarily be conjoined with other selves as well, since there is no difference in their proximity and so forth.

Furthermore, since there is no distinction in the cause, there would be no distinction in the result; thus, when one self is joined with pleasure and pain, it would follow that all selves are equally subject to pleasure and pain. // 50 //
It might be argued:
"The restriction will have an unperceived cause.
He says: No.
Because there would be no restriction regarding the unseen (adṛṣṭa).

[BBs 2.3.51] Since many selves are omnipresent like space and are present in every body without distinction between internal and external, the unseen merit or demerit (dharma-lakṣaṇa-adṛṣṭa) is accumulated through mind, speech, and body.

For the Sāṃkhyas, however, that [unseen force] does not inhere in the self but resides in primordial matter (pradhāna); because it is common to the pradhāna, it cannot logically serve as the regulator for the individual experience of pleasure and pain for each self.

For the followers of Kaṇāda as well, there is this same defect: because there is no cause for the restriction that "this unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) belongs to this very self," even though the unseen merit is produced by the common conjunction of the self and the mind as previously described.
It might be argued:

"Intentions (abhisaṃdhi) and so forth—such as 'I shall obtain this fruit,' 'I shall avoid this,' 'I shall strive thus,' or 'I shall act thus'—which operate individually within each self, [are the cause]. Regarding the unseen merit and the selves...
[The opponent claims: "They will restrict the relationship between owner and owned.
[The author] says: No;
for it would be the same even in the case of intentions and so forth. (BBs 2.3.52)

Even in the case of intentions (*abhisaṃdhi*) and so forth, since they are produced in the proximity of all selves through the very same common conjunction of self and mind, it is impossible for them to serve as the cause for restriction; thus, the aforementioned fault remains attached. // 52 //
If it is argued that [the distinction] is due to location (*pradeśa*), we say no, because there is no internal division.

(BBs 2.3.53) Now, it might be said: "Even though the self is all-pervading, its conjunction with the mind—which resides in the body—will occur only in that portion of the self delimited by the body; therefore, the restriction of intention and so forth, as well as of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and pleasure and pain, will be established on the basis of location."
That too is not tenable.
Why?
Because it is included [within the others].
For, because there is no distinction in their omnipresence (*vibhutva*), all selves (*ātman*) are indeed contained within all bodies.
In this regard, it is not possible for the Vaiśeṣikas to postulate even a spatially delimited portion (*pradeśa*) of the self within a body.
Even if such a portion were postulated, being merely a conceptual construct of a self that is actually partless, it could not determine any ultimate (*pāramārthika*) effect.
Furthermore, it is impossible to determine that a body, even though it arises in proximity to all selves, belongs to this self alone and not to others;
for even if one were to admit specific locations [for each self], there could still be the possibility of experience through a single body by two selves sharing identical pleasure and pain,
since it is possible for both selves to possess unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) in the same location.
For instance, when Devadatta’s body has departed from a certain place where he experienced pleasure or pain,

and Yajñadatta’s body arrives at that same place, the experience of pleasure and pain is seen to be identical for both; this would not occur if there were no undesirable [contact] with the same location for both Devadatta and Yajñadatta.
Furthermore, for one who maintains the doctrine of spatial limitation (*pradeśavāda*), there would follow the consequence that the enjoyment of heaven and so forth is impossible;
for the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is produced in the specific regions of the body such as those of a Brāhmaṇa, whereas the enjoyment of heaven occurs in a different location.
Moreover, it is logically untenable for many selves to be omnipresent.
Because there is no supporting example.
First, tell me: what things are both many and occupy the same location?
If you say "form and so forth," it is not so.
For even those [universals], there is non-difference insofar as they possess the nature of being *dharma*, yet there is a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
However, there is no difference in defining characteristics among the many selves (*ātman*).
If it is argued that the establishment of difference occurs by virtue of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), we say no.
Because the conceptualization of difference and the conceptualization of ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*) are mutually dependent;
furthermore, even the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of ether and so forth is not established for the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*), since they admit that these are effects.
Therefore, it is established that only in the position of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*) is there an absence of all defects. // 53 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
The Fourth Quarter of the Second Chapter.
In this quarter, the contradictions regarding the scriptural texts concerning the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) are resolved.
Section 1: The Origin of the Vital Breaths (*prāṇa*). Sūtras 1–4.
Likewise, regarding the vital breaths (prāṇas):
the contradiction in scripture concerning the objects such as ether and so forth has been resolved by the third section;
now, in this fourth section, the contradiction concerning the vital breaths is resolved.

In those passages concerning origination, such as "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3) and "From this very Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), the origination of the vital breaths is not mentioned; moreover, in some places their non-origination is explicitly taught, as in: "Non-being indeed was this in the beginning" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).

Regarding this they say: "What was that non-existent (asat) which existed in the beginning?"—"The sages (ṛṣis), indeed, were that non-existent in the beginning."—Regarding this they ask: "Who are those sages?"—"The vital breaths (prāṇas), indeed, are the sages. Since this passage declares the existence of the vital breaths prior to creation, [the objection does not hold].

In other places, however, the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is also taught: "Just as small sparks fly forth from a blazing fire, even so from this Self all the vital breaths [proceed]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20);
"From this is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3);
and "From that the seven vital breaths arise" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.8).
Thus, in such passages as "He created Prāṇa; from Prāṇa, faith, space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, mind, and food" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4), and in other similar locations,
a state of non-comprehension arises due to the contradiction between the various scriptural statements and the failure to determine a means for deciding between them.
Alternatively, since their existence is heard of prior to origination, it follows that the origination of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is figurative.
To this, he reads the following reply: "The vital breaths are likewise.
But how, in this case, is there a conformity of the syllable *tathā* (likewise), given the absence of a relevant object of comparison?

The refutation of those who assert a self that is omnipresent and manifold, which was introduced at the end of the preceding section, is as follows: first of all, an analogy is not possible here because of the absence of similarity.
For an analogy would exist only if there were similarity, such as:
"As is a lion, so is Balavarman."
If it should be argued that this is for the purpose of establishing a similarity with what is observed—
that just as that which arises in the proximity of all selves is indeterminate, so too the vital breaths are indeterminate with respect to each self—
then even that would be a mere repetition, since it has already been stated by means of the very indeterminacy of the bodies.

Furthermore, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) cannot be compared with the individual soul (*jīva*), because that would contradict our established doctrine; for the non-origination of the soul has been declared,
whereas the origination of the vital breaths is what we intend to explain.
Therefore, the phrase "thus [it is]" appears as if it were unconnected. This is not so;
for a connection is established even by means of a comparison introduced through an illustration.

In this context, the collection of statements from those who maintain that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) originate [from Brahman] serves as the illustration: "From this Self, all vital breaths, all worlds, all gods, and all beings emerge" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.20).
Such is the nature of this [passage].
The meaning therein is that just as the worlds and so forth arise from the supreme Brahman, so too do the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).

Likewise: "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs; [as well as] space, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3).
In such passages as these, it should be understood that the origination of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) occurs just like that of ether (*ākāśa*) and the other elements;
or else, because even a connection with a remote object of comparison is accepted in cases such as "And the failure of the *apāna* is like that" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.15).

Just as ether and the other elements mentioned in the immediately preceding section were established as modifications of the supreme Brahman, so too must it be applied that the vital breaths (prāṇas) are also modifications of the supreme Brahman.
What, then, is the reason for the vital breaths being modifications?
It is simply because they are so stated in scripture (śruti).
Now, as for the claim that in certain passages the origination of the vital breaths (prāṇas) is not heard, that is incorrect;
for it is heard in other passages. Indeed, the non-mention of something in one place does not have the power to negate what is explicitly stated elsewhere.
Therefore, since there is no difference in their being mentioned in scripture, it is well stated that the vital breaths (prāṇas) also originate, just like ether and the other elements. [Note:
The subject matter concerns the vital breaths; the scope includes their origination, number, true nature, and so forth.
*Ānulomya* means consistency or logical coherence.]

Just as in the third chapter, fourth section, the principle of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding "non-receiving" is referred to in the case of vomiting soma—even though it is separated by many sūtras—so too should it be understood here.
This is because a figurative sense (*gauṇī*) is impossible.

As for what was stated previously—that the scriptural account of the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) must be taken figuratively because of the hearing of their existence prior to creation—that is not so.
To this he replies: "Because of the impossibility of it being figurative" (*gauṇyasaṃbhavāt*). The impossibility of it being figurative is "the impossibility of figurativeness.
For the scriptural statement regarding the origination of the vital breaths cannot possibly be figurative.
Because it would entail the fallacy of abandoning one's own proposition (*pratijñāhāni*).
For, having first proposed that "O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known?

(Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3), the scripture then teaches "From Him is born the vital breath" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3) and so forth, in order to establish that proposition through the knowledge of a single thing.

And that proposition is established provided that the entire world, beginning with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman, since there can be no modification apart from its material cause (*prakṛti*).
However, if the scriptural statement regarding the origin of the vital breaths were taken in a figurative sense, this proposition would be abandoned.
Accordingly, the text concludes the subject matter of the proposition: "The Person alone is all this—the work, austerity, Brahman, and the supreme immortal" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).
Thus [it is said], "Brahman alone is this universe, this most excellent" (Muṇḍaka 2.2.11).
Likewise, in such scriptural passages as, "Verily, my dear, by the seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing of the Self, all this is known," this very same proposition is to be applied.
But how can there be a scriptural statement regarding the existence of the vital breaths prior to creation?
This does not refer to the root-prakṛti;
for in the passage, "Indeed, he is without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2),
it is determined that the root-prakṛti is devoid of all specific attributes such as breath and the like.

However, it should be understood that this determination of the existence of the vital breaths prior to their origination refers to an intermediate state of nature (*prakṛti*) in relation to its own modifications (*vikāra*).

This is because, among the numerous states belonging to the realm of the evolved (*vyākṛta*), the relationship of cause and effect between the primary nature and its modifications is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.

Indeed, in the section concerning ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*), under the prima facie argument sūtra "On account of the impossibility of a secondary [sense]" (*gauṇyasaṃbhavāt*), it was explained that the scriptural statement regarding birth is secondary because [otherwise] it would be impossible.

In that [previous] case, a contradiction with the initial proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) was stated because a tenet (*siddhānta*) had been asserted; however, here, since it is a sūtra stating a tenet, it has been explained as "because a literal sense of birth is impossible. If, however, one were to explain this case in accordance with that [previous logic] by saying "because a figurative sense of birth is possible," then the contradiction with the initial proposition would have been overlooked. // 2 //
"And because of its mention prior [to the others].
(BBs 2.4.3) For this reason as well, the scriptural statement regarding the birth of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) is primary, just like that of ether (*ākāśa*) and the rest.
This is because the single word expressing birth, "is born" (*jāyate*), being heard first in relation to the vital breaths, continues to apply to the subsequent elements such as ether.

In the passage, "From this [Brahman] is born breath" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3), it has been established that birth in the case of ether and the other elements is primary; by virtue of that commonality, birth in the case of the vital breaths (prāṇas) must also be primary.

For it is not possible to determine that within a single context and a single sentence, a single word uttered once, while connected with many things, is primary in one instance and secondary in another.
Because it would lead to the consequence of inconsistency.

Likewise, in the passage, "He created the vital breath (prāṇa); from the vital breath, faith (śraddhā)" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4), the verb "creates" (sṛjati), which is heard in relation to the vital breaths, is also connected to the subsequent entities such as faith that possess an origin.
Even in cases where a word expressing origination is heard later but is connected with preceding terms, this same principle applies.
For example, the word "vyuccaranti" (they issue forth), which is read at the end in the phrase "all beings issue forth," is also connected with the preceding terms such as "prāṇas" and so on. // 3 //
Because speech is preceded by that [mind].

Even though the origin of the vital breaths is not explicitly mentioned in this context in the passage, "It created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), [they are nonetheless understood to originate from Brahman].

Furthermore, since the origin of only three elements—fire, water, and food—is heard [in scripture], even so, because it is stated that speech, breath, and mind have fire, water, and food as their material causes, and because they share that same nature, it is established that all vital breaths (*prāṇa*) originate from Brahman.

For instance, in this very context, the fact that speech, breath, and mind are preceded by fire, water, and food is recorded: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food; breath consists of water; and speech consists of fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4).
Thus it is said.
In this regard, if their consisting of food and so forth is indeed primary, then their origin from Brahman certainly exists.

Even if it is figurative, nevertheless, because it is heard that the differentiation of names and forms has Brahman as its agent—as in the passage, "By which the unheard becomes heard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3)—[the origin from Brahman remains established].

Thus, from the opening statement and from the concluding statement, "All this has that as its self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), as well as from what is well-known in other scriptural passages, it is understood that the description of the mind and the rest as consisting of food and so forth is intended solely to elaborate upon their being effects of Brahman.
Therefore, the fact that the vital breaths are modifications of Brahman is established. // 4 //
2. Section on the Seven Courses of Rebirth. Sūtras 5–6:
"And because the courses of rebirth are specified as seven.
The scriptural contradiction regarding the origin of the vital breaths has been resolved.
Now, the subject of enumeration is being resolved.
Among those, he will explain the primary vital breath (prāṇa) later on;
for now, however, he determines how many other vital breaths there are.
Furthermore, there is a point of doubt here due to conflicting scriptural statements (*śrutivipratipatti*).
In some places, seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are mentioned: "From him the seven vital breaths arise" (Muṇḍaka 2.1.8).
In other places, eight vital breaths are mentioned by way of their quality as "seizers" (*grahas*): "There are eight seizers and eight over-seizers" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.2.1).
In one place [the number] is nine: "There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head and two directed downwards" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.7.1).

In another place it is ten: "There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person; the navel is the tenth. In yet another place it is eleven: "These ten are the vital breaths in a person; the self is the eleventh" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.4).

In one place there are twelve, as in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.11: "The skin is the single point of convergence for all objects of touch. In another place there are thirteen, as in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.8: "The eye and the object to be seen.
Thus, the Śruti texts are indeed in disagreement regarding the number of vital breaths (prāṇas).
What, then, is the position reached? That there are exactly seven vital breaths. Why? Because of their departure.
For that many [seven] are understood from such scriptural passages as, "From him the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) arise" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.8),
and these are specifically designated in the passage, "There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head."
But surely, the repetition "the prāṇas, dwelling in the cave, are deposited seven by seven" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.8) is heard;
that [repetition] implies prāṇas in addition to the seven.

This is not a fault; this distributive repetition— “seven, seven vital breaths for each person”— is intended with respect to the distinction between persons, not with respect to a distinction in principles, as if there were seven different sets of vital breaths.
But surely, a number such as eight and so forth has also been cited regarding the vital breaths; how then can there be only seven?
True, they have been cited;
however, due to contradiction, one or another of those numbers must be determined as the correct one.
In this regard, the determination of the number seven is based on the adherence to a concise conceptualization;
furthermore, it is held that the hearing of other numbers is due to the consideration of different modes of functioning (vṛtti). (5) [Note:
*viṣaya* means doubt.]
The state of being a *graha* is the state of being a binder.
The *grahas* are the sense faculties (*indriya*), so called because they seize and bind. The *atigrahas* are those which transcend the *grahas*; the meaning is that they are the objects (*viṣaya*).
The anus and the generative organ are directed downward;
this is because of their movement and their function.
To this, it is said:
But since hands and so forth exist, it is not thus.

For other vital breaths, such as hands and the rest, are heard of in scripture as being distinct from the [seven] mentioned above: "The hands, indeed, are the grasper; they are seized by action as the over-grasper, for with the hands one performs action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8), and so on in such scriptural passages.
And since there exists a number exceeding seven, it is possible to conceive of [the others] as being included within that number of seven.

For when there is a disagreement regarding a number that is either too low or too high, the higher number is to be accepted, because the lower is included within it, but the higher is not included within the lower.
Therefore, one should not think that there must be exactly seven vital breaths simply out of deference to a more parsimonious hypothesis.
However, in accordance with the higher number, those vital breaths (*prāṇas*) must be exactly eleven;
thus the cited scripture states: "These ten are the vital breaths in a person, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.4).
And here, by the word *ātman*, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is intended.
Because the section concerns the instruments [of action].
Now, it may be argued that twelve and thirteen have also been cited as being greater than eleven.
