True, they have been cited.
Is it not the case that there exists a class of effects greater than the eleven, for the sake of which an additional instrument would have to be postulated?
There are five distinct types of cognition—having sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as their objects—and for those purposes there are the five sense organs.
There are five distinct types of action—speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure—and for those purposes there are the five organs of action.

The mind has all objects as its domain, functions throughout the three periods of time, and though it is one, it possesses manifold functions. Due to the difference in these functions, it is designated in various ways—as if it were distinct—being called "mind" (*manas*), "intellect" (*buddhi*), "ego-sense" (*ahaṃkāra*), and "consciousness" (*citta*). Thus, the Śruti, after enumerating its various functions such as desire and so forth, declares: "All this is indeed the mind alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
Furthermore, for one who considers only the seven vital breaths located in the head, there would be only four vital breaths accepted;
for these, being four, are counted as seven due to the difference in their locations—namely, "two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, and one speech.
Nor can it be said that the other vital breaths are merely different functions of those same [four].
Because the functions of the hands and so forth are absolutely heterogeneous;

likewise, in the passage, "There are nine breaths in a person, with the navel as the tenth," the ten breaths are mentioned solely with reference to the various openings of the body, not with reference to a distinction in the principles of the breaths themselves.
Because of the statement "the navel as the tenth," for there is no vital breath (prāṇa) well-known by the name "navel.
However, since the navel is also one specific seat of the primary vital breath, it is said that "the navel is the tenth."

In some places, a certain number of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are enumerated for the sake of meditation, while in others they are enumerated for the sake of illustration. Thus, since there are various scriptural traditions regarding the number of vital breaths, one must discern which enumeration has what as its ultimate purport. However, it is established that the scriptural authority concerning the vital breaths as being eleven in number is based on the necessity of their functions.
This is another way of connecting the two scriptural passages.

There would be only seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*), because the departure of only seven is heard [in scripture]: "When he departs, the *prāṇa* departs after him; all the *prāṇas* depart after him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). But is it not the case that the word "all" (*sarva*) is also recited here?
How then is it asserted that there is a departure for only seven?
He says: "Because they are specifically distinguished.

For it is these seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*), beginning with the eye and ending with the skin, that are specifically distinguished as the subject under discussion here: "When the person who consists of the eye turns away, then he becomes one who no longer knows forms" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).
This is shown by the sequence beginning with, "He becomes one; they say he does not see" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).

Furthermore, the word *sarva* (all) refers to those things under discussion, just as in the expression "All the Brāhmaṇas are to be fed," where only those Brāhmaṇas who have been invited and are the subject at hand are denoted by the word *sarva*, and no others.
In the same way here as well, only those seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) that are under discussion are denoted by the word "all," and no others.
But surely, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is enumerated as the eighth here;
how then can there be an enumeration of only seven?
This is not a fault;
for although there is a difference in their functions, the number seven is established because there is no difference in the reality of the mind and the mental consciousness.
Therefore, there are exactly seven vital breaths.

This being the case, we reply: other vital breaths, such as the hands and so forth, are perceived in addition to the seven, in scriptural passages such as "The two hands, indeed, are the grasper" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).
And "grasper-ness" (grahatva) consists in the state of being a binder, for [the senses] are held fast.
The knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is bound by this bondage known as "grasping" (graha). Moreover, that knower of the field is not bound in one body alone,
because the nature of the bondage is the same in other bodies as well.
Therefore, it follows by implication that this bondage, termed "graha" (seizing), migrates from one body to another.
And so says the Smṛti: "He is joined with the eightfold subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) as his mark, consisting of the vital breaths and the rest;
for him who is bound by it, there is bondage, and for him who is liberated from it, there is liberation."
Thus, prior to liberation, he demonstrates non-separation from this bondage known as the "seizer" (graha).

Furthermore, in the *Ātharvaṇa* [Upaniṣad], during the enumeration of the objects and the senses, after stating "the eye and the visible," he enumerates the other senses together with their objects in the same manner: "the two hands and the graspable, the organ of generation and that which is to be enjoyed, the anus and that which is to be excreted."
And [it says], "the two feet and that which is to be gone to" (Praśna 4.8).

Likewise, [the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad] shows the departure of eleven prāṇas: "These ten are the prāṇas in a person, with the self as the eleventh; when they depart from this mortal body, then they cause one to weep" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.4).
Moreover, the word "all" (sarva), when connected with the word "vital breaths" (prāṇa), denotes all vital breaths without exception;
and even though the word "all" is connected with the word "vital breaths" and thus expresses all vital breaths, it cannot be restricted to only seven by virtue of the context,
because the direct word is more powerful than the context.

In the case of the injunction "all Brāhmaṇas are to be fed," it would logically follow that all Brāhmaṇas residing on the earth are to be understood, owing to the force of the word "all. However, because feeding everyone is impossible, the application of the word "all" in that context is restricted to those who have been invited.
But here, there is no reason whatsoever for restricting the meaning of the word "all. Therefore, by the word "all," there is an inclusion of all vital breaths without exception;
and the enumeration of seven is for the sake of illustration—thus it is faultless.
Therefore, it is established that there are exactly eleven vital breaths (*prāṇas*), both according to scripture and according to their functions.
[Note: They are called "dwelling in the cave" because they lie within the cave of the heart; they are "placed" or deposited in their respective locations.
By action, they are "grasped," meaning connected, through the act of seizing performed by the hand.]
The three times constitute *traikālya*; that whose function has those as its object is "functioning through the three times" (*traikālyavṛtti*).
The [senses] beginning with the eye and ending with the skin have been specified in the context of departure (*utkrānti*) here in this section on departure.

The pentad beginning with *prāṇa*, the pentad of subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), the pentad of organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the pentad of organs of action (*karmendriya*), the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and ignorance (*avidyā*), desire (*kāma*), and action (*karman*)—this constitutes the group of eight.
[This concludes] the section on the atomicity of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Sūtra 7:
"And they are atomic" (BBs 2.4.7).
Now he further establishes another characteristic of the vital breaths themselves:
these vital breaths under discussion must be understood as atomic (*aṇu*).
And their atomicity consists in subtlety and limited dimension, not in being equal to an atom (*paramāṇu*).
Because it would follow that there could be no functioning [of the senses] pervading the entire body;

these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are subtle, for if they were gross, they would be perceived by those standing beside a dying person as they exit the body at the time of death, like a snake from its hole.
Furthermore, these vital breaths are limited in extent; if they were all-pervading, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural teachings regarding their departure, movement, and return.
Furthermore, the fact that the individual soul (jīva) has those [sensory] qualities as its essence would not be established.

If it is argued that even for [senses] that are all-pervading, their functional activity occurs within the region of the body, we say no; for it is logically consistent that the instrument consists of the functional activity alone.

For whether it be the function (*vṛtti*) or something else that is the means of apprehension, that alone constitutes its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*) for us; the dispute is merely over terminology. Thus, the hypothesis that the instruments are all-pervading is pointless.
Therefore, we conclude that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are subtle and limited. (7) [Note: Subtlety consists in having unmanifest color and touch.]
Limitation means smallness.
Section 4: On the Preeminence of Breath. Sūtra 8:
"And [breath] is the most excellent. (BBs 2.4.8)
And he extends this principle by stating that the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), like the other vital breaths, is a modification of Brahman;
for it has been declared without distinction that all vital breaths are modifications of Brahman:
"From Him [Brahman] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3).
Thus, because the origin of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is heard of as being distinct from the sense organs and the mind,
and because of such scriptural passages as, "He created the vital breath" (*Praśna Upaniṣad* 6.4).
But for what purpose is this extended application (*atideśa*)? It is for the purpose of removing further doubts.
For in the hymn *Nāsadāsīya*, which has Brahman as its primary subject, there occurs this scriptural passage: "There was neither death nor immortality then; there was no sign of night or day."
"By its own power, that One breathed without wind; other than that, nothing whatsoever existed" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.7.17).
Because of the mention of the activity of breathing through the word "breathed" (*ānīt*), it suggests that breath existed as if present even prior to creation.
Therefore, the notion may arise in someone's mind that breath is unborn (*aja*).
He removes that [objection] by means of an extended application (atideśa):
the word "non-moving" (*anīccha*) also does not indicate the existence of breath prior to creation,
because of the qualification "without wind" (*avātam*).

Furthermore, because it has been shown that the root-prakṛti is devoid of all specific attributes such as the vital breaths by the statement, "For it is without breath, without mind, and pure" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2), this word *ānīc* is intended solely to demonstrate the existence of the cause.
Moreover, the word *śreṣṭha* denotes the principal vital breath (*mukhya prāṇa*), as in: "The vital breath, indeed, is the eldest and the best" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.1).
This is because of the scriptural instruction;

moreover, the vital breath (prāṇa) is the eldest, since it acquires its functional activity from the very moment of the emission of the semen. For if it did not acquire its functional activity at that time, the semen emitted into the womb would either putrefy or fail to coagulate.
However, because the ear and the other senses obtain their functioning only upon the formation of their respective locations, such as the ear-cavity, they do not possess seniority.

Furthermore, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the most excellent due to its superiority of qualities, according to the Vedic scripture: "Indeed, we shall not be able to live without you" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.13). // 8 //
FN: At that time, during the period of dissolution (pralaya), there was no death—the destroyer—or the product of death;
there was no ambrosia (amṛta) to be enjoyed by the gods;
and neither the moon, which is the sign of night, nor the sun, which is the sign of day, existed.
By means of *svadhā*, together with the fire to be offered to the ancestors (*pitṛ*), he performed the ritual action.
5. Section on the Function of Air. Sūtras 9–12.
"The vital breath is not the wind, because it is taught separately.
Now, it is desired to know what the nature of this primary vital breath (prāṇa) is.
On this point, it is first suggested that the vital breath is the wind, according to scriptural authority.
For it is heard thus: "That which is prāṇa is indeed vāyu; this very vāyu is fivefold: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.
Alternatively, according to the intention of other systems (tantrāntara), it follows that prāṇa is the function of the aggregate of the organs.
For those belonging to other systems declare: "The common function of the organs consists of the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa."
To this it is replied: Prāṇa is neither air nor the functioning of the organs.
Why? Because of its separate teaching.
There is indeed a separate teaching of prāṇa from air: "Prāṇa alone is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and glows with air as its light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.4).
For if it were merely air, it would not be taught as distinct from air;

likewise, there is a teaching of the prāṇa as distinct even from the functioning of the organs, because after enumerating the organs such as speech and so forth, the prāṇa is enumerated separately in each instance.

And because there is no difference between the function and that which possesses the function, for the mere activity of an instrument would not be taught as something separate from the instruments themselves.
Likewise: "From this [Self] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs."
Statements such as "Space and air" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3) and others should also be understood as teaching that the vital breath (prāṇa) is distinct from both the air and the sense organs.
Furthermore, a single unified function for all the sense organs collectively is not possible.
Because each [element] functions individually and the aggregate as a whole lacks causal agency.
But surely this will occur according to the analogy of moving a cage:
just as eleven birds residing within a cage, each possessing its own specific function, together move the single cage by acting in concert.

Thus, it might be argued that the eleven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) residing within a single body, while each possessing its own specific function, will together attain a single collective function called "breath" (*prāṇa*). To this, we reply: "No. It is logical that birds, endowed with individual functions and intermediate activities corresponding to the movement of a cage, should together move a single cage. However, [the case of the vital breaths] is not analogous.
Because it is observed to be so [in other cases];
however, in this case, it is not logical that the vital breaths (prāṇas), though endowed with intermediate functions such as hearing and so forth, should breathe together as a collective,
because there is a lack of evidence for such a thing.
Furthermore, because breathing is absolutely heterogeneous from hearing and the other [sensory functions],
as well as the proclamation of the pre-eminence of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the subordination of speech and the others toward it,
these are not possible if prāṇa were merely the functioning of the sense organs.
Therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa) is distinct from both air (vāyu) and its functional activity (kriyā).
How then is this scriptural statement to be understood: "That which is prāṇa is air"?

It is said in reply: This very air, having entered the microcosm (adhyātma), assuming a fivefold arrangement and abiding in a specialized form, is called by the name prāṇa; it is neither a separate ontological principle (tattvāntara) nor is it merely air.
Therefore, both the scriptural passages concerning difference and non-difference are not contradictory. // 9 //
This might be so: in that case, the vital breath (prāṇa) would also attain independence within this body, just like the individual soul (jīva),
because of its preeminence and because the organs such as speech and the rest have entered into a state of subordination toward it.

For thus, the manifold majesty of the vital breath (prāṇa) is heard in scripture: "While speech and the other organs sleep, the vital breath alone remains awake; the vital breath alone is not overtaken by death; the vital breath is the absorber (saṃvarga), for it absorbs speech and the others; the vital breath protects the other organs as a mother protects her sons."
Therefore, it would follow that the vital breath (prāṇa), like the individual soul (jīva), possesses independence; he refutes this [objection] as follows:
"But [the vital breath is subordinate], like the eye and other organs, because of its being taught together with them, and so forth. (BBs 2.4.10)
The word "but" (tu) excludes the independence of the vital breath (prāṇa) from the individual soul (jīva).
Just as the eyes and other senses are instruments for the agentship and enjoyership of the soul— like the ministers of a king— and are not independent,
so too the primary vital breath, like a royal minister, is an instrument for the soul by performing all its purposes and is not independent.
Why?
Because of its being taught together with them and other reasons;
for in the dialogues concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and elsewhere, the vital breath is taught precisely along with those [organs] such as the eye.
Furthermore, it is logical that those things possessing common characteristics should be taught together, as in the case of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he indicates the reasons for refuting the independence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), such as its being composite and its being insentient. // 10 //
This might be so:
if the vital breath were accepted as being an instrument for the living self, as the eye and other organs are,
it would follow that it must have another object, just like form and the other sense-objects.

Through their respective functions, such as the perception of form and so forth, the eyes and other organs serve as instruments for the individual soul (jīva). Furthermore, only eleven classes of effects—namely, the perception of form and so forth—are enumerated for the sake of which the eleven vital breaths (prāṇas) are comprised; no twelfth class of effect is found for the sake of which this twelfth vital breath might be postulated.
To this, he recites the following: "And because it is non-productive, there is no fault; for thus [the scripture] shows" (BBs 2.4.11).
First of all, the fault of the consequence of [the mind] engaging with other objects does not apply.
Because the prāṇa is not an instrument;
for the status of being an instrument is not attributed to the prāṇa through the delimitation of objects, as is the case with the eyes and other senses.
Yet, it does not follow from this that it lacks any function whatsoever.
Why?

Because scripture, in such passages as the Dialogue of the Vital Breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), demonstrates a distinctive function of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) that is impossible for the other breaths; beginning with "Then indeed the vital breaths disputed among themselves as to who was the best," it continues, "When you depart... [and so on].

Having introduced the passage, "The body appears as if most wretched; yet he is the best among you" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.1.6–7), [the text] demonstrates that when each of the faculties beginning with speech departs, life continues just as before, though deprived of their respective functions; and it further shows that when the vital breath (prāṇa) desires to depart, there occurs a loosening of speech and the other organs, leading to the consequence of the body's collapse.
The Śruti shows that the maintenance of the body and the senses is caused by the vital breath (prāṇa).
"Then the most excellent Prāṇa said: 'Do not fall into delusion; it is I who, having divided myself fivefold, support and sustain this body.
And the Śruti expresses this very same meaning: 'Protecting the lower nest by means of the prāṇa... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).
And by the passage, "4.3.12)," it shows that when the eyes and other senses are asleep, the protection of the body is caused by the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Furthermore, by the passages, "From whichever limb the *prāṇa* departs, at that very moment it withers" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.19),
and "By what one eats and by what one drinks, one sustains the other *prāṇas*," it shows that the nourishment of the body and the sense organs is caused by the *prāṇa*.
"Upon whose departure shall I depart, and upon whose staying shall I stay?
and "He created the vital breath (prāṇa)"—these [passages] show that the departure and staying of the individual soul (jīva) are caused by the vital breath. // 11 // [FN:
*Ahaṃśreyasi* means for the sake of one's own superiority.]
They contended; they engaged in dispute.
"Another" refers to the lowly nest, the house known as the body.
It is designated as having five functions, like the mind.
For this reason also, the principal prāṇa has a specific function of its own:
because it is designated in the Śrutis as having five functions—“prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
This differentiation of functions depends upon the difference in their effects:
*prāṇa* has an upward function consisting of the action of exhalation and so forth; *apāna* has a downward function consisting of the action of inhalation and so forth.
Vyāna, abiding at the junction of those two, is the cause of vigorous actions.
Udāna has an upward movement and is the cause of departure from the body and so forth.
Samāna is that which carries the essence of food equally throughout all the limbs.
Thus, the prāṇa has five functions, like the mind;
the meaning is that just as the mind has five functions, so too does the prāṇa.
It is well known that the five functions of the mind have sound and other objects as their domains, with the ear and other senses as their instruments.
But [if you argue that] desire, volition, and so forth, as recited in the scripture, should be included [among the modifications], then the number five would be exceeded.

Now, even here, there exists another modification of the mind—such as that directed toward past or future objects—which is independent of the ear and other senses; thus, the excess over the number five remains the same.

In that case, according to the maxim that "what is not prohibited by another is accepted," the five well-known fluctuations of the mind from the Yogaśāstra— namely, "valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory" (Pātañjala Yogasūtra 1.6)— are also adopted here.
Or rather, it should be understood that the mind serves as an illustration for the vital breath (prāṇa) merely by virtue of having many functions.

Furthermore, the fact that the vital breath is an instrument of the individual soul (jīva) should be applied [to the argument] on the grounds that it possesses five functions, just like the mind. // 12 // [FN:
Pramāṇa is valid cognition.]
Error is delusion; conceptual construction is that which follows upon verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object; and sleep is a modification of the mind characterized by tamas.
6. The Section on the Excellence of Atomicity. Sūtra 13:
"And atomic.
(BBs 2.4.13) This principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) is to be understood as atomic, just like the other vital breaths.
And here too, "atomicity" (aṇutva) refers to subtlety and limited dimension, not to equality with an atom;
for the vital breath pervades the entire body through its five functions. It is subtle because, at the time of departure, it is not perceived by someone standing nearby.
Furthermore, [the individual soul] is limited because of the scriptural texts concerning its departure, going, and returning.

But is not the all-pervasiveness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) also recorded in such passages as: "He is equal to a gnat, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, equal to this whole universe" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.22)?

This is explained as follows: This omnipresence is taught with reference to the cosmic (ādhidaivika) Prāṇa alone—both in its collective (samaṣṭi) and individual (vyaṣṭi) forms belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha—and not with reference to the internal (ādhyātmika) Prāṇa.

Furthermore, by the statement of equality beginning with "equal to a gnat" (pluṣi), it is shown that the Prāṇa residing in each individual living being is indeed limited; therefore, there is no fault. [Note:
*Pluṣi* is a creature smaller even than a mosquito; *nāga* means an elephant.]
7. Section on Light and the Others (Jyotirādy-adhikaraṇa). Sūtras 14–16.
But light and the others are the presiding deities, because of the scriptural teaching regarding them.
(BBs 2.4.14) Furthermore, do these aforementioned vital breaths (prāṇas) operate for their respective functions by their own power alone, or are they presided over by deities?

It is now examined whether [the vital breaths] function [independently]: in this regard, it is first established that the vital breaths would proceed by their own power alone, through the possession of the capacity for their own respective functions.

Furthermore, if it were admitted that the vital breaths proceed under the superintendence of deities, it would follow that those presiding deities themselves would be the enjoyers, and thus the body’s status as the enjoyer would be lost.
Therefore, it follows that their activity proceeds by their own inherent power alone.
To this, the following is stated: "But the presiding over light and so forth. By the word "but" (tu), the prima facie view is set aside.

He asserts that the collection of instruments, such as speech and the rest, presided over by deities who identify with fire and so forth—namely light and the rest—proceeds toward their respective functions.
He explains the reason for this with the words: "Because of the scriptural teaching regarding them" (*tadāmananāt*).
For thus they teach: "Fire, having become speech, entered the mouth" (*Aitareya Upaniṣad* 2.4), and so forth.
This statement—that fire becomes speech and enters the mouth—is made by accepting that the deity as the presiding self exercises control over them;
for apart from such a connection with a deity, no specific relationship is observed between fire and either speech or the mouth.
Likewise: "Vāyu, having become breath, entered the nostrils" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 2.4).
This and other such passages are also to be applied accordingly.

Likewise, elsewhere as well—in the passage, "Speech alone is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and glows with fire as its light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.3)—the text confirms this very point by stating that speech and the other organs have fire and the others as their lights.

Furthermore, by stating that speech and the other organs attain the state of fire and the other deities—through such passages as, "He indeed carried speech across first; when it was released from death, it became fire" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.12)—the text illuminates this very point.

Moreover, throughout the text, the sequential enumeration of speech and the others with fire and the others occurs through this same immediate proximity, distinguished by the internal (ādhyātmika) and celestial (ādhidaivika) divisions.

In the *Samhitā* as well, it is shown in detail that speech and the other faculties are presided over by deities such as Agni, through such passages as: "The Brahmins who perceive reality say that speech is the adhyātma;
that which is to be spoken is the adhibhūta, while fire is the adhidaiva therein. And so forth.
As for the claim that the vital breaths (prāṇas) would proceed by their own power alone, through the possession of the capacity for their own functions— that is incorrect;
for we observe that even capable things such as carts proceed only when presided over by oxen and the like.
And since both [explanations] are possible, it is determined from scripture that it is indeed due to being presided over by a deity;
[the word *bhāti* means] it shines, it blazes;
[the word *tapati* means] it performs its own function.

That Prāṇa, having carried speech—the first among the functions of the Udgītha—beyond death in the form of evil such as falsehood, making it free from death and leading it to the state of having Agni as its presiding deity, [accomplished this].
As for the objection raised—that the status of being the enjoyer would logically belong only to the presiding deities and not to the embodied soul (śārīra)—that is refuted by the sūtra:
"By the one possessed of Prāṇa, because of the scriptural statement" (BBs 2.4.15).

Even though there are deities presiding over the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), it is understood from scripture that the connection of these *prāṇas* is with the embodied self (*śārīra*) alone—the possessor of the *prāṇas* and the master of the aggregate of causes and effects.

For thus says the scripture: "Now, where this eye is directed toward space, that is the person in the eye for the purpose of seeing; and he who knows, 'Let me smell this,' he is the Self (*ātman*), and the nose is for the purpose of smelling" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.4).

Thus, this kind of passage declares the connection of the vital breaths with the embodied self alone. Furthermore, because there are many presiding deities for each sense organ, their status as the enjoyer within this body is not tenable;
for it is understood that there is only one embodied self as the enjoyer in this body, since the possibility of recognition and so forth exists only for him. (Sūtra 15)

FN: Now, immediately after entering the body, that Self who identifies with the eye—that is, the visual one—is located in the eyeball where this cavity has entered; his eye is for the purpose of seeing forms. And because he is eternal, [the eye is his instrument]. (BBs 2.4.16)

And because that embodied self, as the enjoyer within this body, is eternal, it is possible for it to be smeared by merit and demerit, and thus possible for it to experience pleasure and pain; this is not the case for the deities.
For they, abiding in a state of supreme sovereignty, are not fit to obtain the status of an enjoyer in this inferior body.
And there is a scriptural text: "Merit alone goes to him; indeed, evil does not go to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
Thus, the connection of the vital breaths with the body is indeed constant, because their persistence is observed during departure and other such states;

for so it is stated in scriptural passages such as: "When he departs, the vital breath departs after him; when the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).
Therefore, even though there are deities who govern the organs, the status of the embodied self as the enjoyer does not depart;
for the deities belong only to the side of the instruments, not to the side of the enjoyer. // 16 //
8. The Section on the Organs (Indriyādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 17–19.
Those are the organs, because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one.
One is the chief, and the others are the eleven vital breaths enumerated.
In this regard, another point is doubted:
are the other vital breaths (prāṇas) merely different functions of the principal prāṇa itself, or are they distinct principles? What, then, is the initial position?
"The others are merely different modes of activity of the principal [prāṇa] alone.
Why? "Because of scripture.

For scripture, having brought together the principal prāṇa and the other prāṇas, declares that the others have the principal as their self: "Come, let us all assume his very form; they all assumed his very form."
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21). Furthermore, because the word *prāṇa* is used as a single term, there is a determination of oneness;
otherwise, the objectionable consequence would follow that the word *prāṇa* has multiple referents.
Otherwise, either one [of the two] would have to be taken in its primary sense and the other in a figurative sense.
Therefore, just as the five functions beginning with *prāṇa* belong to the single *prāṇa*, so too the eleven beginning with speech (*vāk*) belong to the same.
This being the position reached, we reply: speech and the others are indeed distinct principles from *prāṇa*.
Why?
Because of the absence of designation.
What is this difference in designation?
Those vital breaths under discussion, excluding the "best" one, are called the eleven organs (*indriya*),
because such a designation is seen in the Śruti:
"From this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the organs" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3).
Thus, in passages of this kind, the vital breath (prāṇa) is designated separately from the sense organs (indriya).
But if this is so, would it not follow that the mind (manas), like the vital breath, should also be excluded from the category of sense organs,
since we see it designated separately in the passage, "the mind and all the sense organs"?
This is true;
however, in the Smṛti, it is stated that there are eleven sense organs (*indriya*), and thus the mind (*manas*) is also included as a sense organ along with the ear and the others.
But the status of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as a sense organ is not well-established in either Śruti or Smṛti.
Furthermore, this distinction in designation is logically consistent with the position that there is a difference in essential nature (*tattva-bheda*).

However, if there were identity of essence (*tattva-ekatva*), it would be contradictory for that same single entity, being Prāṇa, to both receive and not receive the designation "sense organ" (*indriya-vyapadeśa*).
Therefore, the others, beginning with the principal [Prāṇa], are distinct entities. (17)
FN: Having formed the resolution, "May we become the sāman," those [organs] such as speech and the rest—[the question is:
why are they subordinate to that very same principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa)?
Because of the scriptural statement of distinction:

everywhere, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is heard of as distinct from speech and the other organs. For instance, beginning with "They said to Speech" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.3.2), after presenting speech and the others as being struck down by the evil of the Asuras and concluding that section on speech and the rest, the text says, "Then they said to this breath within the mouth" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.3.7), thus referring to the primary breath which destroys the Asuras.
Because they are introduced separately;
likewise, other scriptural passages concerning distinctions, such as "He made the mind, speech, and breath for himself," should also be cited.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the others are distinct entities from the principal [breath]. 18.
And for what further reason are they distinct entities?
Because of their difference in characteristics (vailakṣaṇya). And there exists a difference in characteristics between the primary [element] and the others.

While speech and the other organs are asleep, this one alone—the principal [prāṇa]—is awake; and it alone is not overtaken by death, whereas the others are overtaken. Furthermore, it is through its staying and its departure that it is the cause of the body's maintenance and its falling, not the sense organs. And while the perception of objects is the function of the sense organs, it is not so for the prāṇa. Such is the manifold difference in characteristics between the prāṇa and the sense organs.
Therefore, their status as distinct principles is established.
As for what was stated— that on the basis of the Vedic text, "All these became his very form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21), the senses are nothing but the vital breath (prāṇa)— [that is refuted].
That is incorrect;
for even there, a distinction is perceived through an examination of the preceding and following context.
To illustrate: "I shall indeed speak," thus he resolved in his speech (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21).

Having thus enumerated the organs beginning with speech, and having stated that speech and the others were seized by death in the form of fatigue—saying, "Death, becoming fatigue, overtook them; therefore, speech indeed fatigues"—it continues: "But he did not reach this one, which is the middle vital breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21).
Thus he follows that individual vital breath which is not overcome by death;
and with the words, "This one indeed is the best among us" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21), he ascertains its preeminence.

Therefore, it should be understood that speech and the other organs obtain their movement and become of that nature (the nature of *prāṇa*) by depending on *prāṇa* without contradicting [their own specific functions], but not through identity (*tādātmya*).
For this very reason, it is established that the word *prāṇa* is used for the sense organs in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*).
And so says the Śruti: "They all became the form of this very one."
"Therefore, these are called 'prāṇas' by this [name]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21).
This passage shows that the word *prāṇa*, which primarily refers to the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), has a figurative application (*lākṣaṇikī vṛtti*) to the sense organs.
Therefore, the sense organs are distinct principles from the vital breath. // 19 //
FN: Death is the fault of attachment.
In the passage concerning the "smelling of the wind," he formed the intention of [teaching] meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
9. The Section on the Fashioning of Names and Forms (Saṃjñāmūrtikḷptyadhikaraṇam), Sūtras 20–22.
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the scriptural instruction.

In the section concerning "Being" (*sat*), after describing the creation of fire, water, and food, it is taught: "That divinity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three divinities with this living self and differentiate names and forms;
let me make each of them threefold'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this differentiation of name and form (nāmarūpavyākaraṇa) performed by the individual soul (jīva), or is it performed by the Supreme Lord?
On this point, the initial position is that this differentiation of name and form is indeed performed by the individual soul.
Why? Because of the qualification "by this living self" (anena jīvenātmanā).

Just as in the world, when one says, "I shall enter the enemy's army through a spy and count it," in such an application, the king— by means of the use of the first person in the phrase "I shall count"— superimposes upon himself the act of counting the army, which is actually performed by the spy, because he is the causal agent; in the same way, [the text] superimposes upon the divine Self the differentiation of names and forms, which is actually performed by the individual soul (jīva), because the Self is the causal agent, by means of the use of the first person in the phrase "I shall differentiate."
Furthermore, in names such as "Ḍittha" and "Ḍavittha," and in forms such as jars and bowls, it is observed that the soul alone is the agent of manifestation.
Therefore, since this manifestation of name and form has the soul as its agent, such being the position reached, [the author] states: "But [it is] the fashioning of names and forms."
By the word "tu" (but), he sets aside the [opposing] position.
"The fashioning of names and forms" means the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa-vyākriyā*).
By the phrase "making tripartite," he indicates the Supreme Lord.

Because in the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), he is designated as the faultless agent; thus, this arrangement of names and arrangement of forms— such as fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning—

as well as the various types found in each genus and each individual, such as among *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, *palāśa* trees, and so forth, as well as among cattle, wild animals, humans, and so on [are his work].
Indeed, that [creation] must be the work of the Supreme Lord alone, the creator of fire, water, and food.
Why? Because of the scriptural instruction.

For instance, beginning with "That divinity thought," and proceeding with the use of the first-person pronoun in the phrase "Let me manifest [the names and forms]," the agency of manifestation is here taught as belonging to the Supreme Brahman alone.
[Objection: Is it not the case that, because of the qualification "by means of the living self" (jīvena), the agency of the creation is determined to belong to the living self?
[Reply: This is not so;
for the term "by means of the living self" is connected with the immediately preceding term "having entered" (anupraviśya).
By the phrase "I shall not explain," [it is implied that he would have explained had he been able].

For if there were a connection [with the capacity to explain], then the use of the first person singular in the sense of "I shall explain" regarding the deity would have to be considered merely figurative.
Furthermore, a living being (jīva) who is not the Lord lacks the power to bring about the manifestation of the various names and forms found in mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth.
Even in those cases where there is capacity, that too is entirely dependent upon the Supreme Lord;
nor is the so-called individual soul (jīva) absolutely different from the Supreme Lord like a servant from a king,
because of the qualification "by the Self" (ātmanā).
Furthermore, because the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) is based solely upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
even the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) effected by that [individual soul] is in fact effected by the Supreme Lord alone.
And it is the established doctrine of all the Upaniṣads that the Supreme Lord alone is the differentiator of names and forms.
This is known from such scriptural passages as, "Space, indeed, by name, is the bringer-out of names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
Therefore, the differentiation of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Lord alone, who effects the tripartition.

It is precisely this differentiation of name and form preceded by triplication that is intended here, because the differentiation of name and form for each individual element has already been stated through the description of the production of fire, water, and food.

And Śruti demonstrates that triplication with respect to fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning: "That which is the red color there is the color of fire; that which is white is the color of water; that which is black is the color of food."
By such passages as [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1],
the form "fire" is first differentiated;
and once the differentiation of form has occurred, the name "fire" is differentiated through the acquisition of its corresponding object.
The same should be understood regarding the sun, the moon, and lightning as well.
By this illustration of fire and the others, it is stated that the threefold compounding (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) applies without distinction to all three substances— earth, water, and fire—
because the opening and the conclusion are common to all.

For thus the introduction is made without distinction: "These three deities, each one becomes tripartite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.4). And likewise the conclusion is made without distinction, beginning with: "That which appeared as if red was the form of fire," and ending with: "That which appeared as if unknown was the combination of these very deities" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.6–7). // 20 //
Note: *Prakriyā* means the process.
The Śruti statement, "I shall make each one of these three deities threefold by means of fire, water, and food," is intended to indicate the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
After those three deities have been made threefold externally, another internal threefold-making is described: "These three deities, having reached the person, each become threefold."
"it becomes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.7).

Now, the Teacher, intending to remove a certain suspected defect, demonstrates this exactly according to the scriptural text: "Flesh and so forth [arise] from the earth; and for the other two, according to the words [of the scripture]. (Brahmasūtra 2.4.21)
From the threefold-constituted earth, when consumed by a person, the effects such as flesh and so forth are produced according to the scriptural texts.

For thus says the Śruti: "Food, once eaten, is divided into three parts: its coarsest constituent becomes feces, its middle constituent becomes flesh, and its finest constituent becomes the mind" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.1).
The intention is that this very earth, made tripartite, is consumed in the form of food such as rice and barley.
Of that [earth], its grossest form goes outwards in the state of excrement;
its middling form nourishes the flesh within the body.
The mind, however, is the subtlest.
In this manner, the effects of the other two—water and fire—should be understood according to the scriptural statements.
Thus, urine, blood, and the vital breath (prāṇa) are the effects of water.
"Bone and marrow are your brilliance," he says. // 21 //

Here [the opponent] says: If all elements and elemental products are indeed made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*) without distinction, based on the scriptural statement, "He made each of those three into a tripartite one," then what is the basis for this specific designation: "this is fire, these are waters, this is food"?
Likewise, regarding the internal self (*adhyātma*), there is this effect of food when eaten, such as flesh and so forth.
"This is the effect of the water that has been drunk, such as blood and so forth;
this is the effect of the fire that has been consumed, such as bone and so forth.
To this, it is replied:
"But on account of its preponderance, it is designated by that; it is designated by that. With the word "but" (tu), he removes the objection raised.
The state of being a distinction is "preponderance" (vaiśeṣya).
"Furthermore, you [should know]" means this much.

Even though there is a threefold combination (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), an abundance of a particular elemental constituent is perceived in some cases: "in fire, an abundance of *tejas*; in water, an abundance of *ap*; in earth, an abundance of food (*anna*).
And this threefold combination is for the sake of establishing common usage (*vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, if there were a merging into oneness like that of a three-stranded rope, worldly empirical usage regarding the three elements would not be established as distinct.

Therefore, even though the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) exists, the discourse concerning the specificities of fire, water, and food is justified with respect to the elements and their derivatives precisely because of their predominance (vaiśeṣya).
The repetition of the phrase "that discourse, that discourse" indicates the completion of the chapter. 22.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the worshipful Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Non-contradiction," in the venerable Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras.
